Court of Appeal for Ontario

R. v. Finta

Date: 19920429

DUBIN
C.J.O. (dissenting):—
,Introduction

I have had the advantage of reading the
carefully detailed reasons for judgment of my colleagues, who have set forth
the many issues which arise on this appeal.

As has been pointed out by them, this appeal
concerns the first prosecution conducted under the legislative scheme
established by Parliament as of September 17, 1987, in response to the recom­mendations
of the Report of the Commission of Inquiry on War Criminals, 1986. That
legislative scheme now appears as
s. 7(3.71)
to
(3.77)
of the
Criminal Code,

R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46.

For my purposes, the principal issue in this
appeal is the effect to be given to this legislation, principally
s. 7(3.71)
,
and how it is to be interpreted. That issue is fundamental to these proceedings
and to any subsequent proceedings of like nature.

As detailed in both the majority judgment and
that of Tarnopol.. sky J.A., the Crown preferred an indictment containing eight
counts, two counts each of forcible confinement, robbery, kidnap­ping and
manslaughter under the
Criminal Code
,
R.S.C. 1927, c. 36, as amended,
four of which counts were said to constitute crimes against humanity and the
other four to constitute war crimes.

Since the acts or omissions alleged against the
respondent were committed in Hungary, in instituting these proceedings the
Crown relied on
s. 7(3.71)
of the
Criminal Code

and contended that,
pursuant to that provision, the acts or omissions alleged against the respondent
were deemed to have been committed in Canada, making the 1927
Criminal Code
provisions
applicable. The rele­vant provisions of
s. 7
read as follows:

7(3.71) Notwithstanding anything in this
Act or any other Act, every person who, either before or after the coming into
force of this subsection, commits an act or omission outside Canada that
constitutes a war crime or a crime against humanity and that, if committed in
Canada, would constitute an offence against the laws of Canada in force at the
time of the act or omission
shall be deemed to
commit that act or omission
in Canada at that time
if,

(a) at the time of the act or omission,

(i) that person is a Canadian citizen or is
employed by Canada in a civilian or military capacity,

(ii) that person is a citizen of, or is
employed in a civilian or military capacity by, a state that is engaged in an
armed conflict against Canada, or

(iii) the victim of the act or omission is
a Canadian citizen or a citizen of a state that is allied with Canada in an
armed conflict; or

(b)
at the
time of the act or omission, Canada could, in conformity with international
law, exercise jurisdiction over the person with respect to the act or omission
on the basis of the person's presence in Canada and, subsequent to the time of
the act or omission, the person is present in Canada.

(3.76) For the purposes of this section,
"conventional international law" means

(a) any convention, treaty or other
international agreement that is in force and to which Canada is party, or

(b) any convention, treaty or other
international agreement that is in force and the provisions of which Canada has
agreed to accept and apply in an armed conflict in which it is involved;

"crime against humanity" means
murder, extermination, enslavement, deportation, persecution or any other
inhumane act or omission that is committed against any civilian population or
any identifiable group of persons, whether or not it constitutes a
contravention of the law in force at the time and in the place of its
commission, and that, at that time and in that place, constitutes a
contravention of customary international law or conventional international law
or is criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the
community of nations;

"war crime" means an act or
omission that is committed during an international armed conflict, whether or
not it constitutes a contraven­tion of the law in force at the time and in the
place of its commission, and that, at that time and in that place, constitutes
a contravention of the customary international law or conventional
international law applicable in international armed conflicts.

(Emphasis added.)

It is with respect to the effect to be given to
these provisions and how they are to be interpreted that I differ from the majority
of the court and the learned trial judge.

In my respectful opinion, both the trial judge
and the majority of my colleagues have misconstrued the purpose, meaning and
effect of
s. 7(3.71)
of the
Criminal Code
,
the respective functions of
the trial judge and jury pursuant to that provision, and the criminal offences
upon which the respondent stood trial.

On this issue, I agree with the conclusion
arrived at by Mr. Justice Tarnopolsky, but since I approach the issue in a
somewhat different manner, I propose to set forth briefly my reasons for coming
to that conclusion.

The ruling of the trial judge

To illustrate how
s. 7(3.71)
was interpreted and
applied by the learned trial judge, I need only refer to counts 1 and 2 of the
indictment since the other counts were dealt with in the same manner and the
same issues arise with respect to all counts. Counts 1 and 2 read as follows:

1 THAT HE, the said IMRE FINTA, between the 16th day of May, 1944, and the 30th day of June, 1944,
at or about Szeged, Hungary, unlawfully did forcibly seize or confine or
imprison approximately 8,617 Jews, thereby committing an offence contrary to

section 297
(b) of the
Criminal Code
,
1927, c. 36,

as amended, said offence constituting a
crime against R.S.C.

humanity pursuant to subsection 6(1.91) of
the
Criminal Code,
R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, as amended by S.C. 1987, c. 37,
ss. 1-2 [now
s. 7(3.71)
].

The further particulars of count 1 are as
follows:

(i) The offence alleged occurred at or
about the brick factory in Szeged, Hungary.

(ii) The act or acts committed constituted
enslavement or deportation or persecution or other inhumane act.

(iii) The act or acts committed constituted
a contravention of customary international law or conventional international
law or were criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by
the community of nations.

(iv) The act or acts committed were against
a civilian population or an identifiable group of persons.

2. AND FURTHER THAT
HE, the said IMRE FINTA, between the 16th day of May, 1944, and the 30th day of June, 1944,
at or about Szeged, Hungary, unlawfully did forcibly seize or confine or
imprison approximately 8,617 Jews, thereby committing an offence contrary to

section 297
(b) of the
Criminal Code
,
R.S.C. 1927, c. 36, as amended,
said offence constituting a war crime pursuant to subsection 6(1.91) of the
Criminal
Code,
R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, as amended by S.C. 1987, c. 37, ss. 1-2 (now
s.
7(3.71)
].

The further particulars of count 2 are as
follows:

(i) The offence alleged occurred at or about
the brick factory in Szeged, Hungary.

(ii) The act or acts committed constituted
a contravention of customary international law or conventional international
law applicable in international armed conflicts.

Prior to the taking of evidence, the learned trial
judge deter­mined that there was a jurisdictional issue in this case. He
concluded that it was a condition precedent to the court having jurisdiction to
try the respondent for the alleged breaches of the 1927
Criminal Code

offences
that the Crown prove that the respondent had committed war crimes or crimes
against humanity. In that regard, the trial judge stated:

This court only has jurisdiction over the
offence if the accused actually in fact committed the act or omission said to
be a war crime or a crime against humanity. It is not the allegation of a war
crime or crime against humanity that gives the court jurisdiction to try the
allegation. It is only the actual commission of an act or omission that
constitutes a war crime or crime against humanity. Jurisdiction to determine
guilt depends on guilt.

and further:

The court has no jurisdiction to determine
whether the accused committed a crime under the 1927
Criminal Code

unless
he committed in fact an act or omission that constitutes a war crime or a crime
against humanity ...

In my view, the effect of the trial judge's
rulings was to elevate the references to war crimes and crimes against humanity
in
s. 7(3.71)
of the
Criminal Code

to the status of two new offences
under the
Criminal Code.
This is further reflected by the additional
following conclusion of the trial judge:

Jurisdiction to try him thus depends on his
guilt or innocence of war crimes and crimes against humanity ..

The condition precedent to jurisdiction is
the actual commission of the acts or omissions with which the accused is
charged.

In his ruling, he concluded that it was for the
jury to decide beyond a reasonable doubt whether the respondent had committed
war crimes or crimes against humanity. The trial judge stated, in part, as
follows:

Where jurisdiction is conferred on the
basis of a finding that the accused committed a crime, and where that finding
deprives the accused of legal protection in the nature of special pleas,
constitutional rights and very important substantive defences, I am reluctant
to take away from the jury those crucial findings of fact.

Whether or not the accused committed
inhumane acts or was guilty of enslavement, deportation, persecution or the
like, are utterly crucial facts in this case. These are findings of fact that
relate to his very guilt or innocence, not to some technical question as to the
territorial jurisdiction of this court as opposed to some other court.

To sum up, I will deal with all the
questions of law and the jury will deal with all the questions of fact.

I will determine the legal meaning of the
words in the definitions of war crime and crime against humanity. I will decide
at the appropriate stage of the trial upon the appropriate motion whether there
is any evidence upon which the jury can properly decide that the accused
committed the acts or omissions which fall within those definitions as I
interpret those definitions.

If I decide that there is some evidence
upon which the jury can properly conclude that the accused committed war crimes
or crimes against humanity, then the jury will decide whether they are
satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused committed the acts or
omissions which constitute war crimes and crimes against humanity as I define
those terms to the jury.

The trial judge's charge to the jury

Given the trial judge's ruling on this issue, in
instructing the jury as to the essential elements of each count in the
indictment which the Crown was required to prove beyond a reasonable doubt, he
instructed them as to the essential elements of each domestic offence and of
what he perceived to be the essential elements of the "offences" of
crimes against humanity and war crimes.

For example, the trial
judge instructed the jury that the essential elements that the Crown had to prove
for Count 1 of the indictment, were as follows:

A. ESSENTIAL ELEMENTS OF COUNT 1:
CONFINEMENT; CRIME V. HUMANITY Has the Crown proven beyond a reasonable doubt
that the accused personally as a principal or as an aider or abetter

(1) Forcibly seized or confined or
imprisoned approximately 8,617 Jews in the Szeged Brickyard and

(2) No reasonable person in the position of
the accused would honestly believe that he had lawful authority
or

Any reasonable person in the position of
the accused would know that the confinement had the factual quality of a crime
against humanity (see 3) below: and

(3) The accused knew that the confinement
had the factual quality of a crime against humanity in the sense that it was

(1) enslavement
or

(2) inhumane or persecutorial deportation
or

(3) racial or religious persecution
or

(4) an inhumane act and

(4) The accused knew that the people
confined were a civilian popula­tion or any identifiable group of persons
and

(5) The accused knew the confinement was in
execution of or in connection
with the conduct of war or any war crime.

The majority judgment

The majority of this court uphold the conclusion
of the trial judge that it was for the jury to decide whether the respondent
actually committed war crimes or crimes against humanity although they arrive
at that conclusion through a different inter­pretation of s. 7(3.71). It is the
view of the majority of this court that in order to obtain a conviction for the
substantive
Criminal Code

offence, it was necessary for the Crown to prove
to a jury beyond a reasonable doubt that the respondent actually committed war
crimes or crimes against humanity. Having in mind the wording of
s. 7(3.71)
of
the
Criminal Code,
it was also necessary for the Crown to prove that had
the alts occurred in Canada, such acts would have amounted to an offence
against the laws of Canada in force at the time of the acts.

Using the allegation of robbery as an example,
the majority expressed the onus on the Crown as follows
[post,
pp.
168-9]:

Where the Crown alleges
robbery
contrary

to
s. 7(3.71)
,
instead of proving that the robbery occurred in Canada,
the Crown must prove that:

— had the act occurred in Canada, it would
have amounted to robbery under the then operative
Criminal Code
,
and

— the act amounted to a war crime or a
crime against humanity.

(Emphasis added.) And further on, the majority
states
[post,
pp. 171-2]:

… in establishing an
offence under s.
7(3.71),
it is necessary not only that the act would have amounted to a
crime in Canada but also that it constituted a war crime or a crime against
humanity ...
Both elements taken together make up the criminal conduct
prohibited by
s. 7(3.71)
.

The language of s. 7(3.71) leaves no doubt
as to its purpose. It was designed to give offences created by the
Criminal
Code

extraterritorial scope provided that the relevant act or omission
would have constituted an offence against the
Criminal Code
when it was
committed had it occurred in Canada, and provided that the relevant act or
omission constituted a war crime or a crime against humanity.
Section
7(3.71)
defines the conduct which by virtue of that section constitutes
a
breach
of the criminal law of Canada. All of the requirements of that section are
essential elements of the offence.
As in any criminal trial by jury, it is
for the jury to determine on all of the evidence whether the Crown has
established each essential element beyond a reasonable doubt. Consequently, it
was for the jury to determine whether the acts or omissions which they held to
be attributable to Finta constituted a war crime or a crime against humanity.

We do not regard the allegations that
Finta's acts or omissions constituted war crimes or crimes against humanity as
going to the jurisdiction of the trial court so as to bring them within the
purview of the judgment in
Balcombe.
Instead,
we view these issues as
integral to the fundamental question of whether Finta committed the offences
which were alleged against him in the indictment.
We see no basis in the language of
s. 7(3.71)
for
distinguishing between issues relating to whether the acts or omissions
constituted war crimes or crimes against humanity and issues relating to
whether the acts or omissions would have constituted an offence against the
laws of Canada, extant at the time the acts were committed.
The two issues
together combine to define the culpable conduct criminalized by the section.

(Emphasis added.)

In my opinion, the upshot of the majority view
is that
s. 7(3.71)
of the
Criminal Code

creates two new offences,
namely, a crime against humanity and a war crime, both of extraterritorial
scope extending the reach of Canadian criminal law throughout the world, and
that therefore, in addition to the question of whether the domestic offence had
been made out, it was also for the jury to determine whether, while in Hungary,
the respondent had commit­ted the offences of crimes against humanity and/or
war crimes. In essence, therefore, the respondent was being tried, not on the
basis that the acts or omissions alleged against him were deemed to have been
committed in Canada and thus subject to Canadian criminal law, but for being a
war criminal while in Hungary, s. 7(3.71) being

the statutory mechanism which renders the
respondent's alleged conduct as a war criminal outside Canada culpable.

With respect to the majority and the learned
trial judge, I am of the view that in this manner they have misconstrued the
purpose, effect and application of s. 7(3.71). In my opinion, that subsection
does not create two new offences, namely, a crime against human­ity and a war
crime, nor does it define the essential elements of the offences with which the
respondent was charged. The subsection did not authorize someone to be put on
trial in Canada for being a war criminal, nor did it require the Crown to prove
that he was. Section 7(3.71) provides a mechanism for persons to be convicted
for violating the
Criminal Code
of Canada for acts or omissions
committed abroad if those acts or omissions are deemed to have been committed
in Canada and thus subject to the
Criminal Code
of Canada. Forcible
confinement, robbery, kidnapping and man­slaughter, contrary to the provisions
of the 1927
Criminal Code,
were the only offences for which the
respondent stood trial.

Analysis

Interpretation of s. 7(3.71)

It is axiomatic that, absent specific
legislation, acts or omissions committed outside Canada are not culpable in
Canada. This principle is codified in
s. 6(2)
of the
Criminal Code
,
which
reads:

6(2) Subject to this Act or any other Act
of Parliament, no person shall be convicted or discharged under section 736 of
an offence committed outside Canada.

Accordingly, only acts or omissions committed in
Canada, or deemed to be committed in Canada, are culpable in Canada. This
proposition has nothing to do with jurisdiction over the person, nor with the
territorial jurisdiction of a court. The question in this case is one of
culpability in Canada for conduct outside Canada.

One method of rendering conduct outside Canada
culpable in Canada is by legislation which specifically makes the commission of
the prohibited conduct outside Canada an offence against the
Criminal Code
of
Canada. The piracy provision of the
Criminal Code
is an example of such
an approach.
Section 74
reads as follows:

74(1) Every one commits piracy who does any
act that, by the law of nations, is piracy.

(2)
Every one who commits piracy while
in or out of Canada is guilty of
an
indictable offence and liable to
imprisonment for life.

(Emphasis added.) Section 75 is a further
example of such legislation and reads as follows:

75. ,Every one who, while in or out of
Canada,

(a) steals a Canadian ship,

(b) steals or without lawful authority
throws overboard, damages or destroys anything that is part of the cargo,
supplies or fittings in a Canadian ship, or

(c) does or attempts to do a mutinous act
on a Canadian ship, or

(d) counsels a person to do anything
mentioned hi paragraph (a), (b) or (c),

is guilty of an indictable offence and
liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen years.

(Emphasis added.) It is to be noted that in such
provisions, if the act or omission complained of takes place outside Canada, it
is immaterial whether such conduct would constitute an offence at the place
where the act or omission was committed.

Section 3(1)
of the
Geneva Conventions Act,
R.S.C.
1985, c. G-3, although worded differently, is a further example of legislation
which specifically makes conduct outside Canada an offence con­trary to the
Criminal
Code
.
It reads as follows:

3(1) Any grave breach of any of the
Geneva
Conventions
of 1949, as defined therein, that would, if committed in
Canada, be an offence under any provision of the
Criminal Code

or other
Act of the Parliament of Canada,
is
an
offence under that provision
of the Criminal Code or other Act if committed outside Canada.

(Emphasis added.)

In my opinion, the interpretation of s. 7(3.71)
by the majority makes s. 7(3.71) read as if Parliament, as it did in the case
of piracy, made it an offence contrary to the
Criminal Code
of Canada
for anyone while in or out of Canada to commit a crime against humanity or a
war crime. In my view that is not the effect of s. 7(3.71).

Another method of rendering conduct outside
Canada culpable in Canada is by legislation which, instead of making the commis­sion
of the conduct outside Canada an offence in Canada, applies a dual criminality
test to the conduct which, if met, deems the conduct committed outside Canada
to have been committed in Canada and thereby makes that conduct culpable in
Canada. The case proceeds as if the conduct actually took place in Canada and
is subject to those provisions of the
Criminal Code

in force at the time
that the conduct was committed. In my view, it is this approach which s.
7(3.71) adopts.

An example of this dual criminality approach is
to be found in s. 465(3) (previously s. 423(3)) of the
Criminal Code
.
Section
465
in its entirety reads:

465(1) Except where otherwise expressly
provided by law, the following provisions apply in respect of conspiracy:

(a) every one who conspires with any one to
commit murder or to cause another person to be murdered, whether in Canada or
not, is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a maximum term of
imprison­ment for life;

(b) every one who conspires with any one to
prosecute a person for an alleged offence, knowing that he did not commit that
offence, is guilty of an indictable offence and liable

(i) to imprisonment for a term not
exceeding ten years, if the alleged offence is one for which, on conviction,
that person would be liable to be sentenced to death or to imprisonment for
life or for a term not exceeding fourteen years, or

(ii) to imprisonment for a term not
exceeding five years, if the alleged offence is one for which, on conviction,
that person would be liable to imprisonment for less than fourteen years; and

(c) every one who conspires with any one to
commit an indictable offence not provided for in paragraph (a) or
(b)
is
guilty of an indictable offence and liable to the same punishment as that to
which an accused who is guilty of that offence would, on conviction, be liable;
and

(d) every one who conspires with any one to
commit an offence punishable on summary conviction is guilty of an offence
punishable on summary conviction.

(3) Every one who, while in Canada,
conspires with any one to do anything referred to in subsection (1)
in a
place outside Canada that is an offence under the laws of that place shall be
deemed to have conspired to do that thing in Canada.

(Emphasis added.)

As noted in the judgments of my colleagues, that
section was considered in the case of
Bolduc
v.
Quebec
(Attorney-General)
(1982),
1982 CanLII 224 (SCC)
, 68 C.C.C. (2d) 413, 137 D.L.R. (3d) 674, [1982]
1 S.C.R. 573. With reference to s. 465(3), then s. 423(3), Chouinard J. stated
at p. 417 C.C.C., p. 678 D.L.R.:

It is apparent on its face that this subsection
does not create an offence.
It creates a
presumption of territoriality so as to make the conspiracy an offence
punishable in Canada. Where, as in the case at bar, persons conspire in Canada
to effect an unlawful purpose in the United States, which would not in itself
be an offence punishable in Canada,
they "shall be deemed to have
conspired to do in Canada that thing". The result is to introduce the
essential aspect which would otherwise be absent, and to make the offence
punishable in Canada.

(emphasis added) and at p. 419 C.C.C., p. 680
D.L.R.:

In my opinion, respondent's interpretation
represents precisely what was intended by the presumption of s. 423(3) [now s.
465(3)]. The persons are deemed to have conspired to commit the offences in
Canada.
When applied to the circumstances here, this means that persons who
have conspired to cause

others to come into the United States
unlawfully are deemed to have conspired to cause persons to come into Canada
unlawfully.

(emphasis added) and at p. 420 C.C.C., p. 681
D,L.R.:

Appellant further argued that the
information itself states the offence as "causing persons to come into the
United States of America unlawfully". To this, respondent replied that
this statement is not an essential component of the offence: it is only a
detail, a statement of fact.
The offence charged is common law conspiracy
committed in Canada, to effect
an
unlawful purpose. Causing persons to
enter the United States unlawfully constitutes an offence under American law,
just as causing persons to come into Canada unlawfully constitutes an offence
under Canadian law. As a consequence of the presumption of s. 423(3), the
conspirators are deemed to have conspired to commit the offence in Canada. It
is as if they had conspired to cause persons to come into Canada unlawfully.

(Emphasis added.)

As pointed out in
Bolduc
,
s. 465(3)
(which is analogous to s. 7(3.71)), does not create an offence. It does not
render the conduct outside Canada, namely, a breach of American law, an offence
in Canada. It is apparent from that decision that whether the acts alleged to
have been committed would constitute offences under American and Canadian law
were questions of law, not questions of fact. Furthermore, the court did not
determine whether Bolduc had in fact committed the acts alleged against him,
namely, whether he had actually conspired to transport persons into the United
States in breach of United States immigra­tion laws. Indeed, in
Bolduc

no
evidence had yet been taken.

Lastly, it was because the acts alleged would in
law constitute an offence under both American and Canadian law that the acts
alleged against Bolduc were deemed to have been committed in Canada. This
introduced "the essential aspect which would other­wise be absent and to
make the offence punishable in Canada". The result was that Bolduc would
be tried for a breach of Canadian law, and it would be for the trier of fact to
decide whether he had committed the acts alleged against him.

Section 7(4)
of the
Criminal Code

is
another example of dual criminality legislation. That section reads as follows:

7(4) Every one who, while employed as an
employee within the meaning of the Public Service Employment Act in a place
outside Canada, commits an act or omission in that place that is an offence under
the laws of that place and that, if committed in Canada, would be an offence
punishable by indictment shall be deemed to have committed that act or omission
in Canada.

(Emphasis added.)

Again, with respect, in my view
s. 7(4)
does not
create an offence, and it is not necessary, before the act or omission can be

deemed to have been committed in Canada, to
prove that the employee had in fact committed an offence in a place outside
Canada. It would be a question of law whether the acts or omissions alleged
would constitute an offence in the place where they were committed, and also
whether such acts or omissions would, if committed in Canada, constitute an
offence under the
Criminal
Code.
If both of these questions of law were
answered in the affirmative, and the acts or omissions were in fact committed,
the acts or omissions would be deemed to have been committed in Canada, thus
making the relevant provisions of the
Criminal Code
applicable.

The employee would be tried for the Canadian
offence just as if he or she had committed the acts or omissions in Canada and
subject to the provisions of the
Criminal Code

in force at the time that
the offence was alleged to have been committed. It would be for the trier of
fact to determine whether the person charged had committed the acts or
omissions alleged.

I now return to s. 7(3.71), a portion of which I
repeat:

7(3.71) Notwithstanding anything in this
Act or any other Act,
every person who,
either before or after the
coming into force of this subsection,
commits
an
act or omission
outside Canada
that constitutes a war crime or a crime against humanity and
that, if committed in Canada, would constitute an offence against the laws of
Canada in force at the time of the act or omission
shall be deemed to commit
that act or omission in Canada
at that time ….

(Emphasis added.)

In enacting s. 7(3.71), Parliament adopted the
dual criminality approach. It did not, as it did in the case of piracy, make it
an offence punishable on indictment for anyone while in or out of Canada to
commit a crime against humanity or a war crime and prescribe a penalty.
Parliament did not prescribe that a breach of s. 7(3.71) constitutes a breach
of the criminal law of Canada. As pointed out by Tarnopolsky J.A., Canada did
not adopt the approach of other countries which have enacted legislation making
war crimes a substantive offence. Yet, as I have noted earlier, that is how the
majority would have s. 7(3.71) read.

The purpose of s. 7(3.71) is to give
jurisdiction to courts in Canada to convict an accused for an offence contrary
to the
Criminal Code
of Canada where the acts or omissions which
constitute such an offence were committed outside Canada. An accused who is on
trial by virtue of the application of s. 7(3.71) is on trial for a breach of the
relevant
Criminal Code
offence, and the indictment need only cite the
relevant
Criminal Code
offence.

The exercise directed to be pursued under s.
7(3.71) is in the end to determine whether the acts or omissions alleged to
have been

committed by an accused outside Canada shall be
deemed to have been committed in Canada, thus making the relevant offences of
the
Criminal Code

applicable.

This section was examined by Callaghan
A.C.J.H.C. in
R.
v.
Finta
(1989),
1989 CanLII 4378 (ON HCJ)
, 50 C.C.C. (3d) 236, 61 D.L.R.
(4th) 85, 69 O.R. (2d) 557. I agree with him when he stated at p. 255 G.C.C.,
p. 105 D.L.R.:

I hold that the legislation in issue does
not create new offences but merely confers jurisdiction on Canadian courts with
respect to acts that would have been offences against Canadian law in force at
the time of their occurrence if such acts had occurred in Canada.

Pursuant to s. 7(3.71), it is for the trial
judge to determine first, that if the accused committed the alleged acts or
omissions outside Canada, whether such acts or omissions would, as a matter of
customary international law or conventional international law or according to
the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations,
constitute a crime against humanity or a war crime. All that the trial judge determines
is whether, as a matter of law, such acts or omissions, if committed, would
constitute a crime against humanity or a war crime within the definition set
forth in s. 7(3.76). The trial judge does not decide whether the accused in
fact had committed the acts or omissions. That issue is left for the trier of
fact. Whether an accused intended or believed that his acts or omissions
constituted a war crime or a crime against humanity is immaterial.

The trial judge must also determine, that if the
accused committed the alleged acts or omissions in Canada, rather than outside
Canada, whether such acts or omissions, as a matter of law, would constitute
the offence against the laws of Canada in force at the time of the act or
omission, with which the accused is charged. In making that determination, the
trial judge does not determine whether the accused had in fact committed that
offence, but only whether if the accused had committed the acts or omissions in
Canada, then, as a matter of law, whether such acts or omissions would be
contrary to the provisions of the
Criminal Code

with which the accused
is charged.

He would also have to determine whether either
of the condi­tions of s. 7(3.71)(a) or (b), reproduced above, had been met.

If the trial judge is satisfied that all those
conditions had been met, he would then determine whether there is sufficient
evidence to go to the jury that the accused had in fact committed the acts or
omissions alleged in the indictment. The case would go to the jury as if the acts
or omissions alleged had in fact been committed in

Canada, thus making the relevant provisions of
the
Criminal Code

in force at that time applicable.

Once the dual criminality test is met, s.
7(3.71) is spent. The jury's fact-finding function is limited to determining
whether the Crown has proven the
Criminal Code

offence beyond a
reasonable doubt. No one submits that, if the respondent had actually committed
the acts or omissions alleged against him in Toronto rather than abroad, he
could be charged with committing the offence of a crime against humanity or a
war crime.

The judge would charge the jury as to the law
which governs the domestic offences set out in the indictment as well as the
provisions of s. 7(3.72), (3.73) and (3.74). If the jury were to find the
accused guilty under those circumstances, the trial judge would record a
conviction since the acts or omissions would then be deemed to have been
committed in Canada.

The application of s. 7(3.71) to (3.76) to
this case

To illustrate the manner in which I think the
above-mentioned provisions of the
Criminal Code

should have been applied
in this case, I propose to use count 1 in the indictment as an example.

As noted earlier, count 1 states as follows:

1. THAT HE, the said IMRE FINTA, between the 16th day of May, 1944, and the 30th day of June, 1944,
at or about Szeged, Hungary unlawfully did forcibly seize or confine or
imprison approximately 8,617 Jews, thereby committing an offence contrary to

section 297
(b) of the
Criminal Code
,
R.S.C. 1927, c. 36, as amended, said offence constituting a crime
against humanity pursuant to subsection 6(1.91) of the
Criminal Code,
R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, as
amended by S.C. 1987, c. 37, ss. 1-2 [now s. 7(3.71)].

In my opinion, the only offence upon which the
respondent stood trial pursuant to count 1 in the indictment was that of
forcible confinement, contrary to s. 297(b) of the 1927
Criminal Code
.
There
is no question in my mind as to the right of the trial judge and the jury to
have tried the respondent for that offence. That jurisdiction is specifically
conferred by s. 7(5), which reads as follows:

7(5) Where a person is alleged to have
committed an act or omission that is an offence by virtue of this section,
proceedings in respect of that offence may, whether or not that person is in
Canada, be commenced in any territorial division in Canada and the accused may
be tried and punished in respect of that offence in the same manner as if the
offence had been committed in that territorial division.

However, the respondent could only be convicted
if the confinement was deemed to have been committed in Canada, thus making
s.
297
(b) applicable. In the resolution of that issue and of the guilt or
innocence of the respondent, both the judge and jury

had their own respective roles to play. To
illustrate those roles, a brief reference to the evidence must be made. Some of
that evidence relevant to count 1 is as follows.

On March 22, 1944, a pro-German government was
installed in Budapest, one that operated in all respects under the
"supervision" of German authorities.

Although the persecution of Hungarian Jews began
long before 1944, a series of decrees was rapidly adopted by the new Hungarian
government after March 19, 1944. The most significant of these was a Ministry
of the Interior order, dated April 7, 1943.

This decree mandated the concentration and
deportation to Reich territory of all Hungarian Jews and placed responsibility
for these measures on "the territorially competent police and the Royal
Hungarian Gendarmerie".

The plan consisted of six phases. First, Jews
were to be identified and isolated by requiring them to wear the yellow star.
Secondly, all Jewish property was to be expropriated. Thirdly, Jews were to be
moved to ghettos established by local civil authorities and guarded by the
gendarmerie. Fourthly, Jews were to be transferred to larger, central
concentration centres by the gendar­merie and the SS, where they again would be
guarded by gendarmerie. Remaining valuables were to be expropriated at this
stage by the investigative subdivision of the gendarmerie. Members of the
Sonderkommando were also present at the concentration centres. Fifthly, Jews
were to be transferred from the concentration centres to transport trains by
the gendarmerie, under the supervision of the local gendarme commander, who was
assisted by a member of the Sonderkommando. Finally, Jews were to be deported
to Reich territory, usually to forced labour and extermination at
Auschwitz/Birkenau, but sometimes to forced labour in Austria. At the Hungarian
border, control of the tran­sports was to be transferred from the Hungarian
Gendarmerie to the German SS.

The above plan was implemented in Szeged shortly
after the decree, and it was the events which were alleged to have occurred at
Szeged which formed the basis of the charges laid against the respondent. On
May 14, 1944, a Jewish ghetto was established by city authorities and fenced
in. After approximately two weeks in the ghetto, Jews were moved to a sports
field, where they camped for two days before being moved to an abandoned brick
factory, the Szeged concentration centre. This was accomplished by June 20,
1944. Those interned in the brickyard were instructed daily to surrender their
hidden valuables to the gendarmes guarding the camp, on pain of death.

By June 20, 1944, approximately 8,617 Jews had
been rounded up and placed in the brickyard. As is detailed in the majority
judgment, the brickyard consisted of a large open area containing a large kiln,
a chimney and several buildings used for drying bricks. It was filthy. The Jews
were crowded together and slept on the ground in drying sheds which had roofs
but no walls. They were not permitted to leave the brickyard which was
surrounded by a fence and guarded by the gendarmes.

Over the loudspeaker, announcements were
repeatedly made ordering them to surrender their remaining valuables, gold or
jewellery, on pain of death. A basket or hamper was presented to them for the
collection of valuables.

There was evidence that the respondent was a
senior gendar­merie officer at the Szeged concentration centre and had
effective control over the operation and guarding of the centre. There was
evidence that as a senior gendarmerie officer the respondent was responsible
for the forcible confinement of the Jews in the brickyard, and that all the
acts and commands given in the brickyard were issued by him or on his behalf.
There was also evidence that the respondent commanded the gendarmes when the
Jews were escorted from the ghetto to the brickyard.

At the end of the evidence, and before the case
went to the jury, there were several questions of law to be resolved by the
trial judge.

First, pursuant to s. 7(3.71) it was for the
trial judge to determine, in the manner previously described, that if the
respond­ent had committed the acts of confinement detailed in the evidence and
in the manner therein alleged, whether, as a matter of law, such acts would
constitute a crime against humanity within the definition found in s. 7(3.76).
By its very definition, the test is an objective one, and I agree with what was
said by Mr. Justice Tarnopolsky on this issue. In determining that issue, it is
quite irrelevant whether the respondent knew that those acts fell within the
legal definition of a crime against humanity or whether he believed such acts
to be inhumane.

However, in determining this legal question, the
trial judge does not decide whether the respondent had in fact committed the
acts or omissions set forth in the evidence.

In my view, the trial judge in this case would
have no difficulty in concluding, as a matter of law, that, if the respondent
had confined the victims in the manner alleged in the evidence, such conduct
would constitute a crime against humanity.

Having come to such a conclusion, the trial
judge would then determine whether, as a matter of law, such acts or omissions,
if

committed, would constitute the offence of
forcible confinement contrary to the 1927
Criminal Code
.
In this case, I
do not think that a trial judge should have had any doubt that such acts, if
committed, would constitute the offence of forcible confinement. Again, the
trial judge does not determine whether the respondent committed the alleged
acts constituting the forcible confinement as alleged, but only the question of
law.

The trial judge would then determine whether
either of the conditions of s. 7(3.71)(a) and
(b)
had been met, with
respect to which there is no issue in this case.

He would then determine whether there was
sufficient evidence to go to the jury that the respondent had in fact committed
the acts or omissions alleged in the evidence.

On this record, there was sufficient evidence
that the respondent had in fact committed the acts or omissions alleged against
him.

That being so, the case would go to the jury on
the premise that the acts or omissions were deemed to have been committed in
Canada. In other words, the case would be tried as if the charge was that the
respondent, in 1944, unlawfully did forcibly seize or confine or imprison
approximately 8,617 Jews at some place in Canada contrary to
s. 297
(b) of the
Criminal
Code
.

The trial judge would instruct the jury as to
the essential elements of that offence, and the case would proceed in the same
manner as any other charge of forcible confinement pursuant to the
Criminal
Code
of Canada, subject to the following provisions of
s. 7(3.72)
,
(3.73)

and
(3.74)
, which read:

7(3.72) Any proceedings with respect to an
act or omission referred to in subsection (3.71) shall be conducted in
accordance with the laws of evidence and procedure in force at the time of the
proceedings.

(3.73) In any proceedings under this Act
with respect to an act or omission referred to in subsection (3.71),
notwithstanding that the act or omission is an offence under the laws of Canada
in force at the time of the act or omission, the accused may, subject to
subsection 607(6), rely on any justification, excuse or defence available under
the laws of Canada or under international law at that time or at the time of
the proceedings.

(3.74) Notwithstanding subsection (3.73)
and section 15, a person may be convicted of an offence in respect of an act or
omission referred to in subsection (3.71) even if the act or omission is
committed in obedience to or in conformity with the law in force at the time
and in the place of its commission.

The trial judge would then instruct the jury,
having regard to the wording in the indictment, that, if they found the
respondent guilty of forcible confinement in the manner alleged, then, as a
matter of law, that would constitute a crime against humanity.

If the jury rendered a verdict of guilty, then
the acts or omissions having been deemed to have been committed in Canada, the
trial judge would proceed to register a conviction.

Conclusion

The proper interpretation and application of s.
7(3.71) to (3.76) to the facts of this case were critical. I agree with the
majority of the court that, if those provisions defined the essential elements
of the offences for which the respondent stood trial, then it would be for the
judge to instruct the jury as to the law and for the jury to make the findings
of fact and decide the guilt or innocence of the accused. Indeed, I do not
think that anybody could quarrel with that proposition. If the essential
elements of each count in the indictment had a domestic component and an
international compo­nent which the Crown was required to prove beyond a
reasonable doubt, then it follows that the trial judge could not try an accused
for one component of the offence and the jury for another.

But, for the reasons which were expressed above,
s. 7(3.71) does not provide that a breach of the conduct referred to in it
constitutes a breach of the substantive criminal law of Canada, nor does it
define the essential elements of any
Criminal Code

offence. The only
offences, in my opinion, upon which the respondent stood trial, were those
offences set forth in the indictment alleging breaches of the 1927
Criminal
Code
which have only a domestic component.

Although the purpose of the legislation was to
deny Canada as a safe haven for persons who come to Canada after having commit­ted
acts or omissions abroad which would constitute a war crime or a crime against
humanity, Parliament did not decree that such acts or omissions committed
abroad would be in breach of the criminal law of Canada. On the contrary,
Parliament decided that such persons could only be convicted in Canada if the
acts or omissions committed abroad were deemed to have been committed in Canada
and would be subject to the provisions of the
Criminal Code

which were
in force at the time the acts or omissions were committed. It is the deeming
provision of s. 7(3.71) which is critical and makes those provisions of the
Criminal
Code
applicable, thus subjecting persons who come to Canada to be convicted
for such offences. If it were the intention of Parliament to make it an offence
for anyone to commit a crime abroad, there would have been no need to provide
that acts or omissions committed abroad would, under certain circumstances, be
deemed to have been committed in Canada. Without such a deeming provision the
acts or omissions alleged to have been committed abroad by the respondent would
not be culpable in Canada.

The case proceeds as if, in fact, the acts or
omissions were committed in Canada. In a trial by jury it is the jury which
makes the findings of fact and determines the guilt or innocence of the accused
with respect to the offence charged. In this manner, there would be no
overlapping of jurisdiction, nor a procedural quagmire as detailed in the
majority judgment.

Since, in my opinion, the learned trial judge
misconstrued and misapplied the relevant provisions of the
Criminal Code
,
the
verdicts cannot stand.

Other issues

If I am right in the conclusions that I have
arrived at, it is apparent that the verdicts cannot stand, and a new trial
would have to be directed. But if I am in error and the proceedings heretofore
have not been misconceived, then I would nevertheless allow the appeal, set
aside the verdicts and direct a new trial for other reasons, which I propose to
deal with briefly.

The trial judge's charge to the jury

Assuming that the learned trial judge was
correct in holding that the Crown had to prove that the respondent committed
not only the domestic offences charged, but also the offence of a War crime or
a crime against humanity, in my respectful opinion, he misdirected the jury as
to the
mens rea
that the Crown had to prove.

The learned trial judge instructed them that it
was not sufficient for the Crown to prove that the respondent intended to commit
the acts alleged against him, namely, forcible confinement, robbery, kidnapping
and manslaughter, but that the Crown also had to prove that he knew that those
acts fell within the legal definition of a war crime or a crime against
humanity.

The learned trial judge instructed the jury, in
part, as follows:

So remember, in respect of each count, the
Crown has to prove against the accused personally the essential element of the
Canadian offence and the essential elements of a war crime or crime against humanity.

It
is
under this heading you will
hear the definitions of war crimes and crimes against humanity and, of course,
the burden is on the Crown to prove this international element beyond a
reasonable doubt, including the necessary knowledge on the part of the accused.

Remember always that before the accused can
be convicted, it has to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt,
whatever he did
to his knowledge rose up to the level of a war crime or rose up to the level of
a crime against humanity.

This principle of universal jurisdiction
only applies if the things the accused did, whatever you find that he did, rose
up to the level of a war crime or rose up to the level of a crime against
humanity.
Even if the Crown proved beyond
a
reasonable doubt the
accused committed confinement, robbery, kidnapping or manslaughter; you must
acquit unless the Crown also proves beyond a reasonable doubt that to the
knowledge of the accused what he did rose up to the level of a war crime or
rose up to the level of a crime against humanity.

Remember the principle of personal
responsibility cuts both ways. It cuts in favour of the accused as well. It
assists the defence because the Crown has to prove beyond a reasonable doubt
the accused personally had the necessary knowledge that makes it a war crime or
crime against humanity.
It isn't enough to prove that the accused confined
or robbed or kidnapped or killed even as
an
aider or abettor unless he
had the requisite knowledge that raises it up
in
each case to the level
of a war crime or crime against humanity, such as persecution, inhumanity or
matters of that nature. So the accused has to know the factual quality of a war
crime or crime against humanity before he can be found guilty.

(Emphasis added.)

This theme persisted throughout the learned
trial judge's charge to the jury. The learned trial judge instructed the jury
at length as to the legal definitions of a crime against humanity and a war
crime, but constantly reminded them again as follows:

Remember, of course, on each count the
Crown has to prove beyond a reasonable doubt not only that the accused
committed the Canadian offence, the Crown has to prove beyond a reasonable
doubt that the act of the accused and
the knowledge of the accused
rose
up to that extra quality factually of a crime against humanity or a war crime
and both of those things, all of those things have to be proved in each count.

(Emphasis added.)

I know of no offence, the essential element of
which is that the accused must know that his or her conduct comes within the
legal definition of the offence charged, and with respect, I think this
constitutes a fundamental misdirection. In this respect, I agree with
Tarnopolsky J.A. and with his extended reasons for arriving at that conclusion.

Furthermore, as I read the learned trial judge's
charge to the jury, in my view the meaning that any reasonable jury would draw
from the trial judge's charge is that, in determining whether the Crown had
proven a crime against humanity, the test was a subjective one, and that it was
essential for the Crown to prove, for example, that the respondent knew that
the act or omission was inhumane. In other words, unless the Crown established
that the act or omission was inhumane according to the standards of inhumanity
of the respondent, the Crown's case failed. Although the learned trial judge
frequently referred to knowledge of the

factual quality of a crime against humanity, he
would invariably return to the requirement of actual knowledge that the act was
inhumane.

Relating that proposition to count 1 in the
indictment (forcible confinement), the learned trial judge instructed the jury
as follows:

One of the ways for the Crown to prove
Count 1 is to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused personally knew
that the confinement had the factual quality of a crime against humanity in the
sense that it was an inhumane act. Now, this is just one element. Of course,
there are six or seven other things the Crown has to prove, but this is one
example of one element the Crown has to prove. So
it is
an
essential
element on that count that the Crown has to prove beyond a reasonable doubt the
accused knew that the confinement was an inhumane act.

(Emphasis added.)

With respect, assuming that it was for the jury
to determine whether the respondent had committed a crime against humanity, in
my opinion it was an error for the trial judge to instruct the jury that the
Crown had to prove beyond a reasonable doubt not only that the acts or
omissions were inhumane, but also that the respondent knew that his conduct was
inhumane. In my opinion, whether the respondent believed his conduct to be
inhumane is completely irrelevant.

In other words, if the jury determined, by
applying an objective test based upon customary international law, conventional
interna­tional law or the general principles of law recognized by the community
of nations, that confining over 8,617 victims in a filthy brickyard, short of
water and sanitary facilities was an act of inhumanity and that the respondent
was responsible for such confinement, then the respondent would be guilty of an
act of inhumanity whether he believed his conduct was inhumane or not.

The requirement of actual knowledge of
inhumanity was a subject constantly commented on by the learned trial judge.
Another example of the requirement of actual knowledge of inhumanity is found
in another portion of the charge, which reads as follows:

Has the Crown proved beyond a reasonable
doubt the accused would know, that
the accused knew that the taking
of
the wedding rings and other valuables was racial or religious persecution or
was
an inhumane act?

(Emphasis added.)

Again, in my opinion, if the jury concluded that
the taking of wedding rings and other valuables from those being forcibly
confined was indeed an inhumane act, it matters not, in my opinion, whether the
respondent knew that such an act was inhumane. Nor, in my opinion, if the
respondent, as an act of

persecution or inhumanity, confined, robbed,
kidnapped or killed, it matters not whether he believed that such conduct were
acts of persecution or of inhumanity.

A similar direction was carried forth with
respect to all counts. With respect to a war crime, the trial judge instructed
the jury, in part, as follows:

Has the Crown proved beyond a reasonable
doubt that the confinement had the factual quality of a war crime, that the
accused
knew
that the
confinement had the factual quality of a war crime in the sense that it was
during an international armed conflict and ill treatment of a civilian
population of occupied territory, unjustified deportation for any other purpose
of a civilian population of occupied territory or a violation of family honour
and rights or individual lives and private property or religious convictions
and liberty.

(Emphasis added.)

With respect to the robbery counts, he gave them
the following instructions:

Now, it is violence and threat of violence
that distinguishes theft from robbery. Theft without violence isn't rdbbery but
theft with violence, with threats of violence is robbery and the Crown has to
prove beyond a reasonable doubt that
the accused
knew
that the taking and threats had the factual
quality of a crime against humanity in the sense that it was racial or
religious persecution or an inhumane act.

(Emphasis added.)

In my respectful opinion, the misdirection to
the jury on the issue of
mens rea
is so fundamental that the verdicts of
acquittal cannot stand.

Whether the calling of the
Kemeny-Ballo-Dallos evidence by the trial judge and the closing address of
defence counsel occasioned a substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice

During the course of the Crown's case in-chief,
the defence applied in the absence of the jury to have the 1947 deposition and
minutes of testimony of Imre Dallos along with the evidence of Mrs. Kemeny and
Mrs. Ballo taken on commission in Hungary introduced into evidence as part of
the Crown's case. The defence's position was that the evidence of these three
witnesses was "crucial" on the issue whether the respondent was in a
position of command in the brickyard. The Crown opposed the application.

In his ruling, the trial judge held that the
Kemeny-Ballo-Dallos evidence was admissible, and I take no issue with him with
respect to that ruling. It was the Crown's position that upon the evidence
being ruled admissible it was for the defence to call such evidence and not the
Crown, and with the introduction of that evidence the Crown would have the
right to address the jury last. The trial judge without finding any improper or
oblique motive in the

Crown's position not to call the evidence
decided that he would do so himself and ruled that the introduction of this
evidence in that manner would not result in the defence having to address the
jury first. He did so before the defence had elected whether to call evidence.

Following the introduction of this evidence, the
defence elected not to call any witnesses, and the trial judge directed Crown
counsel to address the jury first. In this manner, the trial judge denied the
Crown the statutory right to address the jury last.

I agree with the majority of my colleagues that
the trial judge erred in proceeding as he did. There was no reason to interfere
with the Crown's decision not to call the evidence, and the trial judge's
consideration motivating him to proceed as he did was for the sole purpose of
affording a tactical advantage for the defence by denying the Crown's
entitlement to address the jury last. However, I do not agree that this error,
which I regard as fundamental, did not occasion a substantial wrong or miscarriage
of justice.

The issue of who was in command of the brickyard
was central to the Crown's case against the respondent on the counts with
respect to forcible confinement, kidnapping and robbery. Many of the Crown
witnesses testified that it was the respondent who was in command, and the
Crown had mounted a strong case to that effect. There was no doubt that the
respondent was present at the brickyard. The defence, a rather frail one, was
that it was a "look alike" who was in command.

As I read the record, the only evidence from
which it could possibly be inferred that the respondent was not in command was
to be found in the Kemeny-Ballo-Dallos evidence, which at the point in time at
which it was introduced at the trial was inadmissi­ble. I do not see how the effect
of this evidence can be discounted when it was properly described by defence
counsel as "crucial". Indeed, with respect to the evidence of Dallos,
that view was shared by the trial judge, who described that evidence, in part,
as follows:

This evidence does, however, involve a
unique perspective, and a piece of evidence that the command of the brickyard,
whatever one makes of the evidence, was in someone other than the accused. Many
witnesses have said that the accused was the commander of the brickyard, but
not one of them was in the unique position of Dallos, because Dallos, as one of
the leaders of the Jewish community, was "put in charge on the side of the
Jews", according to his material, and thus had an opportunity to observe
that is not shared by any other witness who has thus far testified.

(emphasis added) and further:

This is evidence that could leave the jury
with a reasonable doubt as to whether the accused was in command of the
brickyard .. .

Certainly on the confinement counts the
evidence of Dallos does tie in with the evidence of Fonyo, who said
there
was another gendarme officer in the brickyard who looked like the accused .. .

(Emphasis added.)

In my opinion, I think it can be said with a
reasonable degree of certainty that had this evidence not been introduced the
outcome may well have been different with respect to the confinement,
kidnapping and robbery counts.

Furthermore, in my view, the ramifications of
the trial judge's error with respect to the introduction of the Kemeny-Ballo-Dallos
evidence cannot be assessed in isolation from the fact that as a direct result
of that error the Crown was denied its statutory right to go last and the
defence was given that privilege.

It may be that had the trial judge not called
that evidence himself, the defence would have at any rate elected to call no
evidence in order to preserve this right to go last to the jury. However, in my
opinion that scenario is entirely speculative and does not touch upon the issue
whether in this regard there has been a substantial wrong or miscarriage of
justice flowing from the error of the trial judge. The order of address of
counsel has always been regarded as a rather critical matter and often has been
determinative when defence counsel are called upon to decide whether to call
evidence. This very matter was stressed by defence counsel in this case as was
the importance of addressing the jury last. Its significance, in my opinion,
cannot be downplayed.

The error of the trial judge in denying the
Crown the right to close last was aggravated, in my opinion, by the very
inflamma­tory address of defence counsel.

As detailed in the majority judgment, my
colleagues take exception to defence counsel's jury address with respect to the
following:

— the expression of
defence counsel's personal opinion as to the respond­ent's innocence;

— defence counsel's
invitation to the jury to ignore the
Criminal Code
's
war crimes
provisions which he characterized as bad law;

— defence counsel's
threatening remarks to the jury;

— defence counsel's
invitation to acquit in order to avoid resurrecting grievances of World War
II;

— defence counsel's
analogy through which he compared the relationship between the Court of Appeal
and the trial judge with the relationship between the respondent's military
superiors and the respondent;

— defence counsel's
intimidating comments suggesting that the jury would in turn be judged by God
just as they judged the respondent;

— defence counsel's
alleged appeal to religious or ethnic prejudice.

My colleagues have set forth passages from the
impugned address, and I need not repeat them.

With respect to the contrary view, I take a much
more serious view of the impropriety of that address. In my opinion, the
inflammatory address tainted the trial, and the trial judge's comments about it
in his charge to the jury fell far short of instructing the jury that they
could not approach their duties in the manner that defence counsel invited them
to do. This resulted in prejudice to the Crown's right to a fair trial, and which
prejudice was not cured by the trial judge's instructions.

In conclusion, I do not think that it can be
said that the cumulative effect of the trial judge's error with respect to the
introduction of the Kemeny-Ballo-Dallos evidence resulted in no substantial
wrong or miscarriage of justice.

Constitutional arguments raised by the
respondent

With respect to the various constitutional
arguments raised by the respondent, I agree with the results arrived at by
Tarnopolsky
J
.A.

Disposition

I am hesitant to set aside a verdict of
acquittal and direct a new trial. I recognize the heavy onus on the Crown to
achieve such a result. In this case, however, I am satisfied that the Crown has
met that burden.

In the result, I would, therefore, set aside the
verdicts of acquittal and direct a new trial. However, like Tarnopolsky J.A., I
think the new trial should be limited to four counts, i.e., one count of
forcible confinement, one count of robbery, one count of kidnapping and one
count of manslaughter.

J.A. (dissenting):

I
The determination of jurisdictional facts
and of essential elements of the offences

A.
The indictment

The indictment, as amended by order of the trial
judge, consists of eight counts charging the respondent with four offences
under

the

The ruling of the trial judge

The Queen

The

principle cannot be mechanically applied to this case because of the

"7(3.71) Notwithstanding anything in

This section, which confers jurisdiction,
only applies if the accused commit­ted an act or omission that constitutes a

committed a crime under the 1927
Criminal
Code

This court cannot try the accused for the

Although the definitions of war crimes and

The first reason ... is because
jurisdiction to try an alleged offence depends on the commission of a crime and
the finding of facts such as specific acts or omissions by the accused,
inhumane conduct, enslavement, deporta­tion, persecution, and all the other

The second reason . .. is because they
deprive the accused of important rights such as the right to plead

convict

to
de facto

[A]lso ... the question, whether the

of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms

Where jurisdiction is conferred on the
basis of a finding that the accused committed a crime, and where that finding
deprives the accused of legal protection in the nature of special pleas,
constitutional rights and very important substantive defences, I am reluctant
to take away from the jury those crucial findings of fact.

Whether or not the accused committed
inhumane acts or was guilty of enslavement, deportation, persecution or the
like, are utterly crucial facts in this case . .. that relate to his very guilt
or innocence, not to some technical question as to the territorial jurisdiction
of this court .

This is not a case like
Balcombe
where
there was a dispute about the location of an alleged offence, and the question
was whether the Ontario courts had jurisdiction or the Quebec courts had
jurisdiction ... In
Balcombe
,
the jurisdictional fact did not go to the
guilt or innocence of the accused ..

There is in this case a very significant
factual dispute as to whether the accused committed war crimes or crimes
against humanity. There is a very significant factual dispute as to whether he
committed acts or omissions such as deportation, persecution, enslavement, or
any other inhumane act or omission.

I am unaware of any other jurisdictional
provision where jurisdiction to try the accused depends on his guilt or
innocence of a crime. Upon the determination of these jurisdictional facts
depends the availability to the accused of
Charter
rights, substantive
defences, and special pleas. Upon

these jurisdictional facts depends the
question, whether he is a war criminal who can be tried in our courts and
deprived of very important legal and constitutional rights.

[J]urisdiction in this case depends upon
the determination of disputed preliminary questions of fact which coincide with
the ultimate question of fact to be decided by the jury. In such cases the
orthodox rule that the judge decides jurisdictional facts must be relaxed
because if it is not relaxed then the judge will determine the ultimate
questions of fact for the jury and thus usurp their function.

There is a powerful analogy here to the
division of function between judge and jury that takes place in evidentiary
matters in conspiracy cases. As Mt Justice Martin said in
R.
v.
Hobart,
Fogel and Doolin
(1982),
1982 CanLII 1975 (ON CA)
, 65 C.C.C. (2d) 518 at pp.
529-30, 36 O.R. (2d) 257, 25 C.R. (3d) 214 (C.A.):

"Thus, the admissibility against an
accused of the acts and declara­tions of alleged co-conspirators depends upon
the determination of a preliminary question of fact, namely, whether the
accused was involved in the conspiracy alleged. This preliminary question of
fact, however, coincides with the ultimate issue which the jury is required to
decide. It is accepted doctrine that where the admissibility of evidence
depends upon the determination of a disputed preliminary question of fact, the
Judge decides the preliminary question of fact ... Where, however, the
preliminary question of fact upon which the admissibility of the evidence
depends, coincides with the ultimate issue required to be decided by the trier
of fact, if the Judge were to decide the preliminary question of fact, he would
also be deciding the ultimate issue which must be decided by the trier of fact.
Where the preliminary question of fact upon which admissibility depends
coincides with the ultimate issue, some modific­ation of the orthodox doctrine
is therefore required."

[This approach] is directly relevant to
this case because the preliminary question of fact, whether the accused
committed acts or omissions that constitute war crimes, involves the same
questions of fact that the jury must ultimately decide in determining whether
the accused is guilty or not guilty.

If the judge determines the preliminary
jurisdictional questions of fact, then the judge would be usurping the function
of the jury to decide the ultimate questions of fact.

To take these jurisdictional facts away
from the jury would be to take into my hands the determination of the guilt or
innocence of the accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Unless he
is guilty of those crimes he cannot be tried in our courts and deprived of
legal rights that would otherwise be available to him.

If these questions are decided by the
judge, it would be necessary to hear all the Crown and defence evidence in the
absence of the jury before determining whether or not the accused committed an
act or omission in the nature of enslavement, deportation, persecution, or any
other inhumane act or omission. If these matters are decided by the judge it
could result in the holding of a complete trial in the absence of the jury
before determining whether or not the court had jurisdiction to empanel the
jury.

Although the difficulties of that procedure
could be lessened by empanel­ling the jury and then arguing the jurisdictional
facts on a motion for nonsuit

in the absence of the jury at the end of
the Crown's case, that could force the accused into the witness-box in a
voir
dire
in order to put forward his evidence in relation to the questions of
jurisdictional fact. In that case, any defence evidence on the issues of
inhumane act, deportation, persecution and the like would be heard in the absence
of the jury at the end of the Crown's case.

That would be a most abnormal way to run a
criminal trial. It would offend the principle that in a jury trial disputed
questions of fact should so far as possible be determined by the jury. For the
judge to hear and determine the issues of credibility in relation to the war
crime facts and the crime against humanity facts, including the defence
evidence, would put it in the hands of the judge and not the jury, to accept or
reject the defence evidence on those crucial areas of fact.

In this case, if any defence evidence as to
the jurisdictional facts of inhumane acts or omissions, deportations,
persecution and the like is heard and judged in absence of the jury, the Crown
would get an unfair preview of the defence evidence in relation to the related
substantive offences, the Crown would get an unfair dry run at the

Although
Balcombe
decided that
jurisdictional facts such as
situs
are decided by the judge and not the
jury, the court noted in
Balcombe

that the facts in issue there did not
go to the guilt or innocence of the accused. This is therefore not a case like
Balcombe.

In this case
situs
is not in issue. In this case the jurisdictional
facts such as enslavement, deportation, persecution or the commission of any
other inhumane act by the accused are facts that go to his very guilt or
innocence. Such questions are for the jury. They go in this case to the very
root of the principle of trial by jury.

This is particularly so when an adverse
determination of those jurisdic­tional facts deprives the accused of important
legal rights including
Charter
rights, special pleas, and the very significant
defence of obedience to
de facto
law.

To take these crucial issues of
jurisdictional fact away from the jury would deprive both him and the community
of the right to have a jury decide all the facts that go to the guilt or
innocence of the accused. Those facts will therefore be decided by the jury.

The questions of international law are in a
quite different category.

It is not necessary to refer to the massive
weight of authority produced by the Crown that demonstrates that questions of
international law are questions for the judge. That principle is as old as
Blackstone.

with the second issue first because it can be dealt with more directly and
briefly.
