knowledge

of each of the factual elements necessary to establish jurisdiction, in
essence requiring proof of a mental element in relation to the
"jurisdictional facts".

I agree.

To start, as set out in
s. 19
of the
Criminal
Code
,
ignorance of the law is not an excuse for committing an offence.
Further, this court held, in
R.
v.
Metro News Ltd.
(1986),
1986 CanLII 148 (ON CA)
, 29 C.C.C.
(3d) 35 at pp. 59-69, 32 D.L.R. (4th) 321 at pp. 345-55, 53 C.R. (3d) 289,

that the accused's belief that a publication was

not
legally obscene is not a defence to a charge of distributing an
obscene publication.

A very similar proposition can be gleaned from
R.

v.
Libman
(1985),
1985 CanLII 51 (SCC)
, 21 C.C.C. (3d) 206, 21 D.L.R. (4th) 174, [1985] 2
S.C.R. 178. In that case, the accused was committed for trial on seven counts
of fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit fraud. As the victims of the
fraudulent scheme were U.S. residents, the accused, by motion, sought to have
the committal for trial quashed on the ground that the alleged offences
occurred outside Canada. Mr. Justice La Forest held that, as a significant
portion of the activities constituting the offence took place in Canada, the
offence was subject to the jurisdiction of Canadian courts. In so ruling, La
Forest J. did not consider whether the accused
knew
that the alleged
offence occurred in Canada. In fact, the accused's
belief
that the
offence had been committed outside Canada was irrelevant to the determination
in law that the offence occurred in Canada.

This is even more pertinent to whether the
accused knew that his voluntary actions, which the jury might determine
amounted to,
e.g. ,
robbery, also constituted a war crime or a crime
against humanity. Such knowledge is almost impossible to expect, much less to
expect the Crown to prove that the accused had it. In 1944, war crimes and
crimes against humanity had not yet authorita­tively been specified. As the
Deschênes Commission expressed it at p. 38 of its Report of the Commission of
Inquiry on War Criminals, 1986 (The Deschênes Commission), "the concept of
crimes commit­ted in times of war has evolved over the centuries and was
eventually crystallized in the 1945
Charter
of the International
Military Tribunal which sat at Nurnberg". Although the definition of war
crimes and crimes against humanity was (at p. 39) "posterior ... to the
commission of the acts with which alleged war criminals are charged ... by no
means does it constitute new law". Nevertheless, how could one expect an
actor in 1944 to know that his actions amounted to war crimes or crimes against
humanity? All that need be proved, beyond a reasonable doubt, as to the
accused's knowledge, was that he knew he was committing those acts which the
court finds, under the
Criminal Code

provisions extant in Canada at that
time, amounted to one or more of forcible confinement, robbery, kidnapping and
manslaughter.

(ii)
Who determines jurisdictional facts —
judge or jury?

The starting point must be, as acknowledged by
the trial judge, the chambers ruling of Fauteux J. for the Supreme Court of
Canada in
Balcombe
v.
The Queen
, supra.
In that case, the
applicant sought leave to appeal this court's dismissal of his appeal

against conviction of murder by the Supreme
Court of Ontario (High Court Division). One ground advanced on the application
was that the trial court was without jurisdiction to convict the appellant. The
trial judge, sitting with a jury, had found on the evidence that the offence
occurred in Ontario, notwithstanding that there was evidence that certain
elements of the offence might also have occurred in Quebec. On appeal, this
court unanimously upheld the trial judge's findings on this point, stating:

[H]aving regard to time factors, location
and condition of the body, and other evidence in this case, the Crown has
proved that the crime was committed in the Province of Ontario and within the
jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of Ontario.

It was submitted before Fauteux J. that the
trial judge erred in making the findings of fact necessary to establish
jurisdiction. Rather, it was said, those issues of fact were for the jury to
decide on the usual criminal standard of "proof beyond a reasonable doubt".
Mr. Justice Fauteux, at p. 148, rejected the submission in these terms:

The question of jurisdiction is a question
of law — consequently, for the presiding Judge — even if, to its determination,
consideration of the evidence is needed. It is a question strictly beyond the
field of these matters which under the law and particularly under the terms of
their oath, the jury have to consider. They are concerned only with the guilt
or innocence of the prisoner at the bar. Indeed the lawful fulfilment of their
duties rests on the assumed existence of the jurisdiction of the Court to try,
at the place where it is held, the accused for the crime charged. They are
concerned with facts as they may be related to guilt or innocence but not to
jurisdiction. There is nothing under the law entitling them, through the whole
course of the execution of their duties, to legally make any other
pronouncement but those as to which a general or special verdict is authorized
by law.

(Emphasis added.)

This statement was considered by this court in
R.

v.
Philips Appliances Ltd.,
1968 CanLII 437 (ON CA)
, [1969] 2 C.C.C. 328, 2 D.L.R. (3d) 558,
57 C.P.R. 45. In that case, the trial judge (sitting alone) had ruled that the
offences charged under the federal
Combines Investigation Act
had
occurred entirely in New Brunswick. He, therefore, found that Ontario courts
were without jurisdiction by virtue of
s. 421(1)
of the
Criminal Code

(now

s. 478(1)
).

The Attorney-General, in seeking to appeal that
finding to the Court of Appeal, was required to show that the question of
jurisdiction was one of law alone, even if it involved consideration of
evidence. Reliance, thus, was placed on the above-quoted words of Fauteux J. in

Balcombe
.
Mr. Justice Jessup, speaking for McGillivray and Laskin JJ.A.,
distinguished
Balcombe
by holding that its
ratio
was confined to
the division of roles between judge

and jury, and did not extend to deciding that
jurisdictional matters are pure issues of law for all purposes. He said at p.
333 C.C.C., pp. 562-3 D.L.R.:

What Fauteux, J., was saying was that a
question of jurisdiction is a question of law in the sense that it is to be
decided by a trial Judge alone and not by a jury. In libel and malicious
prosecution actions for instance many questions are to be decided by a trial
Judge alone and hence are called matters of law although they depend on an
examination of the evidence. I have no doubt that the question of jurisdiction
before the learned trial Judge in this case did not involve "a question of
law alone" within the meaning of
s. 584
of the
Criminal Code

and,
in relation to that section, was a question of fact or of mixed fact and law.

It is apparent, therefore, that this court has
interpreted
Balcombe

as settling the allocation, as between judge and
jury, of the duty to determine facts necessary to the establishment of
jurisdiction. The determination of jurisdictional facts is the func­tion of the
judge and not the jury.

In
R. v. Martel
(1986),
1986 CanLII 6428 (PE SCTD)
, 55 C.R. (3d) 63,
61 Nfld. & PE.I.R. 219, 17 W.C.B. 380 (PE.I.S.C.), the accused applied for
certiorari

to quash committals for trial following a preliminary inquiry into charges
of importing narcotics. The ground for the application was that the committing
judge had erred in finding jurisdiction in the absence of any evidence of a
connection between the charges and Prince Edward Island. The issue before the
Supreme Court was whether, for the purposes of appeal, the committing judge's
finding of jurisdiction disclosed a pure error of law. In the course of his
decision, MacDonald J. stated at p. 76:

[A]s Jessup J.A. pointed out in
Philips,

what Fauteux J. was saying [in
Balcombe
]
was that a question of
jurisdiction is a question of law in the sense that it is to be decided by a
trial judge alone and not by a jury.

In both the
Philips
and
Balcombe

cases,
while the question of jurisdiction was to be decided by a judge, it was clearly
indicated that such a decision in those cases would include a determination of
evidence.

That case also, then, interpreted
Balcombe

as
deciding only the narrow procedural issue of who determines facts relevant to
jurisdiction, and not the broader issue of whether a determination of
jurisdiction is a pure question of law for purposes of appellate review.

However,
R.
v.
Moore and Grazier
(1970),

1970 CanLII 1037 (BC CA)
, 1 C.C.C. (2d) 521, [1971] 1 W.W.R. 656 (B.C.C.A.), is a decision that endorses
a procedure inconsistent with that set out in
Balcombe
,
albeit without
referring to that case. Moore and Grazier were charged with committing rape in
a moving car that crossed the boundary between two counties some time before,
during or after the offence. However, the allegation referred to one only of
the

counties. The trial judge instructed the jury
that, notwithstanding evidence showing that the rape occurred in the county not
mentioned in the allegation,
they
could apply the s. 419(c) (now s.
476(c)) deeming provision of the
Criminal Code

to find that the rape
occurred in the county alleged.

The issue on appeal was whether the word
"deemed" in s. 419(c) meant "deemed until the contrary is
proven", or was a conclusive presumption. After holding that
"deemed" in this context meant "deemed conclusively", Bull
J.A. for the Court of Appeal went on to say at p. 536:

In any event, in the case at bar it cannot
be said that it was proved that the offence took place after the vehicle
entered the other county than that charged.
That was a matter for the jury
to determine
and, of course, we do not know whether they accepted the
evidence of the appellants on that issue or not.

I think that s. 419(c) was clearly pertinent
and applicable to the case at bar, and that
the learned trial Judge made no
error
in
directing the jury in the
manner
that he did.

(Emphasis added.)

It should be emphasized that these words were
written in
obiter,
the earlier conclusion of Bull J.A. on the meaning of
"deemed" being conclusive of this issue. Further, no mention is made
by him of the judgment of Fauteux J. in
Balcombe
.
Indeed, the issue of
locale appears to have been approached as a constituent element of the offence,
rather than as an issue of territorial jurisdiction of the court. For all those
reasons, this judgment cannot be taken as detracting from the position taken in

Balcombe
, Philips
and
Martel.

A review of the literature on criminal procedure
discloses uniform treatment of the question of who, as between judge and jury,
decides jurisdictional facts. Béliveau, Bellemare and Lussier,
On Criminal
Procedure
(1982) (Eng. ed. by Muskatel), merely observe, at p. 146, that:
"In
R.
v.
Balcombe,
the Supreme Court declared that the
judge must decide whether the territorial juris­diction has been
established." The same view of the issue was taken in Ewaschuk,
Criminal
Pleadings and Practice in Canada,
2nd ed. (1987), at 111:4280, where,
citing
Balcombe
,
it is stated: "The
situs
of a crime in so
far as it relates to the jurisdiction of a court to try the offence is a
question of law"

It is clear, therefore, that the law on the
matter is that it is strictly up to the trial judge, and not the jury, to
determine questions of fact relevant to the court's territorial jurisdiction.
Is there any reason to decide, as did the learned trial judge, that this
fundamental rule is to be altered because of the unique nature ofs. 7(3.71) to
(3.77) of the present
Criminal Code
?

I do not think
so.

As Callaghan A.C.J.H.C. held, in the pre-trial
application to quash the indictment on the grounds of contraventions of
ss. 7

and
15
of the
Charter
,
s. 7(3.71)
of the
Criminal Code

does not create
new substantive
Criminal Code
offences. Instead, s. 7(3.71) is merely
procedural

in nature, in that it confers jurisdiction on Canadian courts with respect
to acts committed outside Canada, which would have been offences against
Canadian law in force at the time of their occurrence, by deeming such acts to
have occurred in Canada. However, s. 7(3.71) only applies to those acts which
also constitute a war crime or a crime against humanity. The trial judge
appeared to recognize this, but then went on to hold that without a prior
finding that the accused had committed a war crime or crime against humanity,
there was no jurisdiction to try the accused and that a determination by the
trial judge of these prior issues would deprive the jury of making those
crucial findings in what I presume he saw as a "second round". This is
where I believe he was in error. I will deal later with the issue of the timing
of the exercise of the functions of the judge and of the jury, but first it is
necessary to expand somewhat on the division of their functions.

The accused, in this case, was charged with
forcible confinement, robbery, kidnapping and manslaughter contrary to the 1927

Criminal Code
.
He was
not
charged with war crimes or crimes
against humanity, even if the four
Criminal Code
offences were described
in four counts as "constituting a crime against humanity" and in four
others as "constituting a war crime". Section 7(3.71) provides the
jurisdiction to try the accused for these crimes today in Canada, even though
they were committed in 1944 in Hungary by the accused, over whom Canada had no
jurisdiction at that time and place. In addition,
s.
7(3.71) to
(3.77)

have added the condition that this retrospective extraterritorial jurisdiction
can only be exercised if the acts or omissions which the jury finds to have
occurred, also amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity as these are
defined in
s. 7(3.76)
.

The section is analogous in its construction,
and operates in the same manner as other sections of the
Criminal Code
,
particularly
the other subsections of
s. 7
, which provide for trial in Canada of offences
committed outside Canada. Thus, while s. 279.1 creates the offence of
hostage-taking in Canada, s. 7(3.1) extends the applicability of this section
beyond Canada's territorial borders in fulfilment of Canada's international
obligations. In its 1984 Work­ing Paper on Extraterritorial Jurisdiction, at
pp. 92-5, the Law

Reform Commission of Canada recommended that s.
6 (now s. 7) of the
Criminal Code

be amended to implement Canada's
obliga­tion under art. 5 of the International Convention against the Taking of
Hostages, which requires a state party to "take meas­ures to establish its
jurisdiction" over hostage-taking by "confer­ring
trial
jurisdiction
over alleged hostage taking offenders" (emphasis added).

Section 7(3.1) does not create a new offence,
but provides for the extraterritorial application of the offence of
hostage-taking by stating the conditions under which an act of hostage-taking
committed outside Canada will constitute an offence under
s. 279.1
of the
Criminal
Code
of Canada.

Similarly, s. 7(3.7) provides that an act
causing bodily harm committed on a ship or aircraft will be deemed to have been
committed in Canada if the ship or aircraft is registered in Canada. Whether
the offence of causing bodily harm was committed is a question of fact to be
determined by the trier of fact. However, whether the act was committed on a
ship or aircraft registered in Canada is a jurisdictional question and,
therefore, as stated in
Balcombe
, supra,
its determination is properly
allocated to the judge.

The construction of s. 7(3.71) necessitates a
similar division of the role of judge and jury. The trier of fact must
determine the culpability of the accused in respect of the offences with which
the accused is charged, in this case, forcible confinement, robbery, kidnapping
and manslaughter. However, whether these acts also constitute war crimes and/or
crimes against humanity, is a jurisdic­tional question and, as such, is
quintessentially
a question for the judge.

The determination as to whether an act
constitutes a war crime or a crime against humanity is a question of both fact
and law and is not unlike the determination by a judge as to international and
foreign law.

The trial judge erred in holding that by
determining this jurisdictional question, the judge is usurping the function of
the jury. The jury's role in the trial is limited to deciding whether the
accused is guilty, beyond a reasonable doubt, of having committed the four 1927

Criminal Code

offences with which he is charged. It is clear that some
of the facts necessary to the invocation of the procedural mechanism of s.
7(3.71) will also be relevant to the jury's determination of the accused's
guilt of the offences with which he is charged. There will, no doubt, be a
degree of overlap as between the elements required for the determination of the
jurisdictional question before the judge and the factual question

before the jury. To the extent that this is so,
findings of fact by the jury should be accepted and applied by the judge in his
ruling on the applicability of s. 7(3.71).

(iii)
At what stage of the proceedings must
jurisdiction be established?

The trial judge approached the jurisdictional
issue in this case by observing, first, that before the s. 7(3.71) presumption
of territori­ality could operate, certain facts required proof. In particular,
he held that the words "every person who ... commits an act or omission
outside Canada that constitutes a war crime or a crime against humanity"
in s. 7(3.71) acted as a condition precedent to the invocation of that
presumption. In other words, he asserted, war crimes or crimes against humanity
had to be proven
before the alleged 1927 Criminal Code offences could be
deemed to have occurred in Canada, i. e. ,
"jurisdiction to determine
guilt depends on guilt":

The court has no jurisdiction to determine
whether the accused committed a crime under the 1927
Criminal Code

unless he committed in
fact an act or omission that constitutes a war crime or a crime against
humanity .. .

Jurisdiction to try him thus depends on his
guilt or innocence of war crimes and crimes against humanity .. .

The condition precedent to jurisdiction is
the actual commission of the acts or omissions with which the accused is
charged.

It is clear from these passages that not only
did the learned trial judge view proof of war crimes or crimes against humanity
as a "gateway" to the s. 7(3.71) presumption, but that he also viewed
the operation of that presumption as a prerequisite to the court's jurisdiction
to
try the 1927 Criminal Code offences.

With respect, I think that these two premises —
that the s. 7(3.71) presumption of territoriality was required to operate
before the court had jurisdiction to inquire into guilt of the
Criminal Code

offences ("first premise"), and that the invocation of s. 7(3.71)
is predicated upon a prior finding of "guilt" of war crimes or crimes
against humanity ("second premise") — are in error. The first point
has been explored and it is my opinion that the operation of s. 7(3.71) is
required by
s. 6(2)
of the
Criminal Code
only just prior to conviction
and not prior to trial of the offences charged.

The second premise might arguably be said to
follow from a literal reading of s. 7(3.71), but, in my view, such a literal
construction is inconsistent with the purpose of that section and the operation
of similar jurisdictional "deeming" provisions in the
Criminal
Code
.
The purpose of this section was examined by

Callaghan A.C.J.H.C. in
R.
v.
Finta
,
supra.
Adverting to debates of the House of Commons at the time of
enactment of the section, the Associate Chief Justice held at p. 255 C.C.C.,
pp. 104-5 D.L.R.:

Section 6(1.91) [now s. 7(3.71)],
therefore, is procedural only ... Section 6(1.91) merely gives this court the
jurisdiction to try these crimes when such crimes constitute a war crime or
crime against humanity as recognized by the general principals [sic] of law
recognized by the community of nations.

I hold that the legislation in issue does
not create new offences but merely confers jurisdiction on Canadian courts with
respect of acts that would have been offences against Canadian law in force at
the time of their occurrence if such acts had occurred in Canada.

Although the learned trial judge acknowledged
this ruling, in my view his approach to s. 7(3.71) had, as its effect, the
elevation of that section's war crime and crime against humanity elements to a
requirement that these be established as though they were offences under the
Criminal
Code
.
This is particularly apparent when he declares: "Jurisdiction to
try him thus depends on his
guilt or innocence
of war crimes and crimes
against humanity" or when he asserts: "The condition precedent to
jurisdiction is the actual commission of the acts or omissions
with which
the accused is charged".
The "acts or omissions" referred to
are war crimes or crimes against humanity.

Other "territorial deeming" provisions
of the
Criminal Code

shed light on the validity of the learned trial
judge's second premise. Section 465(3) of the
Code
provides:

465(3) Every one who, while in Canada,
conspires with any one to do anything referred to in subsection (1) in a place
outside Canada that is an offence under the laws of that place shall be deemed
to have conspired to do that thing in Canada.

(Section 465(1) refers to various
Code
offences.)
The clear parallel between s. 7(3.71) and s. 465(3) is in their reference to
acts that are unlawful according to some external norm,
i.e. ,
"anything
.. . that is an offence under the laws of the place [outside Canada]" in
s. 465(3), and "act or omission ... that constitutes a war crime or crime
against humanity" in s. 7(3.71).

The case of Gunn
v. The Queen
(1982),
1982 CanLII 174 (SCC)
, 66
C.C.C. (2d) 294, 135 D.L.R. (3d) 237, [1982] 1 S.C.R. 522, involved a
prosecution under s. 465(3) (then s. 423(3)) for an alleged conspiracy
illegally to export arms from the U.S.A. The indictment, however, failed to
allege a violation of U.S. law At trial, the charges were dismissed on the
basis of insufficient evidence to support the indictment. The Manitoba Court of
Appeal ordered a new trial, holding that an amendment of the indictment should
have been allowed to include

a reference to U.S. law The Supreme Court of
Canada restored the acquittal on other grounds, but Laskin C.J.C. added, in
obiter,

at p. 299 C.C.C., p. 243 D.L.R.:

This is not a case where this Court finds
it necessary to give any direction in detail as to how a charge of conspiracy
involving breach of foreign criminal law, as envisaged by
Criminal Code,
s.
423(3), should be framed. It is enough to say that
the statutory fiction of
a conspiracy in Canada in violation of foreign law can only become operative if
a breach of the foreign law is charged.

(Emphasis added.)

Bolduc
v.
Quebec
(Attorney-General)

(1982),
1982 CanLII 224 (SCC)
, 68 C.C.C. (2d) 413, 137 D.L.R. (3d) 674, [1982]
1 S.C.R. 573, also dealt with a prosecution under then
s. 423(3)
(now s.
465(3)) for conspiring to transport persons into the U.S. in breach of U.S.
immigration laws. At the preliminary inquiry the information was quashed on the
ground that it did not allege an offence known to Canadian
law.
The
Attorney-General successfully appealed that decision to the Superior Court, and
a further appeal to the Court of Appeal was dismissed.

On appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada,
Chouinard J., for the court, observed at p. 420 C.C.C., p. 681 D.L.R.:

The offence
charged
is common law
conspiracy committed in Canada, to effect an unlawful purpose. Causing persons
to enter the United. States unlawfully constitutes an offence under American
law, just as causing persons to come into Canada unlawfully constitutes an
offence under Canadian law. As
a consequence of the presumption of
s. 423(3)
, the conspirators
are deemed
to
have conspired to commit the offence in Canada.
It is as if they had
conspired to cause persons to come into Canada unlawfully.

(Emphasis added.) It is significant, in my view,
that this statement was made at a point in the proceedings where no evidence
had yet been taken.

The effect of these dicta is to suggest that
once a charge has been laid, alleging a conspiracy in Canada to violate some
foreign law, s. 465(3) becomes operative, at least provisionally, to allow
convictions of the substantive offences charged.

The operation of such "provisional
deeming" also appears to be a logical necessity in the application of the
special jurisdiction provisions of
s. 476
of the
Criminal Code
.
For
example, paras. (a) and
(b)
of that section provide:

476. For purposes of this Act,

(a) where an offence is committed in or on
any water or on a bridge between two or more territorial divisions, the offence
shall be deemed to have been committed in any of the territorial divisions;

(b) where an offence is committed on the
boundary of two or more territorial divisions or within five hundred metres of
any such

boundary, or the offence was commenced
within one territorial division and completed within another, the offence shall
be deemed to have been committed in any of the territorial divisions;

Applying the learned trial judge's literal
construction to these provisions would require that there be convictions of the
offences before the deeming provisions could operate. However, such convictions
could not occur until the deeming provisions can be invoked provisionally to
permit convictions, otherwise the sections become dead letters. Assuming that
Parliament could not have intended such a result, it seems clear that a literal
reading of such territorial deeming provisions is inappropriate, and that these
provisions must be allowed to operate provisionally throughout the trial
proceedings until evidence exists either to justify or to disqualify the
presumption. I note also that it is unlikely that this procedure would result
in prejudice to the accused because, if the evidence fails to establish the
occurrence of the offence, acquittal will follow regardless of where the
"offence" is deemed to have occurred.

Other sections of the
Criminal Code

containing
jurisdictional presumptions with similar wording are
ss. 477.1
,
477.2
and

477.4
.

I think that these
Criminal Code

provisions
illustrate the difficulty with the trial judge's reasoning, and show that
Parlia­ment cannot have intended to require proof of a war crime or a crime
against humanity offences before invocation of s. 7(3.71).

The learned trial judge went on to hold that
because, in his view, the operation of s. 7(3.71) required a finding of guilt
of war crimes and crimes against humanity, and because such findings would
require determinations of fact coinciding with the ultimate issues to be
decided by the jury,
all
factual determinations required for the operation of s. 7(3.71)
should be made by the jury:

Whether or not the accused committed
inhumane acts or was guilty of enslavement, deportation, persecution or the
like, are utterly crucial facts in this case. These are findings of fact that relate to his very guilt or
innocence , not to some technical question as to the territorial jurisdiction
of this court as opposed to some other court.

(Emphasis added.)

I tend to agree with him that, where
jurisdictional facts coincide with the ultimate factual issues before the jury,
those facts should be left to that body. On a practical level, since the jury
ultimately must make those findings anyway (albeit in the context of their
verdict and not the determination of jurisdiction), there seems to be little
use in having them determined a second time by the trial judge (assuming, of
course, that both findings are required on the same standard of proof).

On a more substantive level, moreover, I think
that leaving such jurisdictional facts to the jury is consistent with the
reasoning of Fauteux J. in
Balcombe
.
That reasoning relied almost
exclusively on the observation that allowing the jury to determine jurisdic­tional
facts,
per se,
was beyond the scope of their lawful duty. Where,
however, such facts are to be determined by the jury in the normal course of
their determinations of guilt or innocence of the offences charged then, in my
view, Fauteux J.'s concern eva­porates.

However, this reasoning is strictly confined to
those issues of fact that
are
ultimately before the jury. In this case,
such issues are those related to guilt or innocence of the offences charged,
that is, the 1927
Criminal Code

offences. Consequently, I think it was
wrong in law for the trial judge to leave to the jury any factual determination
not strictly coterminous with those required by the 1927
Criminal Code
offences.
In the emphasized portions of the extract of the trial judge's ruling quoted
above, he appears to say — erroneously in my view — that the accused's guilt or
inno­cence of crimes under the 1927
Criminal Code
depends on whether the
jury first finds him guilty of war crimes and/or crimes against humanity. In my
opinion, it is clear that such "purely" jurisdictional facts should
be determined by the trial judge.

It follows, as well, from my determination of
this issue, that the Crown was in error in charging the accused with two counts
concerning each of the four
Criminal Code

offences. It matters not
whether what is proved with respect to robbery, for example, constitutes a war
crime or a crime against humanity. The accused could not, as the trial judge
did recognize, be convicted of robbery twice on the same facts, merely because
the act of robbery constituted
both
a crime against humanity and a war
crime.

I must emphasize that, in my opinion, there is
no section in the
Criminal Code

which creates the offence of a war crime
or a crime against humanity, nor does s. 7(3.71) create such an offence. Rather
than creating a substantive offence of war crime or crime against humanity,
Parliament chose, on the recommendation of the Deschênes Commission, to extend
the applicability of existing
Criminal Code
provisions extant at the
time of the acts. Thus, s. 7(3.71) provides that
all
of Canada's
substantive criminal law will apply extraterritorially to those who commit
offences outside Canada, if the acts committed are so grave in nature that they
constitute war crimes or crimes against humanity. This approach is different
than that which may have been adopted in other coun­tries, which have enacted
legislation establishing war crime as a substantive offence.

(iv)
Conclusion

Therefore, I am of the opinion that the correct
approach to s.
7(3.71)
is the following:

First, by virtue of
s. 6(2)
of the
Criminal
Code
,
there is no need to determine finally the issue of territorial
jurisdiction until the moment of conviction. Accordingly, it is unnecessary to
ascertain the applicability of s. 7(3.71) to the facts of a given case until
the end of that case. In a trial by jury, some of the facts necessary to the
invocation of s. 7(3.71) will be determined by the jury in the course of their
determinations of guilt of the offences charged — in this case those in the
1927
Criminal Code.
Such findings of fact should be accepted and applied
by the judge in his ruling on the applicability of s. 7(3.71). On the authority
of
Balcombe
,
all other factual determinations relevant to s. 7(3.71),
concerning interna­tional law and war crimes and crimes against humanity,
should be made by the judge on the usual criminal standard of proof.

The trial judge's ruling on the availability of
s. 7(3.71) should be made after all the evidence is heard (or, perhaps, at the
close of the Crown's case). If, at that point, the trial judge determines that
any factual issue within his or her province has not been established beyond a
reasonable doubt, the trial judge should rule that s. 7(3.71) cannot be invoked
and that the court is without jurisdic­tion. In such a case, the jury is not
then required to return a verdict.

If, however, the trial judge is satisfied that
all facts required for s. 7(3.71) (other than those to be determined in the
jury's verdict on the offences charged), have been established, the jury should
return a verdict and the trial judge should apply that finding in determining
whether s. 7(3.71) shall apply. If the verdict is "guilty", the trial
judge presumably would find jurisdiction and then enter a conviction formally.
If the verdict is "not guilty", then the jurisdictional point becomes
moot and need not be determined by the trial judge.

Section 7

Extraterritoriality

The respondent submitted that s. 7(3.71)

It is necessary to start this discussion with

26 C.R. (3d) 121 at p. 125,

A

A
retrospective

consequences of an act done prior to proclamation are to be given a different
legal effect after proclamation as a result of the enactment of the statute. It

an event which occurred prior to proclamation.

concluded, at p. 245 C.C.G., p. 95 D.L.R., that a retrospective statute, as in

C.
The position of the parties at trial

At trial, the Crown contended that Finta was the
senior gendarmerie officer at the Szeged concentration centre, and had
effective control over the operation and guarding of the centre. The Crown
asserted that, as the senior gendarmerie officer, Finta was responsible for the
forced confinement of the Jews in the brickyard, the confiscation of their
valuables while interned, their forced removal from the concentration centre to
the train station and, ultimately, the deaths which occurred during the
deportation out of Hungary. It was the position of the Crown that Finta either

committed the acts in question, or through his
supervisory role, procured, aided or abetted others who actually performed the
acts.

By the end of the trial, Finta through his
counsel acknowledged that he had been a gendarmerie captain, that he had been
present at the brickyard and that he had participated in the confiscation of
valuables. However, Finta's position was that he was not in a position of
authority at the brickyard, but was subject to the command of the German SS.
The defence position was that, while Finta supervised the confiscation of
valuables in the brickyard, he did so pursuant to orders that were either
lawful, or not manifestly unlawful.

Next, it was argued that Finta was not
responsible for the removal of the Jews from the brickyard to the train station,
or for their deportation out of Hungary by train and that he played no role in
these events. It was also argued on his behalf that the deportation was not
unlawful, or at least not manifestly unlawful.

Finally, the defence trial position was that the
internment and deportation of the Hungarian Jews was a necessary wartime
security measure, and that, given the circumstances of wartime, their treatment
was not unduly brutal or inhumane.

Finta did not call a defence. However, after the
close of the Crown's case, the trial judge, at the request of the defence,
placed before the jury the videotaped testimony of two witnesses taken by way
of commission evidence and the statements and minutes of testimony given by a
witness at Finta's Hungarian trial in 1947-48. The admissibility of that
evidence and the trial judge's decision to call the evidence himself are
challenged on this appeal. We will detail that evidence when we address that
ground of appeal.

D.
Summary of the evidence
1.
Background
evidence

The Second World War began in Europe in
September, 1939, and ended on May 8, 1945. As one of the Allied powers, Canada
was engaged in an armed conflict with the Axis powers, which included Germany.
Hungary joined the Axis powers in 1940 and was engaged in an armed conflict
with Canada between December 7, 1941, and January 20, 1945.

Germany was governed by the National Socialist
German Workers Party (NSDAP) led by Adolf Hitler, the German Chancel­lor. That
government pursued an anti-Jewish policy which, with the outbreak of the war,
was extended to the areas under German influence and occupation, including
Hungary. The implementation of the "final solution" both in Germany
and the occupied areas resulted in the deprivation of all means of existence
for Jews, and

their deportation to camps in eastern Europe for
the purpose of forced labour and extermination.

In March, 1944, German troops invaded Hungary
and ousted the existing Hungarian government; a more servile, pro-German
government was installed in its place. Thus, after March, 1944, while
de
jure
Hungary remained a sovereign state,
de facto
Hungary was an
occupied state. To maintain control over Hun­gary's economic and military
resources, the German government established a command structure which flowed
directly from Heinrich Himmler, the Reichsfuehrer SS and chief of German
police, to the German-appointed Higher SS and police leader for Hungary, in
Budapest, to the various German police and SS units operating in Hungary, the
Royal Hungarian Gendarmerie and the Hungarian police force.

The Royal Hungarian Gendarmerie was an armed
paramilitary public security organization. It provided police services in rural
areas and functioned as a political police force. When the German armed forces
occupied Hungary, they were instructed not to disarm the gendarmerie as it was
in the process of being restruc­tured to be available to the Hungarian Higher
SS and Police Leader.

Anti-Jewish measures began in Hungary prior to
the German occupation. A series of anti-Jewish laws were passed between 1941
and 1944, culminating in the promulgation of a law containing a racial formula
for the identification of Jews. The Jews were therefore an identifiable group
for the purposes of Hungarian law.

Following the German occupation, a series of anti-Jewish
laws and decrees was rapidly adopted by the new Hungarian govern­ment. The plan
for the purging of Jews from Hungary was incorporated in Ministry of the
Interior Order 6163/1944, the so-called Baky Order, dated April 7, 1944. The
government never passed a statute or decree authorizing this plan. Thus, the
Baky Order was the only "authority" for the confinement of all Hun­garian
Jews, the confiscation of their property and their deporta­tion out of Hungary.

The Baky Order provided the master plan for the
implementa­tion of the "final solution" in Hungary, which was to
occur in six phases, namely, isolation, expropriation, ghettoization, concentra­tion,
entrainment and deportation. For the purpose of carrying out this plan, Hungary
was divided into six zones under the command of the Hungarian Gendarmerie. The
City of Szeged was designated as one of seven concentration centres in Zone 4.
The Baky Order was addressed to a number of officials, including all gendarme
district commands, all commanding officers of the gendarme

detective (investigative) subdivisions and the
central detective headquarters of the gendarmerie. It placed responsibility for
carrying out the plan on the territorially competent police and the Royal
Hungarian Gendarmerie.

2.
Events at Szeged

Shortly after the Baky Order was passed, the six
phases of the "final solution" were implemented in Szeged. The city's
Jews were rounded up and forced into a fenced-in Jewish ghetto. On average, the
Jews remained in the ghetto for a couple of weeks before being transferred
directly to the brickyard, or a sports field and then, after a few days, to the
brickyard. The concentration in the brickyard of the approximately 8,617 Jews
of Szeged and its surrounding area was completed by June 20, 1944.

The brickyard, which was filthy, consisted of a
large open area containing an enormous kiln, a chimney and several buildings
used for drying b
ri
cks. The Jews were crowded together and slept on the ground in the
drying sheds which had roofs but no walls. They were not permitted to leave the
brick factory, which was sur­rounded by a fence and guarded by the gendarmes.

Announcements were made repeatedly over the
loudspeaker ordering the Jews to surrender their remaining valuables, gold or
jewellery, on pain of death. When the Jews were gathered for these
announcements, a basket or hamper was presented for the collec­tion of the
valuables.

Between June 24 and 30, 1944, the Jews
imprisoned in the brickyard were marched by the gendarmes to the Rokus train
station, where they were forcibly loaded into railway boxcars to be deported
out of Hungary on three train transports, one to Auschwitz and two to
Strasshof.

Approximately 70 to 90 Jews with their luggage
were crammed into each boxcar measuring roughly eight meters by two meters. As
a result, many were forced to remain standing. The doors on the boxcars were
padlocked shut. The only openings for air were the very small windows with
grilles located in each of the four upper corners of the boxcar. There was no
artificial lighting.

Usually, the boxcars contained two buckets, one
for water and the other for toilet facilities. However, during the transport
the toilet bucket quickly overflowed with human excrement. Due to the crowded
conditions, the buckets were inaccessible to many of
the
prisoners so that they
were forced to relieve themselves where

they stood or sat.

As a result of the inhumane conditions in the
boxcars, some of the Jews, mostly elderly people, died during the journey.
Normally,

the gendarme or German guards did not permit the
bodies to be removed prior to reaching the train's destination, resulting in a
terrible stench in some of the cars. Despite the harsh and deplorable
conditions, with rare exception, the doors of the boxcars remained shut
throughout the journey.

Expert evidence on legality

Dr. Revesz testified that the Baky Order was not
only illegal, but manifestly so. Furthermore, he also testified that, as
members of the gendarmerie were involved in the conduct of criminal investi­gations,
they were required to have thorough training in Hun­garian law and procedure.
Accordingly, Dr. Revesz concluded that, given a gendarme's knowledge of the law
and the decrees pub­lished prior to the Baky Order, a gendarme officer would
have known that the Baky Order was beyond the prerogative of the (under-)
Secretary of State and contained at least 14 violations of Hungarian law.

The trial judge directed the jury that the Baky
Order was unlawful as violating Hungarian law, including a number of principles
of the Hungarian Constitution.

Imre Finta

Imre Finta was born on September 2, 1912, in
Kolosvar, Hungary (now in Romania). He lived and studied law at the university
in Szeged in the 1930's. In 1935, Pinta enrolled at the Royal Hungarian
Military Academy and, on January 1, 1939, was commissioned as a second
lieutenant in the Royal Hungarian Gendarmerie. On April 5, 1942, he was
promoted to the rank of captain. On March 1, 1944, he was transferred to Szeged
as commander of the investigative subdivision of the gendarmerie.

In 1947-48, Finta was tried
in absentia
in
the People's Tribunal of Szeged and convicted of "crimes against the
people". He was sentenced to five years forced labour (later commuted to
five years' imprisonment), confiscation of property, loss of employment and
loss of right to political participation for 10 years. In 1951, Pinta emigrated
to Canada and in 1956, he became a Canadian citizen. He has lived in Canada
since that time.

After January 27, 1958, by operation of a
statutory limitation under Hungarian law, punishment of Finta became statute
barred. In 1970, the Presidential Council of the Hungarian People's Council
issued a general amnesty or pardon which, by its terms, applied to Finta.

The trial judge found that the general amnesty
did not, in its own terms or by operation of Hungarian law, constitute a pardon

and farther, that as the Hungarian trial and
conviction were nullities at Canadian law, any purported pardon based on those
nullities, would be itself a nullity. Accordingly, the trial judge held that
Finta was not entitled to plead
autrefois convict
or pardon.

5.
Evidence regarding Finta's involvement in
events at Szeged

While the trial presented many unique and
complex legal issues, the case for the Crown depended in large measure on the testimony
of 19 witnesses who had been interned in the brickyard and deported on one of
the three trains. Some of these survivors gave viva
voce
evidence before
the jury. Others were examined by way of commission evidence taken in Israel
and Hungary and their evidence was presented at trial on videotape.

In addition, the trial judge, at the request of
the defence, directed that a videotape of the commission evidence of two other
survivors be played for the jury.

The evidence of the survivors fell into four general
groups. Six witnesses who knew Finta before the events in issue testified as to
things said and done by Finta at the brickyard and at the train station. A
second group, consisting of three witnesses who did not know Finta beforehand,
identified him as having said or done certain things at the brickyard and at
the train station. A third group, consisting of four witnesses who did not know
Finta beforehand also testified as to things said and done by Finta at the
brickyard and at the train station. However, this group based their
identification of Finta on statements made to them by others. The fourth group,
consisting of eight witnesses, who did not know Finta beforehand and did not
identify him, testified as to events which occurred at the brickyard and at the
train station.

Of the six witnesses who testified that they
knew Finta before their imprisonment in the brickyard, four testified that
Finta was in charge of the brickyard and one testified that everyone referred
to Finta as the commander of the brickyard. Two of these six witnesses
testified that Finta made the daily announcements in the brickyard demanding
that the prisoners relinquish all valuables on pain of death, and three of
these six witnesses testified that he supervised the confiscation of the
detainees' valuables. Two of these six witnesses testified that Finta was at
the train station supervising the loading of the prisoners into the boxcars.

Among the second group of witnesses, one witness
testified that, as Finta was in charge of the brickyard, all the announcements
made or commands given in the brickyard were issued by him or on his behalf and
that he supervised the confiscations. This witness

testified further that Finta commanded the
gendarmes when the Jews were escorted from the ghetto to the brickyard and that
he supervised the loading of the Jews by the gendarmes at the train station.
Another witness in this group testified that Finta broke the silver handle off
her mother's cane and confiscated it.

Several witnesses who identified Finta on the
basis of what had been said by others gave testimony to the effect that Finta
was in charge of the brickyard and supervised the confiscation. One of these
witnesses testified that she saw a person identified to her as Finta give the
announcements for the surrender of valuables and that, from her observations,
that person was in charge at the railway station. Three other witnesses in this
group testified that they were told by others that the person making the
announce­ments, and in one case, the person in charge at the railway station,
was Finta. The trial judge instructed the jury that they could not rely on the
identification of Finta by these witnesses in so far as it depended on what
others had told these witnesses as to the identity of the person they believed
to be Finta.

The eight witnesses who did not identify Finta
described the conditions in the brickyard, the deportation from Szeged and the
conditions in the boxcars.

In addition to the evidence of the survivors,
the Crown relied on photographs, handwriting and fingerprint evidence to
identify Finta as a captain in the gendarmerie at Szeged at the relevant time.

Expert and documentary evidence was tendered to
establish the historical context of the evidence, the relevant command structure
in place in Hungary in 1944 and the state of international law in 1944.

II.
The grounds of appeal

The Crown advanced numerous grounds of appeal.
Several did not require oral argument by the respondent and can be disposed of
with brief reasons.

A.
The absence of any instruction as to the
doctrine of wilful blindness

The trial judge instructed the jury that Finta
had to have known that the Baky Order was manifestly unlawful. The Crown argues
that if knowledge of the manifest unlawfulness of the order was a prerequisite
to liability, the trial judge should have instructed the jury that wilful
blindness of the manifest illegality of the order would suffice.

In criminal law, wilful blindness of the
existence of a fact or circumstance is distinct from but very close to actual
knowledge of the existence of that fact or circumstance: see, e.g.,
R.
v.

Sansregret
(1985),
1985 CanLII 79 (SCC)
, 18 C.C.C. (3d) 223 at pp. 235-7, 17 D.L.R. (4th) 577
at pp. 588-90, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 570.

The Crown contended at trial that Finta, like
any other senior gendarme officer, knew of the blatant illegality of the Baky
Order. The Crown did not suggest that Finta was merely wilfully blind as to its
manifest illegality. While it cannot be said that it would have been wrong to
instruct the jury as to the potential application of the doctrine of wilful
blindness, the instruction was not necessary. The charge was already a lengthy
and complex one. Reference to the somewhat difficult concept of wilful
blindness, especially when its potential significance in the case was minimal
and somewhat contrary to the actual position advanced by the Crown, would have
served only to further and unnecessarily complicate the charge.

In our opinion, the trial judge did not err in
failing to charge the jury on the potential application of the doctrine of
wilful blindness.

B.
Whether the trial judge erred in failing
to relate the evidence to issues of knowledge and intention

The Crown did not press this point in oral
argument and we doubt whether it raises a question of law alone: see
R.
v.

Pilon,
1990 CanLII 36 (SCC)
, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1422, 28 Q.A.C. 160n,
105 N.R. 77
n. The trial
judge properly instructed the jury that Finta's mental state as it related to
his knowledge and intention could be inferred from his conduct. That conduct
was extensively reviewed by the trial judge. It would be self-evident to the
jury that the conduct reviewed by the trial judge could be looked to by them in
determining whether the Crown had established the necessary intent and
knowledge.

C.
Whether the trial judge erred in refusing
to admit the statement made by Finta after his arrest

The Crown does not challenge the trial judge's
finding that the statement was obtained following an infringement of Finta's
right to retain and instruct counsel as guaranteed by
s. 10(b)
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.
The Crown argues, however, that the trial
judge erred in excluding the evidence pursuant to
s. 24(2)
of the Charter.

Prejudicial incriminatory statements obtained
following a viola­tion of
s. 10(b)
of the
Charter
will generally, although not
always, be excluded:
R.
v.
Elshaw
(1991),
1991 CanLII 28 (SCC)
, 67 C.C.C. (3d) 97 at
pp. 124-8, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 24, 7 C.R. (4th) 333. There was ample basis, in this
record, for the trial judge's conclusion that the general rule of

exclusion should apply in this case. We would
not give effect to this ground of appeal.

D.
Whether the trial judge erred in admitting
the exchange between the Hungarian judge and defence counsel during the taking
of the commission evidence

In the course of the examination of one witness,
during the taking of commission evidence, Judge Strauss, the Hungarian judge,
and defence counsel engaged in a considerable debate concerning the propriety
of defence counsel's questions. At trial, defence counsel argued that Judge
Strauss improperly interfered with his cross-examination of the witness and
that the evidence should be excluded for that reason. The trial judge
disagreed.

Counsel for Finta then argued that the jury
should hear the exchange between himself and Judge Strauss, since it could
affect their assessment of the credibility of the witness. The trial judge
agreed with this submission and the Crown tendered the evidence, complete with
the exchange between counsel and Judge Strauss.

We cannot agree with the trial judge's holding that
the exchange between counsel and Judge Strauss was relevant to the credibility
of the witness being examined when the exchange occurred. It may, however, have
had some relevance to the over-all assessment of that witness's evidence, in so
far as it may have assisted the jury in considering whether defence counsel's
cross-examination was curtailed. The trial judge was anxious to minimize any
disadvan­tage to the defence by the introduction of the evidence
via
videotape
as opposed to the actual attendance of the witness. This ruling was reflective
of that approach.

It is doubtful that the exchange between Judge
Strauss and counsel would have been of much assistance to the jury. It may have
been preferable to exclude the exchange from the material heard by the jury.
Editing of this kind was done in respect of the videotaped evidence of other
witnesses.

We are satisfied that the inclusion of the
exchange between Judge Strauss and counsel could not have adversely affected
the case for the Crown and cannot be viewed as prejudicial much less reversible
error.

E.
Whether the trial judge erred in his
direction to the jury with respect to the evidence of the witness Solti

Another of the issues raised at trial concerned
the alleged persecution of Jews on racial or religious grounds. Evidence of
Finta's attitude towards Jews had some relevance to this issue. Mrs. Solti, a
Jew, gave evidence that she knew Finta prior to the

detention of the Jews in the brickyard and that
he had always dealt with her in an appropriate manner. Her evidence was
relevant to Finta's attitude toward Jews. The trial judge properly related the
evidence to the question of motive or animus, although he mischaracterized it
as "character" evidence. We find no merit in this ground of appeal.

F.
Whether evidence concerning the existence
of gas chambers and extermination camps was relevant

Initially, the Crown sought to adduce evidence
concerning the extermination process at the death camp at Auschwitz. Some of
the Jews deported by train from Szeged were taken to Auschwitz. The issue had
little, if any, relevance to the case against Finta as it was not alleged by
the Crown that Finta had any involvement in, or knowledge of, the operation of
that camp. The trial judge had a discretion to exclude that evidence when
tendered by the Crown and, in our view, did not err in so doing.

Later during the course of the trial, counsel
for Finta cross-examined Crown expert witnesses about various matters relevant
to the historical context in which the alleged offences occurred. In the course
of these cross-examinations, there was reference to the various practices
followed in camps like Auschwitz. The trial judge permitted this
cross-examination as relevant to test the expertise of the experts who were
providing historical information for the jury. We see no error in that ruling.

There is no inconsistency in disallowing
questions asked by the Crown which have minimal relevance to the case, while at
the same time permitting questions of a similar nature asked by the defence as
part of a challenge to the expertise of other witnesses offered by the Crown as
expert witnesses. Crown counsel was, of course, free to pursue this area with
the expert on re-examination in order to buttress the witness's expertise.

We now turn to the issues on which we did
require argument from the respondent.

G.

jury

1

Overview

It is hornbook law that in a trial by a court
composed of a judge and jury, the judge decides questions of law and instructs
the jury as to the relevant law. The jury weighs the evidence, determines the
facts, applies the law to those facts and renders a verdict: see Williams,
Thxtbook
of Criminal Law,
2nd ed. (1978), pp. 124-5;
Stauroff v. The Queen

(1979),

411

The designation of

the judge as the master of the law and the jury
as the master of the facts is fundamental to the institution of trial by jury.
It is the Crown's position that the trial judge and not the jury was required
to weigh the evidence, determine the relevant facts and decide if Finta's acts
constituted war crimes or crimes against humanity. The jury, says the Crown,
was required to determine only whether Finta's acts constituted violations of
the relevant sections of the
Criminal Code

If the Crown's argument is correct, Parliament has chosen to
abandon this fundamental distinction in prosecutions involving allegations of
war crimes or crimes against humanity, by requiring the trial judge to make

roles traditionally played by the judge and jury is said to flow by necessary
implication from the language of
s. 7(3.71)
of the
Criminal Code.

We say at the outset that we cannot accept this
submission. The trial judge was correct in holding that the jury was required
to determine whether Finta's acts constituted a breach of the 1927
Code
and
whether those acts amounted to war crimes or crimes against humanity. Before
turning to the reasons for so holding, it is necessary to set out the relevant

The indictment must be read with an eye to both
the applicable statutory definitions and the generally applicable principles of
criminal culpability. The former addresses conduct primarily, and the latter
the mental component which must coexist with the prohibited conduct to
establish criminal fault.

The definitions of war crimes and crimes against
humanity found in s. 7(3.76) do not expressly require proof of any mental state
which must accompany the existence of the facts or cir­cumstances which bring
an act within those definitions. In this regard, those definitions are no
different than many others in the
Code
which define culpable conduct. In
our view, since the international component of the charges is central to
Finta's culpability, it is necessary to read a fault requirement into those
definitions.

Knowledge of the existence of the facts or
circumstances which bring the conduct within the definition of the prohibited
conduct is commonly required where a definition of culpable conduct is silent
as to the necessary fault requirement. We would, as the trial judge did, hold
that knowledge of the circumstances or facts which bring an act within the
definition of a war crime or crime against humanity constitutes the mental
component which must coexist with the prohibited acts to establish culpability
for those acts.

(4) that Finta knew

(5) that Finta knew
that the people confined were a civilian population or an identifiable group;

Szeged, and

—
that the confinement was done without lawful authority.

The first element, confinement, was relatively
straightforward and required that the Crown establish that Finta was a knowing
party to the confinement of the Jews in the brickyard.

The second element, the absence of lawful authority,
raised a potentially more complex factual issue. The Crown could establish the
absence of lawful authority by proving beyond a reasonable

doubt that there was no lawful authority for the
confinement and that Finta did not believe there was any such authority. The
Crown could also prove the absence of a lawful authority by demonstrat­ing
beyond a reasonable doubt that despite the existence of an order from the
Hungarian government authorizing the confinement, the confinement constituted a
crime against humanity as defined in the
Code
and that Finta knew of the
facts which gave the confinement the quality of a crime against humanity. If
the confinement had that quality it was unlawful by virtue of
s. 7(3.74)
,
despite the existence of an order of the Hungarian government. That section
specifically excludes reliance on the local law of the place where the act
occurred, if the act constitutes a crime against humanity.

In this case, it was central to Finta's defence
on count 1 that he acted under lawful orders from the Hungarian government. It
was equally central to the Crown's case that Pinta knew that the acts directed
by these orders had the factual qualities required to make those acts a crime
against humanity as defined in the
Code.
In light of the evidence
adduced and the position of the parties, it is entirely possible that, in
deciding whether the Crown had proved that the confinement was done without
lawful authority, the jury would have been required to determine both whether
the confinement amounted to a crime against humanity, and whether Finta was
aware of the facts that gave the confinement the quality of a crime against
humanity.

An identical overlap is found in count 2, where
the Crown was also required to show an absence of lawful authority in order to
prove an unlawful confinement. In determining that fact, the jury may, not
must, have had to decide whether the confinement amounted to a war crime and
whether Pinta was aware of the facts which made the confinement a war crime.

The same problem also appears in counts 5 and 6
which require that the Crown establish the absence of lawful authority as an
element of the offence of kidnapping.

A similar overlapping of the domestic and
international com­ponents also occurs in counts 3 and 4. Both allege robbery
arising out of the confiscation of valuables from persons held in the
brickyard. To establish robbery, the Crown was required to prove beyond a
reasonable doubt that Pinta did not act under any colour of right. The Crown
could meet this burden in one of two ways. First, by proving that no such right
existed and that Finta did not believe he had any such right. Secondly, the
Crown could prove that even though the law of Hungary authorized the seizure of
the valuables, the taking of the valuables constituted a crime against

humanity or a war crime and that Finta knew of
the facts which made the taking of the valuables a war crime or a crime against
humanity. If this second route was successfully pursued by the Crown, s.
7(3.74) precluded reliance on the local law as a basis for a colour of right
defence.

The second potential overlap flows from the
"positive" defences advanced by Finta. In addition to arguing that
the Crown had not established the essential elements of each charge, Finta also
advanced two "positive" defences which he contended justified or
excused his conduct. He relied on the exercise of the lawful authority defence,
and the obedience to military orders defence. If these defences were not
negated by the Crown, Finta's liability for the domestic component of the
charges against him could not be made out by the Crown. These defences
generated a further blending of the domestic and international components of
the offences.

For example, the domestic component of count 7
alleged that Finta committed manslaughter, in that he loaded people into
boxcars in circumstances which caused their death, or in that he caused the
death of those he placed in the boxcars by failing to provide certain basic
necessities when he was required to do so, thereby showing a wanton or reckless
disregard for the lives of those placed in the boxcars. In answer to this
charge, the defence contended in part that Finta was entitled to rely on s. 25
of the
Code.
That section reads in part:

25(1) Every one who is required .. . by law
to do anything in the administration or enforcement of the law

(a) ...

(b) as a peace officer .. .

(c) ...

(d)
...

is, if he acts on reasonable grounds,
justified in doing what he is required or authorized to do and in using as much
force as is necessary for that purpose.

That defence was available to Finta by virtue of
s. 7(3.73) of the
Code,
unless Finta's act constituted a crime against
humanity or a war crime, in which case s. 7(3.74) precluded reliance on s. 25
in so far as that reliance was premised in Hungarian law. To establish Finta's
culpability for manslaughter, the Crown was required to negate that defence.
The Crown could do so by establishing

— that the accused did not believe on reasonable
grounds that he had lawful authority to perform the acts which were said to
constitute the offence of manslaughter, or

—
that the accused used excessive force in performing those acts, or

—
that the acts in question constituted a crime against humanity and
Finta knew of the facts which gave those acts that quality.

The third alternative was made available to the
Crown by s. 7(3.74) which excludes reliance on local law where the act
constitutes a war crime or crime against humanity.

If, in order to negate the s. 25 defence, the
Crown was driven to the third of these alternatives, the jury could not decide
whether the defence had been negated and the crime of manslaughter made out
without deciding whether the acts constituted a crime against humanity and
whether Finta had the requisite knowledge.

On the evidence, the s. 25 defence was
potentially available on each count and the jury had to address the issues
outlined above in relation to each charge.

The common law defence of obedience to military
orders was also potentially applicable through s. 7(3.73) and, if applicable,
excused Finta's conduct and negated his liability for the domestic offences
alleged in each count. The onus rested on the Crown to prove beyond a
reasonable doubt that the defence was not available. The Crown could do so in
one of two ways:

—
by proving that Finta did not believe he acted under lawful orders,
or

—
by proving that the acts which constituted the domestic crimes
alleged in each count had the quality of a crime against humanity or a war
crime, that Finta had the requisite knowl­edge, and that Finta had a moral
choice to disobey those orders.

As with the s. 25 defence, the issues raised by
the obedience to military orders defence related to each count and raised very
real issues between the Crown and Finta.

This review of the indictment demonstrates that
there were not two separate packages of facts to be determined in this case,
one which could be assigned Ito a fact-finder who was responsible for domestic
matters, and the other to a different fact-finder who was responsible for the
international components of the offences. A decision with respect to Finta's
culpability for the domestic compo­nent of any of the offences alleged against
him could well have required findings of fact on issues which were identical to
those which had to be addressed in deciding whether the international component
of each offence had been made out.

4
. The position of the parties

a.
The Crown's position

The language of s. 7(3.71) lies at the core of
the Crown's position. For convenience we will repeat the subsection:

7(3.71) Notwithstanding anything in this
Act or any other Act, every person who, either before or after the coming into
force of this subsection, commits an act or omission outside Canada that
constitutes a war crime or a crime against humanity and that, if committed in
Canada, would constitute an offence against the laws of Canada in force at the
time of the act or omission shall be deemed to commit that act or omission in
Canada at that time if,

(a) at the time of the act or omission,

(i) that person is a Canadian citizen or is
employed by Canada in a civilian or military capacity,

(ii) that person is a citizen of, or is
employed in a civilian or military capacity by, a state that is engaged in an
armed conflict against Canada, or

(iii) the victim of the act or omission is
a Canadian citizen or a citizen of a state that is allied with Canada in an
armed conflict; or

(b) at the time of the act or omission,
Canada could, in conformity with international law, exercise jurisdiction over
the person with respect to the act or omission on the basis of the person's
presence in Canada and, subsequent to the time of the act or omission, the
person is present in Canada.

Mr. Amerasinghe, for the Crown, submits
that the section does not create new crimes, and does not give war crimes or
crimes against humanity the status of separate crimes. Instead, the section
gives limited extraterritorial effect to the other offence creating provisions
of the
Criminal Code
.
On this view, the allegations in the indictment
referable to the various provisions of the 1927
Code
constitute the
substance of the charges made against Finta. According to this argument, the
section extends the territorial jurisdiction of Canadian criminal courts to
Criminal
Code
offences committed outside Canada where those
Criminal Code
violations
amount to war crimes or crimes against humanity. The section achieves this
extraterritoriality by "deeming"
Crimi­nal Code
offences which
also constitute war crimes or crimes against humanity to have occurred within
Canada and hence within the territorial jurisdiction of Canadian criminal
courts.

Having distinguished between allegations which
go to the content of the crime alleged and allegations which go to the court's
territorial jurisdiction, Mr. Amerasinghe relies on
Balcombe
v.
The
Queen

(1954),
1954 CanLII 75 (SCC)
, 110 C.C.C. 146, [1954] S.C.R. 303
(per
Fauteux J. in
chambers), as authority for the proposition that issues going to

the territorial jurisdiction of the court must
be determined by the judge and not the jury, even where those issues have a
factual component. Mr. Amerasinghe refers to facts which are relevant to the
establishment of territorial jurisdiction as "jurisdictional facts".
He says that the question of whether Finta's acts constituted a crime against
humanity or a war crime were "jurisdictional facts" and were within
the domain of the trial judge.

b.
The respondent's position

Finta relies on the reasons and conclusions of
the trial judge and his position is best understood by a review of the trial
judge's reasons. His ruling was delivered after an extensive voir
dire
held
prior to the commencement of the evidence.

c
. The ruling of the trial judge

The trial judge accepted the Crown's argument
that
s. 7(3.71)
conferred a new jurisdiction on the court and that the
allegations that Finta's acts constituted war crimes or crimes against human­ity
went to the jurisdiction of the court. He also agreed, referring to
Balcombe,

that normally jurisdictional facts had to be resolved by the trial judge
and not by the jury. He went on to hold that the orthodox view could not
pertain in the unique circumstances before him and that it would be for the
jury to determine whether Finta's acts amounted to a war crime or a crime
against humanity.

He so held for four reasons. First, he
emphasized the unique nature of the jurisdictional facts raised by the
allegations. These jurisdictional facts were in and of themselves allegations
of criminal wrongdoing which, if established, operated by virtue of s. 7(3.74)
to deny to the accused certain substantive defences to the domestic component
of the charges. The above review of the indictment demonstrates the validity of
this conclusion.

Secondly, the trial judge contrasted the nature
of the factual issues raised by the allegation that Finta had committed war
crimes or crimes against humanity with the factual issues com­monly associated
with jurisdictional issues. In Finta's case, the allegations went to the very
root of his culpability. In a typical case like
Balcombe,
the jurisdictional
facts in dispute went to an issue (the provincial
sites
of the offence)
which had nothing to do with the accused's ultimate culpability. In the trial
judge's assessment, if he was to decide whether Finta committed a war crime or
a crime against humanity, he would be deciding in large measure Finta's
culpability. Such fact-finding was the essence of the jury's function.

Thirdly, the trial judge pointed to the
significant overlap which existed between factual issues relevant to the
jurisdictional facts

and those which were relevant to Finta's guilt
on the substantive charges.

Lastly, the trial judge referred to the immense
practical difficul­ties which would arise if he were to determine the
jurisdictional facts while the jury were to determine facts relating to Finta's
liability for the substantive
Criminal Code

offences. In describing
these difficulties, the trial judge made the logical assumption that he would
be required to determine all jurisdictional facts before the jury could
consider Finta's liability for the substantive offences. We will return to
those practical difficulties at a subsequent point in these reasons. However,
we note now that the trial judge's concerns were well founded and exist
regardless of the order in which the judge and the jury perform their
respective fact-finding functions.

The trial judge's closing words eloquently and
effectively sum­marize the reasons for his conclusion:

Although
Balcombe
decided that
jurisdictional facts such as
situs
are decided by the judge and not the
jury, the court noted in
Balcombe

that the facts in issue there did not
go to the guilt or innocence of the accused. This is therefore not a case like
Balcombe.

In this case
situe
is not in issue. In this case the jurisdictional
facts such as enslavement, deportation, persecution or the commission of any
other inhumane act by the accused are facts that go to his very guilt or
innocence. Such questions are for the jury. They go in this case to the very
root of the principle of trial by jury.

This is particularly so when an adverse
determination of those jurisdictional facts deprives the accused of important
legal rights including
Charter
rights, special pleas, and the very significant
defence of obedience to
de
facto
law.

To take these crucial issues of jurisdictional
fact away from the jury would deprive both him and the community of the right
to have a jury decide all the facts that go to the guilt or innocence of the
accused. Those facts will therefore be decided by the jury.

5
.
Analysis

a.
Does Balcombe apply

The Crown's argument stands or falls on the
applicability of the reasoning in
Balcombe

to the case at bar. In
Balcombe

the indictment alleged that the accused committed murder "... at the
County of Dundas in the Province of Ontario" [at p. 1461. He was tried and
convicted in Ontario by a court composed of a judge and jury. At trial, he
sought a directed verdict, arguing that the homicide had occurred in Quebec.
The trial judge dismissed the motion and the Court of Appeal affirmed his
ruling. The appellant then applied for leave to the Supreme Court of Canada,
arguing at p. 146:

"That the evidence does not
substantiate nor prove that the offence alleged was committed within the
province of Ontario and therefore there is no jurisdiction in any Ontario Court
to try the accused on the said charge."

In dismissing the application for leave to
appeal, Fauteux J. said at pp. 147-8:

That Marie Annie Carrier was murdered is
not open to question. And so far as the situs, where the fatal blows were
inflicted or where the death actually occurred, was material to determine
whether or not the accused was the author of the crime, the jury was
sufficiently directed. The submission is simply that they should have been
instructed to determine, as a matter related to jurisdiction and not as a
matter related to guilt or innocence, whether, upon the view taken by them of
the evidence, they were satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that either the
wounds were inflicted or the death occurred within the Province of Ontario.

The question of jurisdiction is a question
of law — consequently, for the presiding Judge — even if, to its determination,
consideration of the evidence is needed. It is a question strictly beyond the
field of these matters which under the law and particularly under the terms of
their oath, the jury have to consider. They are concerned only with the guilt
or innocence of the prisoner at the bar. Indeed the lawful fulfilment of their
duties rests on the assumed existence of the jurisdiction of the Court to try,
at the place where it is held, the accused for the crime charged. They are
concerned with facts as they may be related to guilt or innocence but not to
jurisdiction. There is nothing under the law entitling them, through the whole
course of the execution of their duties, to legally make any other
pronouncements but those as to which a general or special verdict is authorized
by law

The applicant also raised the point that
the evidence failed to establish that the offence charged was committed at the
County of Dundas as alleged in the indictment. This ground was also related to
the jurisdiction of the Court and as such must be disposed of in the same
manner as the preceding ones.

(Emphasis added.)

The Crown contends that the words of Fauteux J.
are equally applicable where the question is not where in Canada the offence
occurred, but rather whether the alleged crime occurred (or is deemed to have
occurred) in Canada at all. We disagree. The Crown's contention fails to
recognize the meaning of the word "jurisdiction" as it is used in
Balcombe

and to distinguish that concept of jurisdiction from another usage of the
word which refers to the territorial scope of the criminal
law.

The meaning of the word "jurisdiction"
is notoriously nebulous and varied:
R.
v.
Botting,
1966 CanLII 229 (ON CA)
, [1966]
3 C.C.C. 373 at p. 388, 56 D.L.R. (2d) 25 at p. 40, [1966] 2 O.R. 121 (C.A.).
In Salhany,
Canadian Criminal Procedure,
5th ed. (1989), it is said at
p. 17:

Jurisdiction over criminal offences may be
said to mean the power of a given court to inquire and determine whether or not
an alleged offence has been committed by a designated person and to apply the
penalty for an offence so determined.

This concept of jurisdiction, which describes
exactly the issue confronted in
Balcombe
,
is directed to the court's
authority to adjudicate and not to an accused's ultimate liability for the
offence charged.

The word "jurisdiction", as defined by
Salhany and used in
Balcombe

requires that one consider both the court's
authority over the accused person and
its
competence to adjudicate with
respect to the alleged offence. A court must have jurisdiction over both the
accused and the offence.

The dual nature of jurisdictional competence is
apparent from a reading of the provisions of Part XIV of the
Criminal Code
.
These
provisions, gathered together under the title "Jurisdiction", provide
the generally applicable rules governing jurisdiction on trials by indictment.
Section 470 provides the general rule regarding jurisdiction over the person.
That section vests jurisdiction over the person only where the court otherwise
has "the power to try an indictable offence". That power depends on
the court's jurisdiction over the particular offence which, in turn, is
predicated on a number of factors, including the nature of the offence, the
accused's election, and the
situs
of the offence. The last of these
factors was the relevant consideration in
Balcombe
.

The opening words of s. 478 of the
Code
provide
the generally applicable rule as regards a court's territorial jurisdiction
over a criminal offence:

478(1) Subject to this Act, a court in a
province shall not try an offence committed entirely in another province.

It was the predecessor of this section that was
relied on by the appellant in
Balcombe.
Subject to certain exceptions,
s. 478 clearly bars prosecution in the courts of one province for an offence
committed entirely in another province. The court must determine if the offence
was committed, at least in part, within the province before it decides the
