merits. That inquiry may require no more than reference to the face of the
indictment, or it may require an analysis of the elements of the charge, a
careful assessment of the evidence, and the application of judge-made rules
respecting the
situs
of crimes which involve conduct in more than one
province: see, e.g.,
R.
v.
Philips Appliances Ltd.
,
1968 CanLII 437 (ON CA)
, [1969] 2
C.C.C. 328 at pp. 332-3, 2 D.L.R. (3d) 558 at pp. 562-3, 57 C.P.R. 45, [1969] 1
O.R. 386 (Ont. C.A.);
Re Bigelow and The Queen
(1982),
1982 CanLII 2046 (ON CA)
, 69 C.C.C. (2d)
204, 37 O.R. (2d) 304, 28 R.F.L. (2d) 1 (C.A.); leave to appeal refused C.C.C.
loc.
cit. ,
45 N.R. 534
n. Regardless of the nature of the inquiry the judge must
decide the issue.

It is important to recognize, however, that s.
478 does not speak to the territorial reach of the
Criminal Code
.
If an
offence is committed entirely in a province other than that in which the
accused is to be tried, the act remains an offence under Canadian criminal law
Section 478 denies adjudicative authority to courts outside the province where
the crime occurred. If the court holds that the offence was committed outside
the province, it cannot acquit or convict the accused both because it has no
jurisdiction and because it has not decided the merits. The court must quash
the indictment.

Questions relating to the territorial scope of
an offence creating provision of the
Criminal Code

are also sometimes
referred to as jurisdictional questions, e.g., see
R.
v.
Libman

(1985),

1985 CanLII 51 (SCC)
, 21 C.C.C. (3d) 206, 21 D.L.R. (4th) 174, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 178;
Macleod
v.

A.-G. N.S.W
[1891] A.C. 455 (P.C.)
; Williams and Castel, Cana­dian
Criminal
Law: International and Transnational Aspects
(1981), at pp. 4-5. Used in
this sense, jurisdiction refers not to the adjudicative competence of any
court, but to the territorial reach of the legislation which creates the crime.

This distinction is well recognized in the
literature. The English law commissioners in their
Report on the Territorial
and Extra­territorial Extent of the Criminal Law
(1978), at p. 1, observe:

The word "jurisdiction" can be
confusing: in this report we are concerned primarily with jurisdiction in the
sense of the extent of the application of the criminal law. We are not
primarily concerned with the narrower question of the jurisdiction of a court
to try particular criminal cases, although we deal with some aspects of this
question .. .

The Law Reform Commission of Canada in
Extraterritorial
Jurisdiction,
Working Paper No. 37 (1984), at pp. 3-4 draws the same
distinction in somewhat different language:

In criminal law, in cases that involve
elements affecting more than one state the same two questions arise: (a) which
state's substantive criminal law applies, and (b) do the courts of that state
have jurisdiction to try the case?

While the same two questions arise in civil
and criminal cases, the same answers may cause quite different results, for it
is a well-established principle that the courts of one state will
not
enforce the criminal law
of other states.

To put it another way, if a court decides
that its own state's criminal law is not applicable in a case before it, then
it will not try the case. Hence it may be said that the choice of criminal law
is conclusive as to jurisdiction.
Neverthe­less it is important, in
considering the extraterritoriality of our criminal law, to bear in mind the
difference between the "applicability of law" on the one hand, and
jurisdiction of courts" on the other, because both must be provided for in
our legislation if criminal conduct outside Canada is to be punishable by a
court in Canada.

We have decided therefore to address in
this Paper both the "applicability" of Canadian criminal law and the
"jurisdiction" of Canadian criminal courts.

The term "jurisdiction" is
commonly used in several different senses in connection with criminal law; for
example, it is used in the sense of legislative power to enact criminal laws —
substantive and procedural; in the sense of executive power to enforce criminal
laws; and in a judicial sense. Internationally, it is used in the sense of the
sovereign power of one state vis-à-vis other states to make, apply and enforce
its criminal law. To avoid
confusion, we will use the term "jurisdiction" in this Paper in the
sense only of the power of a court to try a person for a criminal offence.

(Additional emphasis added.)

See also G. Williams, "Venue and the Ambit
of the Criminal Law" (1965), 81 M.L.R. 276, where the author by reference
to English legislation discusses the distinction between the territorial ambit
of legislation and the jurisdictional competence of a particu­lar court.

The structural organization of the
Criminal
Code

also recog­nizes that the territorial reach of the criminal law is
distinct from the territorial jurisdiction of a court. As indicated earlier,
the territorial jurisdiction of a court is dealt with in Part XIV entitled
"Jurisdiction" and speaks to the provincial
situs
of crimes.
Section 478 limits the power of all courts to the trial of indictable offences
which have a territorial nexus to the province where the court is located.

Section 6(2) sets out the generally applicable
rule with respect to the territorial scope of the criminal law:

6(2) Subject to this Act or any other Act
of Parliament, no person shall be convicted or discharged under section 736 of
an offence committed outside Canada.

Two distinctions between
ss. 6(2)
and 478 are
immediately apparent.
Section 6(2)
is found not in Part XIV but in Part I, the
general part of the
Code.
Part I deals with various aspects of the
criminal law but it does not speak to jurisdictional matters. Also, s. 6(2),
unlike s. 478, does not address a court's power to try offences, but instead
prohibits convictions. Section 6(2) forecloses culpability where the acts
occurred outside Canada. It does not merely deny jurisdictional competence.

The language of s. 6(2) is virtually identical
to that found in ss. 9, 13, 15 and 16, all of which bar convictions based
either on the nature of the act or on the status of the accused. For example,
s. 9 declares in part:

9. Notwithstanding anything in this Act or
any other Act, no person shall be convicted or discharged under section 736

(a) of an offence at common law ..

Section 9 holds that there can be no culpability
for common law offences because they are not crimes in the eyes of the Canadian
criminal
law.
Section 6(2) makes the same declaration (subject to Parliament
declaring to the contrary) with respect to offences which did not occur in
Canada.

In our view, the different treatment hi the
Criminal
Code

of territorial concerns as they relate to the national and provincial
situs

of crime reflects the essential difference between acts which are not
culpable because they did not occur in Canada, and acts which while culpable
are not triable in a particular court, because they occurred entirely outside
the province.

References to this distinction can be found in
the case-law.

In
R.
v.
Martin,
[1956] 2 Q.B. 272
(C.C.C.)
, Devlin J. had to decide if a section of the
Civil Aviation Act,
1949
rendered the accused criminally liable for possession of certain drugs
when the possession occurred on a British airplane travelling in the Far East.
He said at pp. 285-6:

There is a distinction, in my judgment,
between what I may call the nature of an offence and the ingredients which have
to be present before an offence is committed at all on the one hand, and, on
the other hand, the question of what courts are to assume or are to be given
jurisdiction when the offence has been committed.

In a crime that is the creation of a
statute, one must look to the terms of the statute for a definition of its
nature; and if the effect of the statute is limited territorially, then so is
the nature of the crime.

In
Treacy a Director of Public Prosecutions,
[1971]
A.C. 537, [1971] 1 All E.R. 110 (H.L.)
, the accused had sent a letter from England
to a woman in West Germany. In the letter he demanded money and threatened to
turn certain photographs over to her husband if he did not receive that money.
He was charged with blackmail. At trial he argued that as the letter was
received in West Germany the offence had occurred in West Germany and he could
not be tried in England. The argument failed at trial and in the Court of
Appeal. A majority of the House of Lords dismissed his further appeal. The
Court of Appeal and the majority of the House of Lords spoke in terms of the
jurisdiction; however, they clearly used the word in reference to the
territorial scope of the crime, not to the adjudicative authority of the court.

Lord Diplock made the distinction explicit at
pp. 559-60 A.C., pp. 119-20 All E.R.:

In view of the way in
which the question is framed and the wide-ranging
argument about "jurisdiction" before your Lordships' House,
I
am prompted

to state at the outset that the question
in this appeal is not whether the Central Criminal Court had jurisdiction to
try the defendant on that charge but whether the facts alleged and proved
against him amounted to a criminal offence under the English Act Parliament.

The fact that the appellant was arrested in
Greater London and committed for trial at the Central Criminal Court
unquestionably gave to that court jurisdiction to determine whether or not he
was guilty of the offence for which he was indicted. That offence was the
statutory offence of "blackmail" as defined in section 21 of the
Theft Act 1968. The Act creates a new code of offences of obtaining or handling
property or causing loss dishonestly or by other improper means. It supersedes
the previous penal enactments in this field of law, and by section 32(1)(a)
abolishes any previously existing offences at common law falling within that
field of crime. These are offences of which the victims are generally private
individuals. The only question for your Lordships' House is what did Parliament
mean when it enacted in 1968 that:

"A person is guilty of blackmail if,
with a view to gain for himself or another or with intent to cause loss to
another, he makes any unwar­ranted demand with menaces"?

The words are quite general. On a literal
construction they are satisfied wherever the unwarranted demand is made. No
mere application of rules of syntax or semantics can cut them down to "if
... he makes any unwar­ranted demand with menaces in England or Wales." If
the meaning of the subsection is to be qualified by implying some geographical
limitation as to the place where the unwarranted demand is made, the limitation
is to be derived not as a matter of linguistics from the actual words used but
from broader considerations of the purpose of the code in which the words
appear.

(Emphasis added.)

His Lordship then considered both the language
of the section and governing principles of international comity to determine
what, if any, territorial limits, Parliament had placed on the definition of
the crime of blackmail. His conclusions in that regard are irrelevant to this
appeal. However, his approach clearly distinguishes between jurisdictional
matters pertaining to a court's authority to try an offence, and substantive
matters referable to the very definition of the offence.

Lord Diplock's approach was adopted by Lord
Keith in
Director of Public Prosecutions
v.
Stonehouse,
[1978]
A.C. 55, [1977] 2 All E.R. 909 (H.L.)
. Stonehouse took out various life
insurance policies in England. He then pretended to have drowned off the coast
of Miami as part of a fraudulent scheme to obtain the proceeds of those
policies for his wife. The scheme failed when Stonehouse was sighted alive and
well after the "drowning". He was charged with attempting to obtain
the proceeds of the policies by deception. He argued that he could not be tried
in England because the acts said to constitute the attempt had occurred outside
England. In agree­ing with the rest of the House of Lords (and the Court of
Appeal)

that the argument failed, Lord Keith said at p.
90 A.C., p. 937 All E.R..

My Lords, the general principle of the
territoriality of crime is of great importance. The English courts do not
assert jurisdiction to try any person whether a citizen of this country or not,
for acts done in a foreign land.
The more correct approach is to say that
such an act cannot in principle
constitute a
crime
by
the
law

of England rather than
that
the
act
is
a
crime hut the
court does
not
have
jurisdiction.

(Emphasis added.)

R.
v.
Hetsberger

(1979),
1979 CanLII 2977 (ON CA)
, 47 C.C.C. (2d) 154 (Ont. C.A.), demonstrates that the distinction between
territorial jurisdiction and the territorial reach of the criminal law is also
recognized by this court. Hetsberger was charged with personation. He had
purchased an airplane ticket for a friend in a false name in order to assist
that friend in gaining entry to the United States. It was argued that the crime
of personation required an intention to gain an advantage and that in this case
the advantage was to be gained in the United States, thus rendering the conduct
no offence against a Canadian criminal law. In granting an extension of time
within which to appeal to this court, Weatherston J.A. observed at pp. 156-7:

It should be said at once that the question
in this case is not one of jurisdiction, but of the proper definition of the
offence created by s. 361(a). Parliament has the power to make any physical act
done in Canada crime, and any person even temporarily in Canada owes a local
allegiance to the law of Canada.

The only question is whether some
limitation should be placed on the plain words of the section so as to restrict
its operation to cases where the evil effect of its breach is felt in Canada.

On the appeal (
1980 CanLII 2986 (ON CA)
, 51 C.C.C. (2d) 257), this court
adopted the approach taken by Weatherston J.A. and went on to hold that there
was no such limitation on the plain meaning of the words in the section.

These authorities clearly differentiate between
territorial
sites
as it relates to a court's jurisdiction and the
territorial ambit of an offence-creating provision. The latter constitutes part
of the definition of the offence. If the offence alleged did not occur within
the territorial reach of crime as defined by Parliament, there is no crime in
the eyes of the Canadian criminal law.

Balcombe
speaks
only to the jurisdictional authority of a particular court and not to the
territorial aspect of the substantive definition of the offence.
Balcombe
is
not authority for the proposition that questions going to the national
sites

of the offence

alleged raise "jurisdictional facts"
which must be determined by the judge and not the jury.

b.
The significance of a finding that an act
is beyond the territorial scope of the criminal law

Absent some statutory provision to the contrary,
s. 6(2) limits the territorial scope of all
Criminal Code

offences to
Canada. The common law arrived at the same result:
Cox
v.
Army
Council,
[1963] A.C. 48 at pp. 67-9, [1962] 1 All E.R. 880 at pp. 882-3
(P.C.)
;
Air-India
v.
Wiggins,
[1980] 1 All E.R. 192 (Q.B.)
. An
act that if committed in Canada would be an offence against the
Criminal
Code
is not an offence if the act is committed outside Canada. The Law
Reform Commission of Canada in
Extraterrito­rial Jurisdiction,
makes the
point when describing the effect of the territoriality principle at p. 13:

As in English legislation, the general
rule, that is, the territorial principle, is not stated expressly in Canadian
legislation. But it is implicit in the way in which the offence-creating
sections of the
Criminal Code

and of other criminal enactments of Canada
are drafted; that is, no mention is made in an offence-creating section as to
the
locus
of the conduct unless the section is to be applicable to
conduct outside Canada, and in that event, the section expressly says so. For
example, compare
sections 218
and
58
of the
Criminal Code
which read in
part:

"218(1) Every one who commits first
degree murder or second degree murder is guilty of an indictable offence and
shall be sentenced to imprisonment for life.

"58(1) Every one who,
while in or
out of Canada, (a)
forges a passport ... is guilty of an indictable offence
and is liable to imprison­ment for fourteen years."

Thus, it is not an offence under
section
218
to commit murder outside Canada, but it is an offence under
section 58
to
forge a (Canadian) passport outside Canada.

(Emphasis added.)

The position taken by the Law Reform Commission
finds full support in
Bolduc
v.
Quebec (Attorney-General)

(1982),

1982 CanLII 224 (SCC)
, 68 C.C.C. (2d) 413 at p. 419, 137 D.L.R. (3d) 674 at p. 681, [1982] 1 S.C.R.
573. Chouinard J., writing for the court, said:

... apart from the exceptions which we have
seen such as piracy, in which an offence committed in another country
constitutes an offence punishable in Canada, an offence is always created in
Canada in terms of its territory. When the
Criminal Code

makes robbery
an offence it refers to robbery committed in Canada, and not robbery committed
in New York: however, it is not necessary to say this in every case, because it
is self-evident and is in keeping with s. 5(2) [now s. 6(2)] of the
Code.

A similar view of the effect of the
territoriality principle is found in
R.
v.
Walkem
(1908),
1908 CanLII 232 (BC SC)
, 14
C.C.C. 122 at pp. 132-3, 8 W.L.R. 857, 14 B.C.R. 1 (S.C.);
R.
v.
Selkirk,

1964 CanLII 143 (ON CA)
, [1965] 2 G.C.C. 353 at pp. 358-9, [1965] 2 O.R. 168, 44 C.R. 170 (C.A.),
and
R.
v.
Stojadinovic,
1966 CanLII 211 (ON CA)
, [1967] 2 C.C.C. 88 at pp. 89-90, [1967] 1
O.R. 388 (C.A.). These cases all hold that where the alleged offence is
committed beyond the borders of Canada there is no breach of the
Criminal
Code
.
In so far as these cases purport to define when it can be said that
an offence occurred in Canada, they reflect a somewhat narrow view which has
been overtaken by
Libman.
However, the conclusion that conduct committed
outside Canada "cannot, in the eye of our law, be an offence against our
law (unless indeed made so by statute)" (per Clement J. in
Walkem
)
remains
valid.

If the Crown fails to prove that the alleged
crime occurred within Canada, the Crown has failed to prove an averment which
is essential to culpability. Reference to three authorities will suffice to
make the point.

In
R.
v.
Baldini and Gullekson
(1984),

1984 ABCA 42 (CanLII)
, 39 C.R. (3d) 43, 31 Alta. L.R. (2d) 69, 51 A.R. 89 (C.A.), the accused were
charged with conspiring to steal a truck which the indictment alleged was
located near Edmonton, Alberta. At trial, an agreement to steal a truck was
established by direct evidence; however, the evidence was equivocal as to the
location of the truck. It could not be said whether the truck was inside Canada
or outside Canada. In quashing the appellant's conviction on the conspiracy
charge, McGillivray C.J.A. for the court said at pp. 47-9:

To my mind this is not a case of the Crown
failing to prove merely a particular of the charge where other particulars
leave the accused in no doubt as to what is alleged against him. This is a case
where an essential ingredient of the conspiracy has not been proven, namely,
that there was an agreement to commit an indictable offence in Edmonton or,
indeed, anywhere else in Canada. Had the Crown's case shown that Gullekson was
calling from Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, or Prince George, British Columbia, I
would have thought that, although the Crown alleged that the theft was to take
place in Edmonton, this would not have affected the essence of the charge,
which was a conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in Canada.

In my opinion, the
Crown has simply failed to prove what is alleged, namely, an agreement to
commit an indictable offence in Canada. For the very reason that the learned
trial judge acquitted Gullekson of attempted theft, he should have acquitted on
the conspiracy and counselling counts. Clearly there was a conspiracy, but the
evidence fails to show that it was to commit or counsel an indictable offence
in Canada. The verdict of acquittal on the attempted theft charge and the
convictions on the conspiracy and counsel charge are inconsistent.

R.
v.
Gauthier

(1983),
1983 CanLII 4045 (NB CA)
, 51 N.B.R. (2d) 90 (C.A.), raised a similar issue to that canvassed
in
Baldini
.
The accused was charged with conspiring to traffic in a
narcotic contrary to s. 423(1)(d) (now s. 465(1)(c)). The evidence established
that other individuals had conspired to traffic in narcotics in New Brunswick
and that the accused, while in Maine, had agreed to supply these individuals
with narcotics. The trial judge directed an acquittal on the basis that the
court had no jurisdiction because the conspiracy involved an agreement made in
Maine to traffic in narcotics in Maine.

The Court of Appeal affirmed the acquittal but
in doing so did not rest their conclusion on any want of jurisdiction. Instead,
the court held that the indictment alleged a conspiracy to traffic in narcotics
in New Brunswick and that the Crown had offered no evidence from which it could
be inferred that the accused was a member of any such conspiracy. The Crown had
failed to prove that Gauthier conspired to traffic in Canada and he was
entitled to an acquittal for that reason.

R.
v.
Bachrack

(1913),
1913 CanLII 530 (ON SCAD)
, 21 C.C.C. 257, 11 D.L.R. 522, 28 O.L.R. 32 (S.C. App. Div.), was a
case where the accused was charged with conspiracy to procure an abortion. The
abortion actually took place in the United States. On appeal from his
conviction, it was argued that he could not be convicted upon proof that the
agreement made in Canada contemplated the commission of the abortion outside
Canada. It was further argued that the trial judge should not have admitted
evidence related to activities in the United States.

The court had little sympathy for the argument
that an agree­ment entered into in Canada to commit a crime outside Canada was
not indictable in Canada. The court went on to consider the case on the basis
that the Crown was required to prove that the object of the conspiracy was to
take place in Canada. Meredith J.A., for the court, said at pp. 265-6 C.C.C.,
p. 528 D.L.R.:

[I]f the law were as contended for, there
would yet be two things to be proved: (1) a conspiracy to do the act; and (2)
to do it within the jurisdiction; and so the evidence as to what took place
without the jurisdiction might be the best of evidence for the Crown on the
first question; as well as helpful to the prisoners on the question of the
place where the thing was to be done. The prisoners wholly denied any
conspiracy to procure an abortion; what took place in the State of New York was
the strongest kind of evidence that they were guilty of such a conspiracy; and
the prosecution, giving it for that purpose, had to take the chances of its
effect as to the place where the wrong was to be done; chances which, in view
of what was proved to have taken place in this Province, might confidently be
taken. There was evidence upon which any jury might find that the prisoners had
conspired to procure the

abortion in Toronto; but, finding it
difficult, if not impossible, to succeed in their nefarious design there, went
further afield.

(Emphasis added.)

As these cases demonstrate, in order to prove
the commission of an offence (barring some extraterritorial statutory
provision), the Crown must prove that the alleged offence occurred in Canada.
If the Crown fails to prove that the offence occurred in Canada, the prosecution
fails, not for want of the trial court's jurisdiction, but because the Crown
has failed to prove that the offence as defined in the
Code
was
committed by the accused. Failure to prove the national
situs
of the
offence is not qualitatively different from a failure to prove any other
essential element of the
actus reus
or
mens rea.
Indeed, the
national
situs
of the offence can be seen as one aspect of the
actus
reus.
The failure to prove any essential element of the offence alleged,
including that it occurred in Canada, necessitates the acquittal of the
accused.

It follows that because the Crown must establish
that an offence occurred in Canada as a step in establishing the accused's
guilt, the question whether the act occurred in Canada relates "to guilt
or innocence"
(per
Fauteux J. in
Balcombe

[at p. 147]), and
must be determined by the jury based on its assessment of the evidence:
Director
of Public Prosecutions
v.
Stonehouse, per
Lord Salmon at p. 78 A.C.,
p. 926 All E.R.

That is not to say that the trial judge may not
have to decide questions relating to the territorial scope of a particular
offence. The trial judge may have to address the question on a motion to quash
an indictment brought pursuant to s. 581 of the
Code,
where it is said
that the indictment alleges an offence which occurred outside Canada. Such an
allegation amounts to an assertion that the indictment does not charge an
offence known to
law.

The trial judge may also have to consider the
question of the territorial reach of a particular offence on a motion for a
directed verdict where it is argued that there is no evidence from which a
reasonable jury could conclude that the offence occurred in Can­ada. Finally,
in cases where there is a live issue at the conclusion of the evidence as to
whether the offence occurred in Canada, the trial judge will have to provide
the jury with the legal rules necessary to determine that factual question.

These problems are not unique to questions
arising out of the territorial scope of a particular offence but may arise in
respect of any element which is essential to the Crown's proof of the offence
alleged.

c. Does s.
7(3.71)
refer to the
jurisdiction of a court or to the territorial scope of the offences referred to
in that subsection

Bearing in mind the distinction developed above,
one turns to the language of s. 7(3.71). We will repeat the section once more:

7(3.71) Notwithstanding anything in this
Act or any other Act, every person who, either before or after the coming into
force of this subsection, commits an act or omission outside Canada that
constitutes a war crime or a crime against humanity and that, if committed in
Canada, would constitute an offence against the laws of Canada in force at the
time of the act or omission shall be deemed to commit that act or omission in
Canada at that time if,

(a) at the time of the act or omission,

(i) that person is a Canadian citizen or is
employed by Canada in a civilian or military capacity,

(ii) that person is a citizen of, or is
employed in a civilian or military capacity by, a state that is engaged in an
armed conflict against Canada, or

(iii) the victim of the act or omission is
a Canadian citizen or a citizen of a state that is allied with Canada in an
armed conflict; or

(b)
at the
time of the act or omission, Canada could, in conformity with international
law, exercise jurisdiction over the person with respect to the act or omission
on the basis of the person's presence in Canada and, subsequent to the time of
the act or omission, the person is present in Canada.

The section provides an express exception to the
general territorial principle set out in s. 6(2). It is the antithesis of the
normal rule; it not only extends the criminal law beyond Canada, it also
specifically provides that the section has no application in Canada. The act or
omission said to constitute the offence must occur "outside Canada".

The section also says nothing about the
jurisdiction of any Canadian court to try the offences referred to in the
section. Jurisdiction is, however, specifically referred to in s. 7(5) which
provides:

7(5) Where a person is alleged to have
committed an act or omission that is an offence by virtue of this section,
proceedings in respect of that offence may, whether or not that person is in
Canada, be commenced in any territorial division in Canada and the accused may
be tried and punished in respect of that offence in the same manner as if the
offence had been committed in that territorial division.

(5.1) For greater certainty, the provisions
of this Act relating to

(a) requirements that an accused appear at
and be present during proceedings, and

(b)
the
exceptions to those requirements,

apply to proceedings commenced in any
territorial division pursuant to subsection (5).

As can be seen, s. 7(5) addresses the
territorial aspect of a court's jurisdiction by providing that any territorial
division (i.e., province, county or other judicial division) in Canada has
jurisdic­tion to try an offence referred to in s. 7(3.71). The section renders
the very jurisdictional issue raised in
Balcombe

irrelevant to
prosecutions based on s. 7(3.71).

Section 7(3.71) has its genesis in the Report of
the Commission of Inquiry on War Criminals. The commission was alert to the
distinction between the territorial scope of offence-creating provi­sions and
the territorial jurisdiction of particular courts. In recommending that the
Code

be amended to provide for the prosecution of war crimes and crimes against
humanity, the commission referred, at pp. 153 and 165, to several basic require­ments
of any such legislation, one of which was that the legislation "contain an
express grant of jurisdiction to specific Canadian courts" (pp. 153, 165).
In recommending that a provision dealing with war crimes and crimes against
humanity be added to s. 6 of the
Code
(now
s. 7
), the commission said at p.
165:

The Code must contain an express grant of
jurisdiction to the courts in Canada. It has been suggested that the matter be
entrusted to the courts of the territorial division in Canada where the suspect
is found. However, ss. 6(3) (now ss. 7(5)] was replaced in 1985 and the new
wording is so wide that it can apply without any change to the new provisions
concerning war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Clearly, the Deschênes Commission saw s. 7(5) as
the operative territorial jurisdiction provision.

The legislation proposed by the Deschênes
Commission was adopted by Parliament, subject to certain changes in the
definitions of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Parliament clearly
intended to, and did address in s. 7(5), the territorial jurisdiction of
Canadian courts to try offences referred to in s. 7(3.71).

In our opinion, s. 7(3.71) speaks not to the
jurisdiction of the court but to the territorial scope of the offences referred
to in that section. It does so by expanding the territorial reach of the
criminal law beyond Canada to the rest of the world whenever the acts or
omissions in question meet the dual criminality requirement of the section.

For example, to establish the commission of a
"normal" charge of robbery the Crown must prove that the robbery
occurred in Canada. Where the Crown alleges robbery contrary to s. 7(3.71),

instead of proving that the robbery occurred in
Canada, the Crown must prove that:

‑‑ had the act occurred in Canada,
it would have amounted to robbery under the then operative
Criminal Code
,
and

‑‑ the act amounted to a war crime
or a crime against humanity.

These two requirements replace the normal
territorial require­ment set out in s. 6(2) of the
Code,
and by the
operation of the legal fiction in s. 7(3.71), deem the acts to have occurred in
Canada assuming the requirements of s. 7(3.71)(a) or
(b)
are met.

In the "normal" case, absent proof
that the robbery occurred in Canada, there is no offence proved and the accused
must be acquitted. Equally, where the Crown alleges robbery contrary to s.
7(3.71) but fails to prove that the act would have constituted robbery under
the
Code
extant at the time the acts were done, and that the acts
constituted a war crime or crime against humanity, there is no crime proved and
the accused must be acquitted.

Finally, in the "normal" case, the
jury decides whether the Crown has proved the offence occurred in Canada in the
course of deciding whether the Crown has proved the accused's guilt. Similarly,
where robbery is alleged but it is said that the act is an offence by virtue of
s. 7(3.71), it is for the jury to decide whether the requirements which bring
the conduct within the territorial reach of the criminal law have been made out
by the Crown.

This interpretation of s. 7(3.71) is consistent
with the interpret­ation placed on the parts of s. 465 which deal with
extraterritorial conspiracies. In
Bolduc
,
the court was required to
interpret s. 465(3) (then
s. 423(3)
), which reads:

465(3) Every one who, while in Canada,
conspires with anyone to do anything referred to in subsection (1) in a place
outside Canada that is an offence under the laws of that place shall be deemed
to have conspired to do that thing in Canada.

In interpreting the section, Chouinard
J.
said at p. 417
C.C.C., p. 678 D.L.R.:

It is apparent on its face that this
subsection does not create on offence. It creates a presumption of
territoriality so as to make the conspiracy an offence punishable in Canada.
Where, as in the case at bar, persons conspire in Canada to effect an unlawful
purpose in the United States, which would not in itself be an offence
punishable in Canada, they "shall be deemed to have conspired to do in
Canada that thing". The result is to introduce the essential aspect which
would otherwise be absent, and to make the offence punishable in Canada.

(Emphasis added.)

We read this passage as meaning that the effect
of s. 465(3) is to substitute for the usual territoriality requirement a deemed
territo­riality requirement which is met by proof that the object of the
agreement is unlawful in both Canada and the country where it is to be
performed. The section speaks not to the jurisdiction of any court but to the
elements of the offence which must be proved to establish culpability, one of
which is the aforementioned double criminality. Section 465(3), like s.
7(3.71), deems an act to have occurred in Canada if a dual criminality
requirement is met.

La Forest J. in
Libman
,
at p. 234
C.C.C., p. 202 D.L.R., interprets s. 465(3) (then
s. 423(3)
) in the same way.
He said:

Parliament has provided, in
s. 423(3)
of
the
Criminal Code
,
that a person who conspires to do anything referred
to in
s. 423(1)
and
(2)
in a place outside Canada that is an offence there
shall be deemed to have conspired to do that thing in Canada.
In
establishing
an
offence under that provision it is necessary not only to
prove that the accused violated foreign law outside Canada, but also that the
act would have constituted a crime in Canada .. .

(Emphasis added.)

Section 465(3) may be compared with s. 465(5).
In
R.
v.
Lai and
Lau (1985),
1985 CanLII 665 (BC CA)
, 24 C.C.C. (3d) 237 at p. 242
(B.C.C.A.), s. 465(5) (then s. 423(5)) was identified as the section which
addressed the territorial jurisdiction of a court in cases where an
extraterritorial conspiracy is alleged. It reads:

465(5) Where a person is alleged to have
conspired to do anything that is an offence by virtue of subsection (3) or (4),
proceedings in respect of that offence may, whether or not that person is in
Canada, be commenced in any territorial division in Canada, and the accused may
be tried and punished in respect of that offence in the same manner as if the
offence had been committed in that territorial division.

Clearly, s. 465(5) parallels s. 7(5) just as s.
465(3) parallels s. 7(3.71). In our view, the pronouncements made with respect
to the conspiracy provisions apply fully to s. 7(3.71) and (5). Indeed,
Chouinard J. in
Bolduc
,
at p. 417 C.C.C., p. 678 D.L.R., appeared to
equate those parts of
s. 7
(then s. 6) which give extraterritorial effect to
parts of the
Criminal Code

in certain situations, with s. 465(3). He
referred specifically to
s. 7(4)
(then s. 6(2)) which provides:

7(4) Every one who, while employed as an
employee within the meaning of the
Public Service EmploymentAct
in a
place outside Canada commits an act or omission in that place that is an
offence under the laws of that place and that, if committed in Canada, would be
an offence punishable by indictment shall be deemed to have committed that act
or omission in Canada.

The format used in s. 7(4) is very similar to
that used in s. 7(3.71).

To borrow the language of La Forest J. in
Libman

quoted above, in establishing an offence under s. 7(3.71), it is necessary
not only that the act would have amounted to a crime in Canada but also that it
constituted a war crime or a crime against humanity: see also Law Reform
Commission of Canada,
Extraterritoriality,
at p. 142. Both elements
taken together make up the criminal conduct prohibited by s. 7(3.71).

Section 7(3.71) also emulates Canada's
pre-existing war crimes legislation, the
Geneva Conventions Act,
S.C.
1985, c. G-3.
Section 3(1)
reads:

3(1) Any grave breach of any of the
Geneva
Conventions
of 1949, as therein defined, that would, if committed in
Canada, be an offence under any provision of the
Criminal Code

or other
Act of the Parliament of Canada, is an offence under such provisions of the
Criminal
Code
or other Act if committed outside Canada.

Section 3(2) provides:

3(2) Where a person has committed an act or
omission that is an offence by virtue of this section, the offence is within
the competence of and may be tried and punished by the court having
jurisdiction in respect of similar offences in the place in Canada where that
person is found in the same manner as if the offence had been committed in that
place, or by any other court to which jurisdiction has been lawfully
transferred.

Section 3(1) parallels s. 7(3.71) in that it
makes grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 committed outside Canada
justiciable in Canada if the acts would also have been a breach of the
Criminal
Code

or some other Act had they occurred in Canada. Like s. 7(3.71), s.
3(1) of the
Geneva Conventions Act

defines the offence by reference to a
double criminality standard, that is, the act must be a grave breach of the
Geneva Conventions of 1949 and an offence against the
Criminal Code
or
some other Act of Parliament.

Section 3(2)
of the
Geneva Conventions Act

indicates
which courts have territorial jurisdiction to try the offences referred to in
s. 3(1) and is similar to
s. 7(5)
.

The Law Reform Commission of Canada in
Extraterritoriality

at pp. 84-6 accurately refers to
s. 3(2)
of the
Geneva Conventions Act

as
the jurisdictional provision and s. 3(1) of the Act as the section which
defines the offences so as to give them extraterrit­orial effect. The same
descriptions fit s. 7(5) and (3.71) respectively.

The language of s. 7(3.71) leaves no doubt as to
its purpose. It was designed to give offences created by the
Criminal Code

extraterritorial
scope provided that the relevant act or omission would have constituted an
offence against the
Criminal Code

when it was committed had it occurred in Canada,
and provided that the relevant act or omission constituted a war crime or a
crime against humanity. Section 7(3.71) defines the conduct which by virtue of
that section constitutes a breach of the criminal law of Canada. All of the
requirements of that section are essential elements of the offence. As in any criminal
trial by jury, it is for the jury to determine on all of the evidence whether
the Crown has established each essential element beyond a reasonable doubt.
Consequently, it was for the jury to determine whether the acts or omissions
which they held to be attributable to Finta constituted a war crime or a crime
against humanity.

As is apparent, we arrive at the same conclusion
reached by the trial judge, although we interpret s. 7(3.71) differently. We do
not regard the allegations that Finta's acts or omissions constituted war
crimes or crimes against humanity as going to the jurisdiction of the trial
court so as to bring them within the purview of the judgment in
Balcombe
.
Instead,
we view these issues as integral to the fundamental question of whether Finta
committed the offences which were alleged against him in the indictment. We see
no basis in the language of s. 7(3.71) for distinguishing between issues
relating to whether the acts or omissions constituted war crimes or crimes
against humanity and issues relating to whether the acts or omissions would
have constituted an offence against the laws of Canada, extant at the time the
acts were committed. The two issues together combine to define the culpable
conduct criminalized by the section. Logically, if one issue raises a
"jurisdictional fact" so too must the other. If both issues go to
jurisdiction, the jury is left with nothing to decide.

We make one further observation relating to the
language of s. 7(3.71). The Crown's position rests on the contention that it is
the status of Finta's acts or omissions as war crimes or crimes against
humanity which triggers the deeming provision so as to bring the conduct within
the territorial jurisdiction of Canadian courts. We have set out at length the
reasons for which we regard this as a misconception of the section. However,
even assuming that the Crown is correct in its contention that the act which
triggers the deeming effect of s. 7(3.71) is a jurisdictional fact, a careful
reading of the section reveals that it is not the fact that the acts constitute
war crimes or crimes against humanity which triggers the deeming action within
the section. Rather, the acts or omissions are deemed to have been committed in
Canada if any of the facts referred to in s. 7(3.71)(a) or
(b)
are
established. The facts in para. (a) relate to the status of the accused or the
victims,

while the facts in para.
(b)
relate to
what is known as the principle of universal jurisdiction.

Consequently, even if the Crown is correct in
its contention that facts which must be established to activate a section which
deems certain conduct to have occurred in Canada are jurisdictional facts, the
Crown misreads s. 7(3.71) when it argues that it is the fact that the acts
constitute a war crime or crime against humanity which deems the conduct to
have occurred in Canada.

d.
Other considerations
(1)
The right
to trial by jury

The conclusion, that it is for the jury to
determine whether Finta's acts constituted a war crime or a crime against
humanity, rests on the fundamental distinction between matters going to the
jurisdiction of a particular court and those going to the substantive
definition of the offence alleged, and on the plain reading of s. 7(3.71). Two
additional factors, both of which were relied on by the trial judge, fortify
our conclusion.

The first relates to the function of a jury in a
criminal case. It is a basic tenet of our criminal law that in cases tried by a
jury, it is the jury which must decide the guilt or innocence of the accused. Findings
of fact which are germane to that task must be left to the jury. As Cory
J.
put
it in
R.
v.
Kirkness
(1990),
1990 CanLII 57 (SCC)
, 60 C.C.C. (3d) 97 at p. 123, [1990]
3 S.C.R. 74, 1 C.R. (4th) 91:

It is not members of the judiciary, but
rather the members of the jury, sitting as members of the community, who make
the decision as to guilt or innocence which is so vitally important both to the
individual accused and the community.

Similarly, Sopinka J. in
R.
v.
Morin
(1988),

1988 CanLII 8 (SCC)
, 44 C.C.C. (3d) 193 at p. 211, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 345, 66 C.R. (3d) 1, said:
"The reason we have juries is so that lay persons and not lawyers decide
the facts."

Many have argued that trial by jury enhances the
reliability of the fact-finding process, makes that process more accountable to
and acceptable by the public, serves to educate the public as to the operation
of the criminal justice system, and provides a valuable protection against the
arbitrary exercise of power by judges and prosecutors. Others regard these
supposed values as part of a legal mythology and maintain that the jury system
provides neither accurate results nor a safe harbour against the arbitrary
exercise of power. These competing views are referred to by the Law Reform
Commission of Canada in
The Jury in Criminal Trials,
Working Paper 27
(1980), ch. 2.

It is doubtful that either side of the debate
will ever prove its case.
Section 11(f)
of the
Charter
has, however, resolved
the debate in favour of the proponents of the jury system by giving constitu­tional
protection to trial by jury in serious criminal cases. Section 11(f) provides:

11. Any person charged with an offence has
the right

(f)
except
in cases of an offence under military law tried before a

military tribunal, to the benefit of trial
by jury where the maximum

punishment for the offence is imprisonment
for five years or a more

severe punishment;

The nature of the right guaranteed by s. 11(f)
and its central role in the criminal justice system was described by Blair J.A.
in
R. v. Bryant
(1984),
1984 CanLII 2026 (ON CA)
, 16 C.C.C. (3d) 408 at p. 423, 15 D.L.R. (4th) 66
at p. 81, 48 O.R. (2d) 732 (C.A.):

[T]he right of trial by jury is not only an
essential part of our criminal justice system but also is an important
constitutional guarantee of the rights of the individual in our democratic
society. In all common law countries it has, for this reason, been treated as
almost sacrosanct and has been interfered with only to a minimal extent ... Now
that the right of jury trial is entrenched in our Constitution it is preserved
both from open attack or subtle erosion.

See also
R.
v.
Tttrpin
(1989),
1989 CanLII 98 (SCC)
, 48
C.C.C. (3d) 8 at p. 18, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1296, 69 C.R. (3d) 97.

In
R. v. Mack
(1988),
1988 CanLII 24 (SCC)
, 44 C.G.C. (3d) 513
at p. 565, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 903, 67 C.R. (3d) 1, the court was required to
decide whether the judge or jury should determine if the defence of entrapment
had been made out. Lamer J. for the court held that it was a matter for the
trial judge to decide after the jury returned its verdict on the merits of the
case. He referred to the possible impact of
s.
11(f)
of the
Charter
on
the procedure he had outlined:

Because the guilt or innocence of the
accused is not in issue at the time an entrapment claim is to be decided, the
right of an accused to the benefit of a jury trial in
s. 11(f)
of the
Charter

is in no way infringed.

(Additional emphasis added.)

These words sound a clear warning; any statutory
or judge-made rule which transfers the fact-finding function as it relates to
issues going to the culpability of the accused, from the jury to a judge is, at
the very least, constitutionally suspect.

The "benefit of trial by jury" must
refer to a trial in which the jury performs its traditional role as the
fact-finder and ultimate arbiter of the accused's guilt. The quintessence of
the jury's role rests in its obligation to blend the law as provided by the
judge with the facts as found by the jury to produce a verdict: see Devlin,
"The Conscience of the Jury" (1991), 107 L.Q.R. 398. If the jury's

authority to determine facts which are relevant
to culpability is transferred to the judge, its ability to reach just verdict
is compromised. Derogation from the fact-finding function of the jury would
"erode" an accused's right to the benefit of trial by jury.

There can be no doubt that the allegations that
Finta committed war crimes and crimes against humanity go to his culpability.
Without these allegations Canada has no interest in and no justification for
bringing Finta before a Canadian criminal court to answer for his conduct. The
moral claim that Canada has against those who have committed the offences
referred to in s. 7(3.71) outside Canada comes not from the mere alleged
violation of Canadian domestic criminal law but from the additional allegation
that the violation reached the dimension and status of a war crime or a crime against
humanity. Canada's international obligation to prosecute such offences rests on
the same foundation.

The statement made by the Minister of Justice
when the Deschênes Commission Report was tabled in the House of Com­mons (House
of Commons of Canada,
Debates,
Second Session — Thirty-Third Parliament,
vol. VII, at p. 4078 (March 12, 1987)), makes it abundantly clear that the
government proposed to introduce legislation, the purpose of which was to call
to account before Canadian courts, those who had engaged in war crimes and
crimes against humanity:

Although the commission found that the
number of war criminals in Canada has been greatly exaggerated, it is clear
that Canadians are not and will not be satisfied with the notion that
individuals guilty of war crimes during the course of World War II should find
in Canada a safe haven from the processes of justice. The Government must be
concerned if even one individual guilty of war crimes has found a refuge from
justice here.

Similar statements were made when the Bill
containing what is now s. 7(3.71) received second reading (House of Commons of
Canada,
Debates,
Second Session — Thirty-Third Parliament, vol. IV at
pp. 8264-65 (August 27, 1987)).

The legislation as passed does not suggest any
modification of the traditional role of the jury. Quite the contrary. Section
7(3.72) provides:

7(3.72) Any proceedings with respect to an
act or omission referred to in subsection (3.71) shall be conducted in
accordance with the laws of evidence and procedure in force at the time of the
proceedings.

This section reflects the position taken in the
Deschênes Com­mission Report, at p. 167:

It goes without saying that the right of
the accused to trial by jury should be protected. It has been argued in some
quarters that there is no room for jury trials in the matter of war crimes: the
Commission disagrees. As these

prosecutions should be heard before
ordinary courts following ordinary rules of evidence, in the same vein the
traditional right to jury trial should be recognized to the accused. Indeed,
this right is enshrined in
art. 11(f)
of the
Charter
.

In our opinion, Pinta is said to merit
prosecution, conviction and punishment in Canada for acts committed almost 45
years ago in Hungary because those acts reached the level of war crimes or
crimes against humanity. To remove those issues from the jury is to deny to
Finta the benefit of trial by jury on the very issues which are the
raison
d'être
for his prosecution in Canada.

In interpreting
Criminal Code

provisions,
a court should factor in values reflected in the
Charter
: see
R.
v.
Landry

(1991),
1991 CanLII 114 (SCC)
, 62 C.C.C. (3d) 117 at p. 127, [1991] 1 S.C.R. 99, 2 C.R. (4th) 268,

per
McLachlin J. (in dissent on another point);
R. v. Collins
(1989),

1989 CanLII 264 (ON CA)
, 48 C.C.C. (3d) 343 at pp. 373-4, 69 C.R. (3d) 235, 41 C.R.R. 193 (Ont. C.A.).
The value reflected in
s. 11(f)
of the Charter would be seriously undermined if
s. 7(3.71) were interpreted so as to leave the jury powerless to determine
factual issues central to Finta's guilt. The language of the section does not
suggest or even hint at a derogation from the traditional role of the jury. The
trial judge's ruling is entirely consistent with the value underlying s. 11(f)
of the Charter.

(2)
The potential procedural quagmire

The argument that the fact-finding should be
split between the judge and jury along international and domestic lines would
have had potentially significant ramifications on the conduct of the trial. The
trial judge was very much alive to the procedural problems which would arise if
he accepted the Crown's argument. He was right to approach the interpretation
of s. 7(3.71) with an eye to the practical effect of his interpretation of the
section on his ability to conduct a trial effectively with a jury. Whatever
interpretation he adopted had to allow for the presentation of evidence in an
intelligible fashion, permit the orderly determination of the various factual
issues raised in the trial, admit of a clear demarcation between his function
and the jury's function, and enable him to direct the jury effectively as to
their responsibilities.

In our view, any effort to bifurcate the
fact-finding function between the international and domestic components of the
offences alleged against Pinta would have resulted in serious procedural
problems and may well have rendered trial by jury a virtual impossibility.

The intricate interrelationship between the
elements comprising the domestic component and those forming the international

component of the charges is evident in the
indictment, As discussed above, the factual questions relating to whether
Finta's acts constituted war crimes or crimes against humanity arose not only
in the context of the international component of the charges, but were also
potentially relevant to one of the essential elements of the domestic
components of the charges in counts 1 through 6 (confinement, robbery,
kidnapping) and to the "positive" defences advanced in relation to
all of the charges. This interrelationship defies segregation of the facts
along the lines required by the Crown's position.

Consider some of the procedural problems which
could have developed had the trial judge held that it was for him to decide
whether Finta had committed war crimes or crimes against humanity but for the
jury to decide whether he had committed the domestic offences. Would the judge
make his findings of fact before instructing the jury? And if so, would the
jury be informed of those findings? One can hardly overestimate the prejudice
to Finta had the trial judge instructed the jury that he had concluded that
Finta was a war criminal or had committed crimes against humanity and they were
to accept and apply that finding in their deliberations concerning his
responsibility for the offences alleged against him.

Assuming the trial judge were to decide the
international component of the case, was he to decide those same issues in so
far as they arose in connection with the domestic elements of the offence? As
indicated earlier, the question whether Finta's acts constituted war crimes or
crimes against humanity arose in connection with the domestic elements of
counts 1 to 6 and the "positive" defences advanced by him to all
charges. If the trial judge were to decide whether the acts constituted war
crimes or crimes against humanity for all purposes, the jury would not be in a
position to determine ultimate guilt or innocence even on the domestic aspects
of the allegations. They would decide only some of the factual issues relevant
to culpability for the
Criminal Code

offences alleged.

For example, if this procedure were followed in
respect of count 1, the jury would decide whether Finta was a party to the
confinement of the Jews in the brickyard. The jury would also decide some, but
not all, of the factual questions potentially relevant to the lawfulness of
that confinement and the two "positive" defences advanced. They could
not return a general verdict as it related to even the domestic component of
the crime. At most, the jury could return a special verdict consisting of an
answer to a series of questions put to them by the trial judge. Special
verdicts in criminal matters are used on rare occasions in

some jurisdictions (e.g. , see
R.
v.
Graham, [1984} V.R. 649 (S.C.)), but are virtually unheard of in Canada.

It would be equally untenable to allow the jury
to decide all factual issues relating to culpability for the domestic offences,
including those which were also relevant to the question whether the acts
constituted a war crime or crime against humanity, only to have the trial
judge, after the verdict was returned, make his own overriding assessment of
those same factual issues. The trial judge would have to make those potentially
overriding findings regard­less of the verdict of the jury since jurisdictional
competence is a condition precedent to acquittal or conviction.

For example, the jury could conclude that the
acts did not amount to war crimes or crimes against humanity and that
consequently the s. 25 defence was available on each charge. If the jury so
found, it would return acquittals as regards the domestic offences. The trial
judge would then consider whether for jurisdic­tional purposes Finta's acts
amounted to war crimes or crimes against humanity. The trial judge might
decide, contrary to the jury's findings, that Finta's acts did constitute war
crimes and crimes against humanity. Based on that finding, he would conclude
that the court had jurisdiction. Faced with the jury's acquittals and his
finding in favour of jurisdiction, the trial judge would presum­ably have no
choice but to affirm the acquittals, despite his conclusion that Finta's
conduct amounted to a war crime or a crime against humanity. Bizarre is an apt
word to describe this result.

The result would be equally strange if the trial
judge happened to agree with the jury's conclusion that the acts did not
constitute war crimes or crimes against humanity. If the trial judge reached
that conclusion, he would hold that the court was without jurisdic­tion, set
aside the acquittals and quash the indictment, although he and the jury were
agreed that Finta was not a war criminal and had not committed a crime against
humanity. Indeed, it would seem that an accused, no matter how demonstrably
innocent of both the domestic crime and the war crime or crime against
humanity, could never be acquitted if the trial judge was satisfied that his
acts did not constitute a war crime or crime against humanity. That finding, if
it went to the court's jurisdiction, would require the quashing of the
indictment, not an acquittal. It is passing strange when a law forecloses the
outright acquittal of the innocent!

These problems cannot be resolved by varying the
procedure described above so as to require the trial judge to accept and apply

the jury's findings of fact regarding
culpability for the domestic offences in so far as they relate to the war
crimes and crimes against humanity issues. In the first place, this would
undermine completely the premise on which the Crown relies, that is that
jurisdictional facts are for the judge and not the jury. In the second place,
the jury's verdict would not reveal what findings of fact, if any, they had
made in relation to those issues. The jury could convict or acquit in regard to
the domestic elements of the offences without deciding whether the acts
constituted a war crime or a crime against humanity. A trial judge would have
no way of knowing by the general verdict returned, what findings of fact, if
any, the jury had made in respect of the facts which were germane to the
international component of the charges.

We cannot formulate any procedure which would
permit the jury and the trial judge to perform effectively and independently
the task allotted to them by the Crown's approach. Nor was counsel, even one as
experienced and capable as Mr. Amerasinghe, able to provide a procedural road
map around these difficulties.

Placed beside the procedural problems
encountered if the fact-finding process was split as suggested by the Crown,
the procedure actually followed by the trial judge was a model of simplicity
and clarity.

The trial judge's charge, which was an
organizational master­piece, put all of the factual issues before the jury in a
comprehen­sive and comprehensible manner. We see no reason to suspect that the
jury was unable to make the findings of fact relevant to questions concerning
the international aspects of the offences, nor do we doubt that the jury was
able to apply the law as given to them by the trial judge to the findings of
fact they made. The effectiveness with which the trial judge was able to present
the case to the jury offers further support for the conclusion that he was
correct in holding that all factual issues would be determined by the jury.

6
.
Conclusion

As with all accused who are tried by a court
composed of a judge and jury, Finta was entitled to have the community, as
represented by the jury, pass on the validity of the charges he faced. It was
for the jury to decide whether Finta should be condemned as a war criminal or
as one who had committed crimes against humanity. The trial judge properly left
this task to the jury.

H.
Did the trial judge properly define the knowledge requirement of the
international component of the charges?

As indicated above, we regard knowledge of the
facts and circumstances necessary to bring Finta's conduct within the
definition of crimes against humanity or war crimes as an essential element of
each charge. That knowledge requirement does not depend on Finta's perception
of whether particular conduct came within the meaning of the relevant words
(e.g. , persecution, inhumanity). The trial judge gave the jury definitions of
those words. If the jury concluded that certain acts fit those definitions, and
if they also concluded that Finta was aware of the facts or circumstances which
brought the acts within those definitions then the required mental element was
established regardless of how Finta might have characterized his acts.

For example, if the jury accepted the evidence
of the various witnesses who described the conditions in the boxcars which
transported the Jews away from Szeged, the jury would have no difficulty
concluding that the treatment was "inhumane" within the definition of
that word supplied by the trial judge. The jury would then have to determine
whether Finta was aware of those conditions. If the jury decided that he was
aware of the relevant conditions, the knowledge requirement was established
regardless of whether Finta believed those conditions to be inhumane.

In our opinion, the trial judge correctly
described the knowledge requirement of the international component of the
offences charged against Finta. For example, in his charge under the specific
heading "the mental element" as it related to crimes against
humanity, he said:

[T]he Crown has the duty to [prove] beyond
a reasonable doubt that the particular offences; robbery, kidnapping,
confinement, manslaughter, to the knowledge of the accused had those factual
qualities that raise them up to a crime against humanity.

The Crown doesn't have to prove the accused
is an international scholar, that he knows the pigeon holes or nooks and crannies of international law. It is sufficient to prove the accused knew his acts had the factual
quality of enslavement or persecutoriai deportation or racial or religious
persecution or inhumanity that raised them up from the level of an ordinary
crime to the international level of a crime against humanity.

The trial judge gave a similar direction when
defining culp­ability for war crimes:

It is the same principle that I referred to
on the mental element of crimes against humanity. The Crown has to prove beyond
a reasonable doubt that the accused knew that his acts had the factual quality
that made them war crimes, such as ill treatment of the civilian population,
all of the other

alternatives listed there and that the
accused knew he was the agent of the occupying forces.

The trial judge's repeated references to Finta's
knowledge of the "factual quality" of his acts clearly referred to
knowledge of the circumstances (e.g., the conditions in the camp) which brought
his acts (e.g., the confinement) within the definition of a crime against
humanity or a war crime read in its entirety. The trial judge's charge limited
the issue to Finta's knowledge of the facts sur­rounding his acts, and did not
suggest that Finta's personal moral code or his own perceptions of
international law had any relevance to his guilt.

I.
Defence counsel's address to the jury

The Crown contends that defence counsel's jury
address was improper when viewed as a whole and in seven specific respects. The
Crown further contends that the trial judge's attempts to correct defence
counsel's improprieties were inadequate, in the circumstances. It is the
Crown's position that the jury's verdicts of acquittal cannot stand in the face
of defence counsel's allegedly improper jury address.

Mr. Amerasinghe, for the appellant, raised these
specific objec­tions to defence counsel's jury address:

‑‑ the
expression of defence counsel's personal opinion as to the respond­ent's
innocence;

‑‑ defence
counsel's invitation to the jury to ignore the
Criminal Code
's
war crimes provisions which he characterized as bad
law;

‑‑ defence
counsel's threatening remarks to the jury;

‑‑ defence
counsel's invitation to acquit in order to avoid resurrecting grievances of
World War II;

‑‑ defence
counsel's analogy through which he compared the relationship between the Court
of Appeal and the trial judge with the relationship between the respondent's
military superiors and the respondent;

‑‑ defence
counsel's intimidating comments suggesting that the jury would in turn be
judged by God just as they judged the respondent;

‑‑ defence
counsel's alleged appeal to religious or ethnic prejudice.

We will deal with these issues in the order set
out above.

1.
The expression of counsel's personal opinion
as to the respondent's innocence

Early in his jury address Mr. Christie dealt
generally with the inconsistencies and contradictions in the evidence. This, of
course, was quite acceptable. He next noted that the respondent did not have to
prove what had happened 45 years ago in the Szeged brickyard. This submission
cannot be criticized, as it does no more than to remind the jury that the onus
throughout was on the

Crown, not the accused. Unfortunately, Mr.
Christie then expanded his submission, by saying:

Is it for me to have to prove what happened
45 years ago in that brickyard? No, it is not. Thank goodness. I wouldn't bring
a case. In
my judgment, there
is no case. If
it was my duty I wouldn't be here. If it was my duty to determine
if
there was a case to bring here,
you wouldn't be here.

(Emphasis added.)

Mr. Amerasinghe did not object to this part of
Mr. Christie's jury address at trial. Nor did the trial judge view it as
sufficiently improper to merit rebuke, correction, or even comment.

Mr. Christie takes the position that he did no
more than submit to the jury that the onus was on the Crown and that it had not
been met. He explained that he did no more, by way of his words, than to submit
that there was no case for the respondent to answer. He further submitted that
his comment concerning what would have happened had he been responsible for the
prosecution was merely a comment on the weight of the evidence. Finally, Mr.
Christie takes the position that only Crown counsel is prohibited from stating
personal opinions about the issues in a criminal trial. As Mr. Christie sees
it, unlike Crown counsel, defence counsel is ". , a partisan advocate for
his client".

In our view, neither Crown nor defence counsel
is entitled to express his personal opinion about a witness, an issue, the
basis upon which the prosecution was commenced, or the case in general.
Counsel's opinion is not relevant. There is no special exemption for defence
counsel. There can be no criticism advanced concerning Mr. Christie's submission
that the evidentiary onus was on the Crown throughout. Nor can there be
criticism concerning his submission that there was no case to be met on the
evidence, We think, however, that the remark "[i]f it was my duty to
determine if there was a case to bring here, you wouldn't be here"
constituted a personal opinion. These remarks were improper and irrelevant.

The trial judge carefully and fairly directed
the jury to the issues they had to consider in proceeding to their verdicts.
Although Mr. Christie's remarks were improper, we do not think they were
prejudicial when counsel's submissions and the trial judge's charge are
considered as a whole.

jury that it was wrong for defence counsel to have made those comments about
the legislation. The trial judge did not accede to Crown counsel's request to
recharge the jury in stronger terms. He advised Crown counsel that, in his
opinion, the direction was clear and strong enough.

Mr. Christie's attempt to justify his personal
characterization of the war crimes legislation as bad law was both complex and
unconvincing. He asserted that the substance of his submission was that the
respondent was in no different position than the jury. He said that both were
faced with bad laws and both had, as a matter of law, to apply the law in
issue. Mr. Christie submitted that his comments had to be read and assessed in
the context of his jury address, taken as a whole. He submitted further that he
made it clear in his jury address that the jury had to obey the law, in
accordance with the trial judge's instructions.

Resort to reasonable rhetoric as part of
counsel's jury address is acceptable. A jury address is, after all, an
argument. There is nothing inappropriate about defence counsel making
submissions as to the strength or weaknesses of the Crown's case, provided
those submissions focus on the evidence, or lack of it. The difficulty here is
that it was the process and legislation, as distinct from the evidence
presented by the Crown, which Mr. Christie referred to as morally, legally and
factually absurd. This reference was improper in the extreme.

We
are, however,
satisfied that the prejudice occasioned by defence counsel's comments was
remedied by the trial judge in his charge. As stated, the trial judge told the
jury that Mr. Christie's opinion of the legislation was "unhelpful".
The trial judge could have resorted to stronger language. However, he clearly
dismissed Mr. Christie's views of the legislation and he directed the jury that
the law, which was the subject-matter of Mr. Christie's acerbic attack, had
passed constitutional scrutiny. He also told the jury that they were obliged to
take and apply the law, in accordance with his instructions.

We are satisfied that, notwithstanding defence
counsel's com­ments, no prejudice accrued to the Crown on this aspect of
defence counsel's jury address.

3.
Defence counsel's threatening remarks to
the jury

The appellant contends that, in his jury
address, defence counsel threatened the jury by his reference to the prospect
of the jury being in the respondent's position in 45 years' time. The theme of
Mr. Christie's submission was the difficulty the jury members would have
defending allegations made against them 45 years after this trial, as a
consequence of convicting the respondent. He stated:

The fundamental injustice of putting
someone on trial at this stage for what happened in 1944 is that no one can
give you any recollection with moral certainty and you had better have moral
certainty if you are to convict, because if somebody 45 years from now puts you
on trial in another country for persecuting Imre Finta and that country might
be as hostile to Jews as we are to Nazis, who would you be calling? Don't call
me.

If you were to place yourselves, as I said,
in another country 45 years from now that told you your laws here were invalid,
no defence to you, they were unconstitutional, you would have no means of
verifying the justification for anything you did but you would never have the
guilty knowledge, a guilty mind or a criminal intent. You are here because the
court and the law says you should be, you are doing what the law requires but
that means that unless you are doing something for yourself, you could never
have a guilty or criminal intent.

You see, you are going to split and go your
own ways after this awful ordeal ... and if you ever were to convict this man,
you would have to justify that to yourself. You see, no one else, it is your
individual conscience and when you are telling the accused he is supposed to
have looked to his conscience to disobey the law, you had better have an answer
that satisfies yourself and remember this 45 years later, because you never
know in this crazy world, what we do today is lawful and might be some kind of

If you were ever accused of doing something
unconstitutional in this time and place, you could certainly say we were
officially induced into believing by the government authorities, we represented
that we were doing what was lawful. I would say you would be absolutely right
and even if the government was wrong in what they told you, you would be
innocent of any criminal intent because you are here under the officially
sanctioned belief that you are trying a constitutionally valid law and that, as
his Lordship will tell you, is, indeed, none of your affair.

If it turned out that what we were doing
here was totally unconstitutional, where does that place you? Does that mean
you acted unlawfully? No, you are here with the official sanction of the
government and how else do we know anything is lawful or unlawful? When the
government says so, we have to take it as such.

If it turns out
later we are wrong, what can we say? It is certainly not with a criminal
intention. I mean, we are all part of a system right here, sitting in this room
and it is the whole room including you, including me, including his Lordship
and in courts that are here, we are all part of a system, keeping a man here
