officially sanctioned actions are not individual responsibilities even if the
State happens to be wrong from time to time.

Mr. Christie submits that this submission did no
more than remind the jury, by what Mr. Christie characterized as moral
exhortation, that human memory is frail after 45 years and that the jury had to
be morally satisfied of the respondent's guilt. He justified his reference as
an attempt to make the jury aware of the respondent's predicament. That
predicament, he said, arose from state sponsored actions being later viewed as
criminal. Mr. Christie denied threatening the jury, or having an intention to
do so.

Crown counsel did not object to this part of
defence counsel's jury address. The trial judge did, however, deal with Mr.
Christie's comments in his charge. He said:

The only reason I stress that point is
because of the unhelpful suggestion from defence counsel that the reason you
better have a moral certainty if you are to convict, is because if someone in
another country puts you on trial 45 years from now for persecuting Imre Finta,
who do you call as a witness in your defence.

I don't propose to dignify that kind of
suggestion by spending much time on it. In the first place you have the
judgment of this court that this law is constitutionally valid and it conforms
to the principles of fundamental justice.

We think the trial judge's response was
sufficient. The trial judge gave this clumsy and inappropriate defence
submission all the time it deserved and dismissed it. He could have resorted to
stronger language; the trial judge, however, had the advantage of being with
the jury over an extended period and was thus able to assess the real impact of
the defence submission on the jury.

A.
Defence counsel's invitation to acquit in order to avoid
resurrecting grievances of World War II

In his jury address Mr. Christie advised the
jury that other countries (Australia and England) were awaiting the jury's
verdict. He also told the jury that a conviction on flimsy evidence would
result in the grievances of World War II being resurrected, and lead to unjust
charges in other countries. Mr. Christie now says he intended to do no more
than to exhort the jury not to convict on flimsy evidence.

The Crown did not object to this part of defence
counsel's jury address at trial. The trial judge, however, dealt with the issue
of the consequences of the jury's verdict, and the more specific issue of the
potential impact of the jury's verdict in other countries. He said:

Don't speculate about the consequences of
your verdict inside this court room or outside this court room. There is only
one consequence at stake here and that is that your verdict should be fair and
just as a consequence of your oath, on the law and the evidence. Don't
speculate about the consequences of your verdict or concern yourself with that
in any way. Your oath requires you to deliver a just and fair verdict on the
law and the evidence and not to send a message to one side or the other in some
dispute in this country or some other country about what policy should be
followed in respect of the suspected war crimes or crimes against humanity.

Don't concern yourselves with the judgment
of history. Concern yourselves with the evidence.

We are satisfied that any prejudice which may
have been occasioned by defence counsel's improper references to the poten­tial
consequences of the jury's verdict was removed by the trial judge's clear
instruction.

B.
Defence counsel's analogy through which he
compared the relationship between the Court of Appeal and the trial judge with
the relationship between the respondent's military superiors and the respondent

A main theme of the defence counsel's jury
address was the contention that in 1944 the respondent was morally justified in
obeying the orders of his superiors, provided that those orders were not
manifestly unlawful. Mr. Christie dealt with that issue directly, and in a
manner which did not result in any criticism. He also approached this issue in
another way; he compared the command hierarchy in a military organization with
the hierarchial structure of our courts. He submitted that the respondent was
bound to obey the orders of his superiors, just as the trial judge was bound to
follow the law as established by the Court of Appeal.

The key thought underlying the submission was at
its conclusion when Mr. Christie submitted, "... we have to trust
authority. And sometimes authority might indeed be wrong".

Crown counsel objected to the analogy. He asked
the trial judge to include in his charge a reference to the fact that the trial
judge was independent and not part of a military style hierarchy.

The trial judge referred to the issue in his
charge in these terms:

Defence counsel said something that needs
to be corrected. He said that that position I just expressed to you is one that
most people in hierarchies of command rely on. He said that position is similar
to the military where a captain follows the order from a lieutenant-colonel,
relying on his superiors, in public acts like the entrainment, and each of us
relies on the government's judgment of authority, which might later on turn out
to be wrong.

Now, that wasn't a very helpful comparison.
You make up your own mind whether a reasonable person in the position of the
accused can honestly believe the Baky Order or the train schedule order were
lawful and did not involve racial or religious persecution or inhumane acts.
Don't get the idea you are following orders or I am following orders. There is
all the difference in the world between someone following government orders and
someone like me who has a duty to apply the law in all due process and all the
principles of fundamental justice and all the rights of the accused.

You are not following orders in this case
from anyone and neither am I. You are independent and so am I. You are judges.
We do not follow any orders. We go wherever the path of the law takes us. No
matter whether we think it will please someone in authority or displease
someone in authority. Your sense of responsibility and mine come from our
oaths, our knowledge that what we do is the right thing. None of us, you or I,
are following government orders. We are going down the path of the law as
interpreted by the independent courts of this country. It isn't helpful to draw
a parallel between someone following government orders and independent judges
like you and me.

This is not a military tribunal, this is
not a field court martial. You and I are applying something called due process
of law. You know what due
process is because you have been part of it for six long months. You see the
degree of protection accorded to the accused in our system of law.

It isn't a military court, it isn't a court
martial. You are not following orders at all. You are independent judges by
your oath and you have bound your conscience to follow the path of the law with
all its constitutional safeguards for the accused.

In our opinion, the trial judge properly
emphasized that he and the jury were not following orders from anyone. He
emphasized that members of the jury were independent judges, bound by their
oath and required to follow "the path of the law with all its
constitutional safeguards for the accused". We are satisfied that this
issue would have been considered by the jury on its own merits, unencumbered by
defence counsel's manifestly imperfect and inappropriate analogy

6. Defence counsel's intimidating comments
suggesting that the jury would in turn be judged by God just as they judged the
respondent

The defence position, generally, was that Crown

[T]wo wrongs don't make a right and

responsibility and a tough job .. .

So as you sit in judgment on Imre Finta,

The way to stop circles of vengeance and

The Crown submits that defence counsel's
rhetoric would have left the jury with the impression that convicting the
respondent would be an act of vengeance for which the jury would in due course
be judged by God. Although the submission was improper, it simply exhorts the
jury to recognize the capacity of the brickyard witnesses to seek vengeance
against an inhumane regime which had become personified in the respondent. He
did, however, take his message much too far in suggesting to the jury that a
conviction would be an act of vengeance, and in expressing (or seeming to
express) his personal opinion that, in the scheme of things, vengeance would be

created by Mr. Christie's excessive language. In his charge, he said:

Don't concern yourselves with the
consequences of your verdict, whatever it may be. Don't concern yourselves with

judgment of God, that isn't my

department. But if you honour your oath,
you will do your duty in every respect. Remember that each of you took this
oath. The Registrar said, as you stood:

"Do you swear that you will well and
truly try and true deliverance make between our sovereign lady the Queen and

Honour that oath, you will do your duty. I
am confident you will go wherever your conscience takes you on the law and the
evidence before you.

We are satisfied that the jury considered the
issues before them without intimidation. The trial judge's response corrected
the excesses in this part of defence counsel's jury address.

7
.
Defence counsel's alleged appeal to
religious or ethnic prejudice

In support of his submission that silence is not
evidence of guilt, defence counsel's address contained a verbatim recital from
the Bible, as follows:

And the chief priests and all the council
sought for witness against Jesus to put him to death; and found none.

For many bear false witness against him,
but their witness agreed not together.

And there arose certain, and bear false
witness against him, saying:

We heard him say, I will destroy this temple
that is made with hands, and within three days I will build another made
without hands.

But neither so did their witness agree
together. And the high priest stood up in the midst, and asked Jesus, saying:
Answerest thou nothing? What is it which these witness against thee?

But he held his peace and answered nothing.

And later before Pilate:

The chief priests accused him of many

And Pilate asked him again, saying,
"Answerest thou nothing? Behold how many things they witness against

But Jesus yet answered nothing.

Crown counsel did not object to this part of the
defence jury address at trial.

The Crown now submits that the biblical
reference was improper and highly inflammatory in that it would suggest that
the respondent, like Jesus, was being falsely accused. The Crown conceded,
however, that defence counsel made it clear he was not comparing Finta to
Jesus.

Mr. Christie contended that the biblical
reference was intended to reinforce his submissions related to the presumption
of inno­cence and the failure of the accused to testify

In our view, the exegesis chosen by defence
counsel was inappropriate in the extreme. None the less, we do not think that
the jury could have realistically compared the circumstances of Jesus and the
respondent. Had a contrary conclusion been obvious, we would have thought this
part of the defence jury address would have been included in the list of Crown
counsel's lengthy objections made immediately after the defence jury address.

Moreover, on repeated occasions the trial judge,
in clear lan­guage, instructed the jury to discharge their responsibilities by
resorting only to the evidence and the law as set out by the trial judge. He
specifically told the jury not to let their decision be affected by sentiment,
emotion, prejudice or sympathy.

Although the reference to the biblical quotation
was unfortu­nate, and in hindsight singularly inappropriate, we do not think it
resulted in prejudice as is now suggested by the Crown, or in the tainting of

Finally, Mr. Amerasinghe has objected to defence

of whom affirmed before giving evidence, and jurors who swore on the Bible upon
taking their oath. The Crown's position is that this was an appeal to a
religious prejudice. We think the distinction drawn by Mr. Christie between
those who swore and those affirmed was unworthy of a counsel of his experience
and inappropriate in the extreme. The trial judge, however, directed the jury
with precision that an oath and an affirmation have the same effect. We are
satisfied that the jury would not have succumbed to defence counsel's
transparent tactics. Moreover, as earlier noted, the trial judge correctly
reminded the jury not to let their decision be affected by sentiment, emotion,
prejudice or sympathy.

8
. Conclusion

The critical issue to be addressed in dealing
with this general ground of the appeal is whether what was said by counsel in
his jury address tainted the trial, with the result that the Crown was
prejudiced.

We are satisfied that the separate and
cumulative effect of those parts of defence counsel's jury address which we
view to have been inappropriate did not, when considered in the light of the
trial judge's charge, deprive the Crown of its right to a fair trial.

J.
The admissibility of the evidence introduced by the trial judge

1. Overview

A central issue in the trial was the identity of
the Hungarian gendarme officer who was the commander of the brickyard concentration
camp in Szeged. Several Crown witnesses testified that Finta was the Hungarian
commander of the camp. However, there was also some evidence, most of which
forms the subject matter of this ground of appeal, to the effect that there was
another gendarme officer present at the brickyard who might have been
responsible for some of the offences attributed to Finta.

Professor Randolph Braham, an expert historian,
testified that the concentration centres were guarded both within and on the
outside by gendarmes and that at Szeged, the gendarmes guarding the outside of
the brick factory were under the command of a Lieutenant Bodolay.

Mrs. Fonyo, one of the eyewitnesses who had been
confined in the brickyard, stated in cross-examination that there was another
gendarme officer in the camp who resembled Finta, although she could tell the
difference between them. She testified that Finta was the commander of the
brickyard and specifically denied that the commander of the gendarmerie
guarding the Jews at the brickyard was named Bodolay. The possibility of a
gendarme named Bodolay having been in charge was not put in cross-examination
to any of the other eyewitnesses called by the Crown.

The testimony of Mrs. Kemeny and Mrs. Ballo,
taken on commission in Hungary, also indicated that there might have been
another gendarme officer in command of the brickyard.

The most cogent evidence of the existence of a
Lieutenant Bodolay, who might have been in charge of the confinement and
deportation of the Jewish population held at the Szeged brickyard, was
contained in statements given by Mr. Dallos as part of Finta's 1947-48 trial in
Hungary.

The trial judge found that the testimony of
Kemeny and Ballo and the Dallos statements were essential to the narrative. The
Crown, however, refused to call this evidence, and the trial judge ruled that
this was not improper. Rather than leaving it to the defence to decide whether
to call this evidence as part of its case, the trial judge called it himself.

The Crown argues that the Dallos statements were
inadmissible hearsay, inherently unreliable and prejudicial to the Crown. Alter­natively,
the Crown submits that, if admissible, the Dallos state­ments should not have
been introduced by the trial judge. The

Crown also submits that the jury was
insufficiently cautioned about the unreliability of the Dallos statements, and
furthermore, that the Dallos statements were improperly linked to the Fonyo
evidence.

2.
The admissibility of the Dallos evidence
a.

The evidence

Dallos had been a witness at Finta's trial in
1947-48 in Hungary before the People's Tribunal of Szeged. Dallos who died,
apparently in 1963, gave two statements in connection with that trial. In those
statements, Dallos, himself a Jew confined in the brickyard, said that he had
been put in charge on the side of the Jews. He said that those in the brickyard
were guarded by a First Lieutenant Bodolay, a commandant of the gendarmerie. He
identified another comman­dant, a gendarme officer by the name of Naray. He
also said that Finta was the commandant of the plain clothes gendarme detec­tives.
Their assignment was to carry out searches for personal valuables, jewellery
and money.

Although incriminating on the robbery count, the
Dallos evi­dence was potentially favourable to the defence in that it pointed
to the possibility that someone else was responsible for the unlawful
confinement and kidnapping. It had no bearing on the manslaugh­ter counts,
which did not relate to the activities at the brickyard.

The statements made by Dallos came in two forms.
The first is a deposition given by Dallos to the Hungarian state police in
Szeged on January 16, 1947. On that occasion, Dallos was instructed of his
obligation to tell the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, according to the
best of his knowledge and conscience, and that he might have to confirm his
testimony by oath. He stated that he was born in 1891, that he was a married
lawyer, and that he first met Finta at the beginning of June, 1944, when the
Jews were in the closed ghetto of Szeged. Dallos said that at that time Finta
was the commanding officer of the gendarmes detective division. He added:

What role he played in the closed ghetto I
do not know, but the so-called Jewish Council communicated with him through
Marcel Gross, former director of the Bank of Commerce.

I did see him a few times in the closed
ghetto and I also know that on one occasion he and Marcel Gross discussed the
matter of apartments and accommodation, at which time he hinted that
we
would
soon be moved on again.

Then a couple of days after June 20th, we
got to the ghetto by the brick factor[y] where the outside Commander of the
Gendarmerie entrusted me with command as one who had been for five and a half
years the director of the Advocacy Office.

The Commandant of the Gendarmerie guarding
us was a certain First Lieutenant Bodolay, but the Gendarme Detachment whose
assignment it was to carry out the most drastic search several times a day, was
under the command of Captain Pinta.

This detachment consisted of plain clothes
gendarme detectives who kept us in trepidation the whole time and always
referring to Captain Finta as their authority, calling on us to hand over our
valuables and monies and always immediately because a search would follow, and
if any of us were to be found in possession of the smallest amount of money or
valuables, the same person would be shot dead and we would also be decimated.

In May, 1947, he made a another statement before
the People's Tribunal of Szeged in the form of a deposition. The trial judge
here described that latter statement in the following manner:

The deposition was taken apparently before
a recording secretary and someone called an examiner. It later had affixed to
it the seal of the court, and I take it to be some kind of a deposition.
Although it was not under oath, it was apparently not subject to
cross-examination. It was read over and signed by the witness and it was
preceded by a caution that he had an obligation to tell the truth and that his
testimony might have to be confirmed by oath and that he would be committing an
indictable offence should he testify falsely.

In the deposition Dallos said:

I met Imre Pinta when we landed in the
closed city ghetto, the beginning of June, 1944. Imre Finta was the commandant of the Gendarme Detective
Sub-Division. In the city ghetto I had no contact with Imre Finta, but I heard
from Marcel Gross that Imre Pinta could have helped with our uncomfortable
accommodations even in the city ghetto.

In the ghetto at the brick factory I was
put in charge on the side of the Jews. The Commandant of the Gendarmerie
guarding us was Gendarme First Lieutenant Bodolay who had come from Ujvidek.
There was another Com­mandant, a Gendarme officer by the name of Narai from
Nagyvarad. Imre Finta was the commandant of the plain-clothes Gendarme
detectives. Imre Pinta strove to give the outward impression of a gentleman but
inwardly he was all the more cruel.

The orders were issued by the Germans, they
were carried out by the Gendarmes. One time I heard myself as Imre Finta issued
the order that we must surrender all of our valuables at the pain of being shot
dead. I have no knowledge of Imre Finta himself searching for our valuables.
The Gendarme detectives were rougher than the Gendarme guards.

I know for certain that even the Germans
did not order the kind of drastic actions that the detectives carried out
against us. I know this from a remark made by one of the German SS soldiers
who, noting the extreme brutality of the Gendarmes, quoted a German saying,
roughly corresponding to the Hungarian proverb, "The fish starts rotting
from the head." Whenever the Gendarme detectives carried out an order,
they always referred to Imre Finta as their authority.

At the end of the minutes of testimony, the
document reads as follows:

The presiding judge shows the witness his
testimony to the police. Witness: I stand by my testimony, it has been recorded
accurately. In the absence of a motion, the witness is not required to take an
oath.

b.
The ruling of the trial fudge

The trial judge found that the Dallos evidence
was capable of sustaining the inference that Finta was not responsible for the
brickyard confinement, and that it was thus capable of leaving the jury with a
reasonable doubt as to Finta's guilt on the kidnapping and forcible confinement
counts.

The trial judge correctly concluded that the
Dallos evidence was hearsay and that it was not admissible under the business
record exception to the hearsay rule contained in
s. 30
of the
Canada
Evidence
Act,
R.S.C. 1985, c. C-5. Even if the Dallos statements were records made
in the usual and ordinary course of business, they would be inadmissible by
virtue of s. 30(10), which declares inadmissible any part of a business record
made in the course of an investigation or inquiry (s. 30(10)(a)(i)), in
contemplation of a legal proceeding (s. 30(10)(a)(ii)), or any transcript or
recording of evidence taken in the course of another legal proceeding (s.
30(10)(c)).

Despite its hearsay nature, the trial judge
ruled that the Dallos evidence was admissible because of the unique features of
the trial. He based his conclusion on the circumstantial
indicia
of
reliability of the Dallos evidence, combined with the necessity to have
recourse to hearsay.

With respect to reliability, the trial judge
said:

Dallos is perhaps far from disinterested,
but his interest, if any, is against the accused, against whom he testified in
1947-48. It is a party adverse in interest who seeks the admission of his
evidence, and I think that is relevant on the question of
indicia
of
reliability, in the sense that the defence seeks to call or seeks to have put
before the court the evidence of someone adverse in interest to the defendant.

There is some circumstantial guarantee of
trustworthiness from the fact that the deposition and testimony of Dallos
emerged during judicial proceed­ings under an obligation to tell the truth.
Though the trial was ruled in these proceedings to be a nullity in the Canadian
jurisdictional sense, because the accused was neither present nor represented
by counsel instructed by him, although the process of the court was subject to
all the frailties pointed out by the defence earlier, because it was political
tribunal, these weaknesses in the circumstantial warranty of authenticity
redound equally in favour of admis­sion because they are frailties which would
bias the 1948 trial against the accused and not in his favour.

As for the need for the Dallos evidence, the
trial judge found that the question of brickyard command was central to the
case and that there was obvious difficulty after 45 years in obtaining evidence
from people who, like Dallos, had direct knowledge of the actual command
structure of the brickyard.

Essentially, the trial judge admitted the
evidence after testing it according to the general principles of reliability
and necessity. As we understand his ruling, the trial judge decided to permit
reliable evidence needed by the defence to be introduced for the truth of its
contents, even though it offended the traditional hearsay rule.

The trial judge also ruled that the evidence was
not to be edited and that it would go before the jury in its entirety. The
defence did not object to the introduction of the incriminating parts of
Dallos' evidence which, in any event, added nothing new to the Crown's case.
However, a substantial portion of the evidence unfavourable to the defence was
in the nature of double hearsay, since the declarant, Dallos, had referred to
matters that had been related to him. The trial judge warned the jury in that
respect.

The trial judge also based his conclusion, in
part, on the constitutional entitlement of the accused to have access to this
evidence to be assured of a fair trial. It is apparent that, for this reason,
the trial judge would only admit the evidence at the request of the defence,
and was not prepared to admit similar evidence if tendered by the Crown.

The Crown argues that the Dallos statements were
inadmissible hearsay, inherently unreliable and prejudicial to the Crown.

C.
Admissibility of the Dallos evidence as an
exception to the hearsay rule

It
is conceded
that the Dallos statements would not be admiss­ible under any of the
established exceptions to the hearsay rule. However, the existing categories of
exceptions, for the most part, have been judicially created and are not
exhaustive.

The recent decision of
R.
v.
Khan
(1990),

1990 CanLII 77 (SCC)
, 59 C.C.C. (3d) 92 at p. 100, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 531, 79 C.R. (3d) 1, reaffirms the
principle that the " `common law is moulded by the judges and it is still
their province to adapt it from time to time so as to make it serve the
interests of those it binds' ":
Ares
v.
Venner
(1970),
1970 CanLII 5 (SCC)
, 14
D.L.R. (3d) 4, [1970] S.C.R. 608, 12 C.R.N.S. 349;
Myers
v.
Director
of Public Prosecutions,
[1965] A.C. 1001 (H.L.) at p. 1047,
per
Lord
Donovan, dissenting. In
Khan
,
the court admitted the hearsay evidence of
a mother whose four-year-old child allegedly had been sexually assaulted by Dr.
Khan. McLachlin J. stated on behalf of the court, at p. 100, that:

The hearsay rule has traditionally been
regarded as an absolute rule, subject to various categories of exceptions, such
as admissions, dying declarations, declarations against interest and
spontaneous declarations. While this approach has provided a degree of
certainty to the law on hearsay, it has frequently proved unduly inflexible in
dealing with new situations and new needs in the law.
This has resulted in
courts in recent years on occasion adopting a more flexible approach, rooted in
the principle and the policy underlying the hearsay rule rather than the
strictures of traditional exceptions.

(Emphasis added.)

The policy underlying the hearsay rule has
undergone considera­ble reassessment and evolution over the years. In an
article appearing in 62 Harv. L. Rev. 177 (1948), at pp. 182-3, Edmund M.
Morgan summarized that evolution in the following way:

Before the opening of the eighteenth
century, then, we find three reasons advanced for excluding hearsay. The court
and jury must base their findings upon what the witness knows and not upon what
he is credulous enough to believe; the witness must make that knowledge known
under sanction of the fear of the consequences which falsehood will bring; and
the adversary must have an opportunity to cross-examine.

At pp. 183-4, Morgan deals with what he calls
the modern basis for the hearsay rule:

Today, the notion that the court and jury
cannot be permitted to rely upon the possible credulity of the witness seems to
have gone by the board, for unless the adversary objects, the court may admit
inadmissible hearsay and the trier of fact may give it such value as is within
the bounds of reason. The trier has the right to only such protection from this
pitfall as the adversary sees fit to insist upon. What of the requirement of
the oath? Here, too, the trier may have to go without such help, if any, as
this stimulus to truth telling may furnish; for if the judge does not insist
that the witness take an oath and the adversary makes no objection to unsworn
testimony, the trier may give it full credence even in a criminal case. On the
other hand, if the adversary is deprived of the opportunity for adequate
cross-examination for any reason other than conduct for which he is
responsible, he is entitled to have the direct examination stricken.

And further, at p. 185:

The theory of the system is that in the
contest between parties, each interested to demonstrate the strength of his own
contentions and to expose the weakness of his opponent's, the truth will
emerge. The purpose of furnishing the safeguards of oath and cross-examination,
therefore, is not to aid the parties to suppress the truth, but to enable them
to avoid the risk that the trier will be misled into mistaking the false for
the true.

Thus, as Morgan has noted, hearsay is no longer
excluded primarily because it is unreliable, but rather, because it is unchal­lenged.
To a large extent, the fact that the evidence is unchal­lenged renders its
reliability suspect. But there is more than reliability to the notion that only
cross-examined evidence should

be admissible. There is a fundamental element of
fairness arising from the right of confrontation implicit in the adversarial
system.

These principles were considered and affirmed
recently by this court in
R.
v.
Miller
(1991),
1991 CanLII 2704 (ON CA)
, 68 C.C.C. (3d)
517, 9 C.R. (4th) 347, 5 O.R. (3d) 678 (C.A.), which applies
Khan
to the
benefit of the accused, In
Miller,
there was evidence that the accused
had visited the deceased in her apartment on the morning of her death, but he
testified that he left at 11:15 a.m. There also was evidence to indicate that
the deceased had contemplated suicide in the preced­ing weeks. The Crown
tendered evidence of a telephone call received by the deceased around 12:15
p.m. from a Mr. Stehr. Stehr testified that in that conversation the deceased
spoke of her plans to go out to a bar with a girl-friend later that night.
Stehr also said that later in the conversation, the deceased told him that a
friend had just left the apartment. The trial judge admitted the first part of
Stehr's evidence as going to the state of mind of the deceased, which was
relevant to whether she had contemplated suicide that day. However, the trial
judge ruled that the decease 's comment to the effect that a friend had just
left the apartment could not be used to prove the truth of its content because
it would offend the hearsay rule. The defence elicited that evidence to support
the inference that the friend who had just left was, in fact, the appellant.
The trial judge had made his ruling prior to the Supreme Court decision in
Khan
.

On appeal, this court found that the jury should have been permitted to use
the hearsay evidence of the deceased's statement.

In our view, the conclusion of the trial judge,
that the Dallos statement should be admitted as an exception to the hearsay
rule, accords with the principles and policies underlying exceptions to the
hearsay rule.

(1)
Necessity

The principle of necessity, which can serve as
the first pillar for the recognition of an exception to the hearsay rule, has
been stated in
Wigmore on Evidence,
3rd. ed. (Chadbourn
rev.
1974), vol. 5,
at p. 253:

§1421.
First principle: Necessity.
The
scope of the first principle may be briefly indicated by terming it the
necessity principle. It implies that since
we
shall lose the benefit of
the evidence entirely unless we accept it untested, there is thus a greater or
less necessity for receiving it. The reason why we shall otherwise lose it may
be one of two:

(1) The person whose assertion is offered
may now be
dead,
or out of the jurisdiction, or insane, or
otherwise
unavailable
for the purpose of testing. This is the commoner and more
palpable reason. It is found in the exception for dying declarations and in the
five ensuing ones. The principle is not always

fully and consistently carried out in the
rules; but the general notion is clear and unmistakable, and it is acknowledged
in these exceptions with more or less directness and strictness.

(2) The assertion may be such that we
cannot expect, again, or at this time, to get
evidence of the same value
from
the same or other sources. This appears more or less fully in the exception for
spontaneous declarations, for reputation, and in part elsewhere. Here we are
not threatened (as in the first case) with the entire loss of a person's
evidence, but merely of some valuable source of evidence. The necessity is not
so great; perhaps hardly a necessity, only an expediency or convenience, can be
predicated. But the principle is the same.

Properly understood, the principle of necessity
means not that the hearsay evidence is necessary for a party to prove his case,
but that hearsay is the only available means of putting that evidence before
the court. To be admissible, the evidence must be relevant to, but not
necessarily dispositive of, an issue, and for hearsay to be admissible, it must
be the only way of tendering that relevant evidence. Furthermore, it must
exhibit
indicia
of reliability not required of evidence capable of being
tested in court by cross-examination.

Here, the requirement of necessity is clearly
met since the declarant is dead. The need to use hearsay here is thus greater,
in view of the death of the declarant, than it was in either
Khan or
Ares v.
Venner
.
Indeed, the death of the declarant is, as stated by Wigmore, the
"commoner and more palpable reason" for having to resort to hearsay
evidence.

(2) Indicia of reliability

Wigmore expresses this second branch of the
foundation of a hearsay exception in the following terms at p. 253:

§1422.
Second principle: Circumstantial
probability of trustworthiness.
The second principle which, combined with
the first, satisfies us to accept the evidence untested, is in the nature of a
practicable substitute for the ordinary test of cross-examination. We see that
under certain circumstances the probability of accuracy and trustworthiness of
statement is practically sufficient, if not quite equivalent to that of
statements tested in the conventional manner. This circumstantial probability
of trustworthiness is found in a variety of circumstances sanctioned by
judicial practice; and it is usually from one of these salient circumstances
that the exception takes its name. There is no comprehensive attempt to secure
uniformity in the degree of trustworthiness which these circumstances
presuppose. It is merely that common sense and experience have from time to
time pointed them out as practically adequate substitutes for the ordinary
test, at least, in view of the necessity of the situation.

The Dallos evidence bears many of the
indicia

of reliability which have been relied upon in other decisions to justify an
exception to the hearsay rule. In fact, the Dallos statements

narrowly miss being admissible as statements
given in a prior judicial proceeding, a recognized exception to the hearsay
rule. Although the admissibility of the Dallos statements is precluded by
s.
30(10)
of the
Canada Evidence Act
,
conceptually, the Dallos evidence
fits within the business record exception.

The trial judge correctly identified the
indicia

of reliability peculiar to this case. The statements were made on a solemn
occasion, somewhat akin to a court proceeding, by a person adverse to the party
seeking to tender the statement. They appear to have been made by a person
having peculiar means of knowl­edge of the events described in the statement,
and the statements themselves distinguish between events within Dallos'
personal knowledge and events about which he had merely received infor­mation
from others.

Finally, the fact that the Dallos statements
were officially recorded and preserved militates towards admissibility. The
Crown contended that it was deprived of an opportunity to cross-examine the
person who heard Dallos make the statement. Such cross-examination could shed
little light on the truth of what D allos said since only he could testify to
that. The cross-examination of which the Crown says it was deprived could only
clarify what was said by Dallos. As in the case of a business record, there is
little reason here to doubt the accuracy, as opposed to the truth, of what
Dallos is reported to have said.

(3)
Fairness

In addition to finding the hearsay evidence both
necessary and reliable, and thus admissible as an exception to the hearsay
rule, the court in
Miller

addressed the issue of fairness in the
following terms at pp. 534-5:

Here, it is the accused, rather than the
Crown, who wishes the hearsay evidence in question to be admitted. It is not
only in his interest to allow admission of this evidence, but its admission
also balances the admission of hearsay evidence at the behest of the Crown to
show the frame of mind of the deceased. Evidence favouring the Crown included
the evidence of the deceased's intention to attend at a bar on the evening of
May 2nd with her friend, Debbie Virtue. In balancing the interests of a fair
trial for both the Crown and the accused, it seems inappropriate to admit
evidence of hearsay utterances by the deceased which were of assistance to the
Crown in showing the deceased's frame of mind, but to reject evidence of
utterances made in the same telephone conversation which could be of assistance
to the accused.

The question remains, then, whether an exception
to the traditional rule which excludes hearsay can be made for the defence,
when the same exception is denied to the Crown.

Because hearsay exceptions have developed on the
basis of a combination of necessity and reliability, and because the modern
foundation of the hearsay rule is the protection of the adversary's right to
cross-examine, the rule and its exceptions usually operate without regard to
whether the party seeking to rely upon the hearsay evidence is the Crown or the
accused. This presents us with a second difficulty, not present in
Khan
,
viz. ,
whether an exception to the hearsay rule may be allowed solely to
the benefit of the accused.

Many rules of evidence, in criminal cases,
operate differently for the Crown and the defence, for example, compellability
of the accused and his or her spouse, character evidence, the discretion of the
trial judge to exclude evidence prejudicial to the defence, and the exclusion
of evidence obtained in violation of a constitutional right. The hearsay rule,
on the other hand, has traditionally been applied with equal vigour in criminal
cases, for or against both the Crown and the accused. Indeed, in
R.
v.
Williams

(1985),
1985 CanLII 113 (ON CA)
, 18 C.C.C. (3d) 356, 50 O.R. (2d) 321, 44 C.R. (3d) 351 (C.A.);
leave to appeal refused C.C.C. & O.R.
loc. cit.,
[1985] 1 S.C.R.
xiv, Mr. Justice Martin remarked, at p. 372:

I take it to be self-evident that an
accused in exercising his right to make full answer and defence must comply
with the established rules of procedure and the rules respecting the
admissibility of evidence. Generally speaking, an accused is not precluded from
making full answer and defence because he is prevented by the laws of evidence
from introducing hearsay, not falling within an exception to the hearsay rule,
in support of his defence. In advancing a defence, the accused must comply with
the law of evidence, just as the prosecution must prove the accused's guilt by
admissible evidence and not by hearsay, unless the evidence comes within a
recognized exception to the hearsay rule. Counsel for the appellant did not
take issue with the proposition that the accused in exercising his right to
make full answer and defence must, as a general rule, comply with the rules of
evidence. He contended, however, that the rules of evidence governing the
admissibility of confessions by third persons which exculpate the accused
require re-examination in the light of the
Charter
.

This view was adopted by Sopinka J. in
Dersch

v.
Canada (Attorney-General)
(1990),
1990 CanLII 3820 (SCC)
, 60 C.C.C. (3d) 132 at p. 141,
77 D.L.R. (4th) 473 at p. 482, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 1505:

The right to full answer and defence does
not imply that an accused can have, under the rubric of the
Charter
, an
overhaul of the whole law of evidence such that a statement inadmissible under,
for instance, the hearsay exclusion, would be admissible if it tended to prove
his or her innocence.

However, in
Williams
,
Martin J.A.
recognized the need for a flexible application of some rules of evidence in
order to prevent a miscarriage of justice. He said, at p. 378:

I would be disposed to hold that, in some
circumstances, precluding an accused by mechanical application of the adverse
witness requirement of s. 9(1), from cross-examining a witness whom he has
called with respect to a prior confession made by the witness that he, rather
than the accused, had committed the crime might deprive the accused of his
constitutional right to a fair trial secured by the
Charter
. It seems to me that
a court has a residual discretion to relax in favour of the accused a strict
rule of evidence where it is necessary to prevent a miscarriage of justice and
where the danger against which an exclusionary rule aims to safeguard does not
exist.

To the same effect, see Paciocco, "The
Constitutional Right to Present Defence Evidence in Criminal Cases", 63
Can. Bar Rev. 519 (1985).

Apart from a constitutional dimension, there is,
at common law, at least one exception to the hearsay rule which presently
operates for the sole benefit of the defence and which provides a fruitful
analogy Declarations against both pecuniary and penal interest have been held
to be admissible on common law principles:
R.
v.
O'Brien
(1977),

1977 CanLII 168 (SCC)
, 35 C.C.C. (2d) 209, 76 D.L.R. (3d) 513, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 591;
R.
v.
Demeter

(1975),
1975 CanLII 685 (ON CA)
, 25 C.C.C. (2d) 417, 10 O.R. (2d) 321 (C.A.).

However, in
R.
y.
Lucier
(1982),

1982 CanLII 153 (SCC)
, 65 C.C.C. (2d) 150, 132 D.L.R. (3d) 244, [1982] 1 S.C.R. 28, statements which
were manifestly against the deceased declarant's penal interest, but which also
incriminated the accused, were held to be inadmissible when tendered by the
Crown. Ritchie J., speaking for the court in
Lucier
,
noted that in both
O'Brien

and
Demeter,
the statements made by an unavailable person had been
tendered by the accused and had an exculpatory effect. In
Lucier
,
the
deceased declarant's statements, although against his penal interest, as noted,
also had the effect of incriminating Lucier and were tendered by the
prosecution for that purpose. Ritchie J. said, at p. 154 C.C.C., p. 248 D.L.R.:

The difference is a very real one because a
statement implicating the accused in the crime with which he is charged
emanating from the lips of one who is no longer available to give evidence robs
the accused of the invaluable weapon of cross-examination which has always been
one of the mainstays of fairness in our Courts.

He then concluded that this was not a
"proper case" for admitting the statements.

It thus appears that the exception to the
hearsay rule permitting the admissibility of statements against penal interest
by a person who is unavailable is a unilateral exception which can be invoked
only by the defence. The rationale for the court's conclusion in
Lucier

seems
to be that it would be unfair to deprive the accused

of his right to cross-examine someone on a
statement which implicates the accused in the crime with which he is charged.

Professor Marc Gold has noted that the absence
of opportunity to cross-examine applies to all evidence admitted as an
exception to the hearsay rule, including hearsay evidence directly incriminat­ing
the accused, such as dying declarations: see M. Gold,
Lucier v. The Queen
,
Case
Comment, 21 Osgoode Ball L.J. 142 (1983), at pp. 146-7. Professor Gold points
out different ways to support the court's conclusion in
Lucier
,
for
instance, by stating that the declarant's incriminating comments about Lucier
were merely collateral to his statements against his penal interest and
therefore fall outside the exception. Ultimately, Professor Gold suggests, at p.
153, that "the boldest way around this problem is to fashion different
rules for the Crown and for the accused".

There is no reason in principle why some
exceptions to the hearsay rule cannot operate like many other rules of
evidence, to give preferential treatment to what Professor Gold refers to as
"the value of liberty", and to address what Ritchie J. perceived as
the unfairness, in
Lucier
,
of depriving the accused of an opportu­nity
to test such evidence by cross-examination.

In our view, the same unfairness would exist in
this case if the Dallos evidence could be called by the prosecution. The
evidence of Dallos is sufficiently reliable to justify its admission as an
exception to the hearsay rule on behalf of the accused. It dealt relatively
contemporaneously with an event which took place 46 years ago and which the
declarant, since deceased, had a unique opportunity to observe. The statements
were given on a solemn judicial or quasi-judicial occasion by a person who
appeared to be opposed to the interest of the party now desirous of having the
evidence tendered. Yet it would be unfair and oppressive for the state to
prosecute an accused today with the assistance of evidence, however reliable,
which has been in existence for some 46 years and which the accused was not
given the opportunity to challenge.

d.
Conclusion

In our view, the trial judge's ruling that the
Dallos statements were Admissible at the behest of the defence despite their
hearsay nature is supported by the approach to hearsay taken in
Khan

and

Miller,
and is consistent with the constitutional considerations
identified in
Williams
,
and reiterated in
R.
v.
Rowbotham
(1988),

1988 CanLII 147 (ON CA)
, 41 C.C.C. (3d) 1 at p. 57, 63 C.R. (3d) 113, 35 C.R.R. 207 (Ont. C.A.).

The trial judge did not err in holding that the
evidence was admissible.

The evidence of Kemeny and Ballo

A substantial part of the evidence in this case
was taken on commission from witnesses residing in Hungary. When the com­mission
evidence was taken, the defence applied to the commis­sioner to compel the
Crown to call Mrs. Kemeny and Mrs. Ballo, two witnesses whose names appeared on
the list of witnesses the Crown proposed to call. The Crown took the position
that their evidence was not necessary and the commissioner declined to compel
the Crown to call them but permitted the defence to do so. As a result of that
ruling, Mrs. Zoltan Kemeny and Mrs. Istvan Ballo were called by the defence and
cross-examined by the Crown.

Mrs. Kemeny testified that she recalled the
Hungarian officer wearing boots who was accompanied by a German officer when­ever
they came into the brickyard office. She said that she had never heard the name
Imre Finta mentioned in the brickyard. She could not identify anyone in the
photograph shown to her.

Mrs. Ballo also testified that she saw a
Hungarian gendarme officer in the brickyard. She gave some description of that
man and said that she heard the name Imre Finta in the brickyard. She also
could not identify any of the men depicted in the photographs shown to her.

4. Whether the evidence of Dallos, Kemeny and
Ballo should have been introduced by the trial judge

At trial, the defence asked the trial judge to
compel the Crown to place the Kemeny and Ballo evidence before the jury as part
of its case. While the Crown did not object to the admissibility of the Kemeny
and Ballo evidence, the Crown took the position that Kemeny and Ballo were
defence witnesses and that, accordingly, their evidence could not be introduced
as part of the Crown's case. A similar issue arose with respect to the Dallos
evidence.

The trial judge was of the view that the Dallos,
Kemeny and Ballo evidence was essential to the unfolding of the narrative on
which the prosecution was based, and that, consequently, it should be
introduced as part of the Crown's case. Although he expressed the firm view
that the Crown should call that evidence, the trial judge ruled that he could
not compel the Crown to introduce it.

The Crown refused to call the evidence and the
trial judge ruled that there was nothing oblique, questionable or improper in
the Crown's decision, At that point, rather than leaving it to the defence to
decide whether to call the evidence of Dallos, Kemeny

and Ballo as part of its case, the trial judge
decided to call the evidence himself. In doing so, he ruled that the evidence
would not form part of the case for the defence and that, therefore, the
defence would retain its right to address the jury last.

The videotaped evidence of Kemeny and Ballo was
played to the jury. In it, as noted earlier, both witnesses were examined
in-chief by defence counsel, and cross-examined by Crown counsel. The Dallos
statements were read to the jury by defence counsel.

The significance of the trial judge's rulings
became apparent when, immediately after that evidence was put before the jury,
the defence elected not to call evidence and thus became entitled to address
the jury last, by virtue of
s. 651(3)
of the
Criminal Code
.

The Crown challenges the correctness of these
rulings. The Crown submits that the trial judge erred in introducing the Dallos
statements and the evidence of Kemeny and Ballo before the defence had elected
whether to call evidence.

In our view, the trial judge erred in proceeding
as he did.

The following consideration was obviously
central to the trial judge's conclusion:

The defence, at the close of the Crown's
case, in every case is faced with a difficult decision whether or not to call
evidence. That decision is hard enough in the ordinary case. In the unique
circumstances of this 45-year-old case, it should not be forced to call a
defence simply for the purpose of putting before the jury evidence readily
available in the form of depositions and videotaped Commission evidence, that
is, evidence which could potentially put a different cast on all the evidence
the jury has heard as to brickyard command, and evidence which is, in my view,
essential to the unfolding of the narrative on which the Crown's case is based.

In light of the manner in which the evidence was
presented to the jury — by videotape and by the reading of statements by
defence counsel — the defence could not possibly have been in a worse position
by having called that evidence as part of its case. The sole consideration,
therefore, motivating the trial judge to proceed as he did, was the preservation
of the defence's entitle­ment to address the jury last. In our opinion, this
was not a proper consideration upon which the trial judge could exercise his
discre­tion to call evidence himself in circumstances where he had found no
reason to interfere with the Crown's decision not to call the evidence.

Although the discretion of a trial judge to call
evidence is a broad discretion, it ought not be exercised for the purpose of
maintaining or providing a party with a tactical advantage. The trial judge
considered this case to be a special one. He said:

I think everything should be done to
relieve the defence of some of the special burdens it faces in defending a case
after close to half a century. One way to

redress that difficulty, to some degree, is
to encourage or require the Crown to put before the jury before the end of the
Crown's case the evidence of Dallos, Kemeny and Ballo, thus putting before the
jury evidence essential to the unfolding of the narrative upon which the Crown
relies, so far as that evidence is available.

There is nothing inherently unfair in requiring
each party to tender the evidence upon which that party wishes to rely. Many
factors may come into play in the decision of the defence whether to call
evidence, including whether the accused will testify.

Section 651(3)
of the
Criminal Code

provides
that:

651(3) Where no witnesses are examined for
an accused, he or his counsel is entitled to address the jury last, but
otherwise counsel for the prosecution is entitled to address the jury last.

To the extent that addressing the jury last may
be considered a strategic advantage — and it surely was sought after by both
parties in this case — it may be a factor that the defence will weigh in
deciding whether to call evidence. Absent an oblique motive by the Crown in the
exercise of its discretion in selecting the evidence to call, the trial judge
should not have attempted to relieve the defence of the statutory consequence
of calling evi­dence, even if the proposed evidence was only from one or two
witnesses.

The special features of this case do not justify
a departure from that general proposition. This may have been a case that was
difficult to defend because the alleged offences took place in 1944. Other
cases are difficult to defend for other reasons. The difficulty in defending
the case did not justify a procedural interference with the basic mechanisms of
the adversarial process. The discretion of a trial judge to call evidence
inevitably interferes with the adver­sarial nature of the trial. Such
discretion should not have been exercised for the sole purpose of assisting the
respondent in presenting his case. There is nothing in the special nature of
this case that required judicial interference with a statutorily pre­scribed
order of addressing the jury.

5.
The trial judge's instruction to the jury

Looked at generally, the trial judge's
instructions about the frailty of eyewitness identification, particularly so
many years after the events in question, were unimpeachable. The trial judge
also explained to the jury that the Dallos statements were hearsay. Having
ruled that evidence admissible as an exception to the hearsay rule, and thus
having found in it some
indicia
of reliability, the trial judge was not
required to caution the jury further about the use they could make of that
evidence. As

indicated above, the trial judge adequately
warned the jury about the double hearsay content of the statements by
emphasizing the distinction between Dallos' personal knowledge and his informa­tion
based on other sources.

The question of linking the evidence of Dallos
and Fonyo is slightly more troubling. The jury could have inferred that the
second gendarme seen by Fonyo at the brickyard was in fact Bodolay, although
she rejected the suggestion that Bodolay was in charge of the brickyard and
said that Finta was. There was nothing in the evidence to link the other
officer seen by Fonyo with either Bodolay or Narai, whom Dallos said were
involved. However, the absence of such a link does not detract from the
strength of Dallos' evidence and could not have affected the jury's conclusions
in that respect.

The expert historian called by the Crown,
Professor Braham, referred to a Lieutenant Bodolay, who was said to be in
charge of the external security of the camp at the brickyard. The Crown
complains that it was precluded by the trial judge from re­examining Braham to
show that the source of his information about Bodolay was the Dallos statement
and that, therefore, his opinion on that point had no more weight than the
Dallos hearsay evidence could supply.

In our view, the trial judge gave adequate
instructions to the jury about the use of Braham's evidence, including a
warning about its hearsay content. This was sufficient to avoid undue weight
being put on Braham's reference to Bodolay.

In our view, the trial judge gave proper and
adequate instruc­tions to the jury with respect to that evidence.

6.
Conclusion

The trial judge was correct in holding that the
Dallos statements were admissible hearsay on behalf of the accused. However, in
the circumstances, he erred in calling that evidence himself, as well as the
testimony of Kemeny and Ballo.

K.
Whether there was a substantial wrong or
miscarriage of justice

This court's jurisdiction, on a Crown appeal
against an acquittal, is set out in
s. 686(4)
of the
Criminal Code
,
which
provides, to the extent that it is relevant:

686(4) Where an appeal is from an
acquittal, the court of appeal may

(a) dismiss the appeal; or

(b) allow the appeal, set aside the verdict
and

(i) order a new trial .. .

On an accused's appeal from conviction, the
conviction may be sustained, in the face of a wrong decision on a question of
law, if the appellate court concludes the error did not give rise to a
substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice: see s. 686(1)(b)(iii). On a Crown
appeal from an acquittal, there is no similar statutory provision controlling
the decision whether, in the face of an error on a question of law, an
acquittal can be sustained, and the Crown's appeal dismissed. However, it has
long been established that a defence appeal from conviction, and a Crown appeal
from an acquittal, both bring into play the issue whether the error on a
question of law occasioned no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice:
Vezeau

v.
The Queen
(1976),
1976 CanLII 7 (SCC)
, 28 C.C.C. (2d) 81, 66 D.L.R. (3d) 418, [1977] 2
S.C.R. 277, and
R.
v.
Morin
, supra.

There is, therefore, a reciprocal parallel
between the analysis required on a defence appeal against conviction and a
Crown appeal against an acquittal. In both cases if an error on a question of
law is found, the appellate court will consider whether the error occasioned no
substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.

The answer to the question whether the error has
occasioned no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice requires the
appellate court to consider the effect of the error. In the case of a defence
appeal against conviction, if an error on a question of law is found, the
appellate court will inquire if the verdict would necessarily have been the same
(guilty), had there been no error. In the case of a Crown appeal against
acquittal the same question, but in its negative form, is frequently posed.
Thus, on a Crown appeal, the issue, as frequently articulated, becomes whether
the verdict would
not
necessarily have been the same, had there been no
error. This articulation of the issue is somewhat confusing, in that its plain
wording (if applied literally), suggests that the Crown bears a less stringent
onus to sustain a conviction on a defence appeal, than it faces when attempting
to set aside a verdict of acquittal on a Crown appeal.

Any lingering confusion resulting from the
meaning to be ascribed to the "not necessarily the same" test, seems
to have been resolved in
Morin
.
In
Morin
,
the accused was acquitted
and the Crown appealed. The appeal was allowed on two bases, both errors in
law, and a new trial was ordered. On a further appeal to the Supreme Court of
Canada, that court held that the trial judge erred in his instructions to the
jury on the application of reasonable doubt. Sopinka J. addressed the burden
that the Crown must

discharge to secure a new trial. His reasons on
this issue were accepted without dissent. He said at p. 221:

I am prepared to accept that the onus is a
heavy one and that the Crown must satisfy the court with a reasonable degree of
certainty. An accused who has been acquitted once should not be sent back to be
tried again
unless it appears that the error at the first trial was such
that there is a reasonable degree of certainty that the outcome
may
well
have been affected by it.
Any more stringent test would require an
appellate court to predict with certainty what happened in the jury room. That
it cannot do.

(Emphasis added.)

Defining the issue in this way generally accords
with Dickson J.'s observations in
Vezeau.
In
Vezeau,
the error on
a question of law found by the Quebec Court of Appeal [
15 C.R.N.S. 336, [1971]
Que. C.A. 682
n], and accepted by the Supreme Court of Canada, consisted of the
trial judge's reference in his charge that the jury could not draw an inference
adverse to the accused from his failure to testify. The accused was acquitted
at trial, and the Quebec Court of Appeal allowed the Crown's appeal and ordered
a new trial. The Supreme Court of Canada dismissed the accused's appeal.
Mart-land J., for the majority, considered the effect of the error at trial and
concluded that the jury's verdict would not necessarily have been the same (not
guilty) had there been no error at trial. Dickson J. (with whom Laskin J.
concurred) came to a different conclusion on the issue of the effect of the
error. Dickson J. put the test in language imposing an even heavier burden upon
the Crown than that set out by Sopinka J. in
Morin
.
Dickson J. said at
p. 91 C.C.C., p. 428 D.L.R.:

Not every error by a trial Judge is fatal,
in the sense of requiring a new trial. An accused appealing reversal of an
acquittal does not have the benefit of a curative section such as s.
613(1)(b)(iii), but it is none the less clear that in order for a new trial to
be ordered
the Crown must satisfy the Court with a substantial degree of
certainty that the jury would necessarily have convicted the accused in the
absence of the offending words.

(Emphasis added.)

It appears that the question posed above by Dickson
J. is whether the verdict (not guilty) would necessarily have been different
(guilty) had the error at trial not occurred. The dominant issue remains — did
the error occasion a substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice?

In the circumstances of this case, for reasons
we will set out shortly, we are not able to conclude with a reasonable degree
of certainty, that had the trial judge not called the Dallos, Kemeny and Ballo
evidence, the jury's verdict of not guilty on all eight

counts in the indictment, might well have been
different, i.e., guilty, on any of the eight counts.

The decision by the trial judge to call the
Dallos, Kemeny and Ballo evidence did not result in the jury receiving
inadmissible evidence. The videotaped examination-in-chief of Mrs. Kemeny and
Mrs. Ballo was undertaken by defence counsel and Crown counsel cross-examined
the witnesses. Thus, as a matter of form, the evidence of Mrs. Kemeny and Mrs.
Ballo had the appearance of defence evidence. The Dallos statement and evidence
were read to the jury by defence counsel. The Dallos evidence, therefore, came
before the jury in the form of defence evidence. Finally, on this point, the
trial judge told the jury that the defence wanted the Dallos, Kemeny and Ballo
evidence to be called.

The error made by the trial judge in calling the
Dallos, Kemeny and Ballo evidence effectively deprived the Crown of its
statutory right to address the jury last. This view is based on the assumption
that the defence would have called that evidence as part of its case had the
judge not called it himself. In that event, the Crown would have been entitled
to address the jury last. Defence counsel did not disclose what position he
would take, should the trial judge decline to have that evidence introduced
prior to the case for the defence. On the final occasion on which this matter
was discussed, in the absence of the jury, defence counsel said:

That's right, my lord. But I must say one
thing that my learned friend Miss Kulaszka mentioned to me, and I think it's a very
important thing for me to say, and that is,
I have to know before I
introduce or I am party to the introduction of this Kemeny and Ballo and Dallos
material, whether this does or does not prejudice
my
position as to the
order of addresses,
because I'd have to — if it does, then I have to consider a different factor in the weighing
of the prejudicial effect as opposed to the beneficial value of the defence of
that evidence. And I apologize for putting you and this court in this position
at this later hour. I didn't hear my learned friend say anything about his
reluctance to do this until four o'clock today, and Tuesday morning the jury
comes up and it's holidays till then and I'm a little surprised that we would
only hear this hour, that the Crown was going to take this position. So in that
reality, I'm afraid I've got to know before I participate in this, what that
does to the order of addresses. You can appreciate, I'm sure, why.

(Emphasis added.)

It is possible that the defence might have
maintained its decision not to call a defence. In that event, the defence still
would have been entitled to address the jury last, but the evidence of Dallos,
Kemeny and Ballo would not have been before the jury.

Just as the presence of the Kemeny and Ballo
evidence added little of substance to the case for and against Finta, its
theoretical absence was not, in our view, matter of significance in the sense

that the jury's verdict would not have been
different had their evidence not been put before the jury. It is the Dallos
evidence which must be looked to, for purposes of assessing the impact or
effect of the trial judge's decision to call the evidence as evidence of the
court. It, therefore, follows that consideration must be given to the issue
whether the jury's verdict might have been different had the Dallos evidence
not been called, either by the court, or by defence counsel.

The Dallos evidence, which has been reviewed
earlier, assisted Finta on the forcible confinement and kidnapping counts,
because it was capable of giving rise to an inference that Finta was not the
commander of the internal operations of the brickyard at relevant times. The
Dallos evidence was harmful to Finta's defence on the robbery counts, and was
of no consequence on the manslaughter counts.

It is, of course, impossible to predict with
certainty what weight or significance the jury gave to Dallos' evidence. It is
significant to note that the jury acquitted Finta, even on the robbery counts
where Dallos' evidence was harmful. Obviously the jury had some other basis
upon which it proceeded to its verdict of not guilty on those counts. This, of
course, does not mean that the jury rejected Dallos' evidence. It appears that
the jury, at least on the robbery counts, did not view the Dallos evidence as
being determinative.

Based upon our assessment of the import of the
Dallos evidence as a whole, we do not think that the Crown has discharged the
heavy onus cast upon it to establish that the trial judge's decision to call
the Dallos evidence, even when that decision is assessed with implications most
favourable to the Crown's position on this appeal, was such that "...
there is a reasonable degree of certainty that the outcome may well have been
affected". Put another way, even though the trial judge was wrong in
calling the Dallos evidence as court evidence, and even if it is assumed that,
had the trial judge not erred, the Dallos evidence would not have been called
by the defence, we do not think it can be said with a reasonable degree of
certainty that the jury's verdict would have been any different.

Thus, in our opinion, the trial judge's decision
to call the Dallos, Kemeny and Ballo evidence occasioned no substantial wrong;
nor does it form the basis for the conclusion that there was a miscarriage of
justice.

L. The constitutional validity of the
legislation and the proceedings below

In the trial court, Mr. Christie unsuccessfully
challenged the constitutional validity of s. 7(3.71) and related sections. He
is entitled, in response to the Crown appeal from Finta's acquittals, to renew
that challenge in this court: see
R.
v.
Morgentaler
(1985),
1985 CanLII 116 (ON CA)
, 22
C.C.C. (3d) 353 at pp. 361-2, 22 D.L.R. (4th) 641 at pp. 649-50, 52 O.R. (2d)
353 (C.A.); reversed on other grounds,
1988 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, 37 C.C.C. (3d) 449, 44 D.L.R. (4th) 385,
[1988] 1 S.C.R. 30.

A brief history of the relevant proceedings in
the court below is necessary. The constitutional validity of these provisions
was first raised by Mr. Christie, by way of a motion for a declaration that the
provisions were constitutionally invalid. That motion was adjourned, and the
same issues were raised on a pre-trial motion before Associate Chief Justice
Callaghan. The Associate Chief Justice heard the motion pursuant to s. 645(5)
of the
Code
as "a judge before whom an accused ... is to be
tried". He held that the impugned sections were constitutional:
R.
v.

Finta

(1989),
1989 CanLII 4378 (ON HCJ)
, 50 C.C.C. (3d) 236, 61 D.L.R. (4th) 85, 69 O.R. (2d) 557
(H.C.J.).

When the Associate Chief Justice heard the
motion it was anticipated that he would preside over the trial. For very good
reasons, which were unique to the circumstances and developed after the
Associate Chief Justice had heard the motion, he could not preside over the
trial and a new trial judge was assigned.

Before the trial judge, Mr. Christie argued that
the Associate Chief Justice's ruling was a nullity because he was no longer the
trial judge and that the motion should be entirely reargued. The trial judge
disagreed, holding that the ruling as to the constitu­tional validity of the
sections remained valid. He also held that absent any good reason meriting a
reopening of the argument, he would apply the ruling of the Associate Chief
Justice to the trial proceedings. No such reason was advanced, so the trial
judge proceeded on the basis of the ruling made by the Associate Chief Justice.

In this court, Mr. Christie advanced the same
arguments he had made before the Associate Chief Justice and the Crown relied
on the reasons of the Associate Chief Justice.

In so far as the reasons of the Associate Chief
Justice consider and reject arguments based on
ss. 7
,
11(a)
, (d), (g)
and

15
of the
Charter
, we agree with and adopt those reasons, with one caveat.

In the course of his reasons at pp. 245, 254-5
C.C.C., pp. 94-5, 103-5 D.L.R., the Associate Chief Justice refers to s.
7(3.71) as procedural and relevant only to the jurisdiction of the court to try

Finta for the domestic offences alleged against
him. As is evident from our reasons as to the respective functions of the judge
and jury, we do not agree with that characterization. That difference of
opinion does not, however, affect our conclusion that the Associate Chief
Justice was correct in upholding the constitutional validity of the
legislation.

In addition to his constitutional challenge to
the legislation itself, Mr. Christie also attacked the constitutional validity
of the proceed­ings on the basis of pre- and post-charge delay, a reasonable
apprehension of bias, and an alleged inability to make full answer and defence.
The trial judge considered and rejected those argu­ments.

Except for the allegation with respect to
post-charge delay, these contentions are essentially fact bound and relate to
the fundamental fairness of the particular proceedings. A review of the trial
record demonstrates that there was no bias, real or apprehended, and that Finta
received a fair trial in which his counsel was able to make full answer and
defence on his behalf. Indeed, the result — eight acquittals — goes a long way
to dispel­ling any claim of bias or unfairness. We are equally satisfied that
there is no merit to the submission that Finta was not tried within a
reasonable time as required by
s. 11(b)
of the
Charter
.

We would not give effect to any of Mr.
Christie's constitutional arguments.

III.
Disposition

For the reasons given above, we would dismiss
the appeal.
Appeal dismissed.
